title: 'Putney pusher' suspect found dead at home
description: Nicholas Brandram was a suspect in the incident where a woman was shoved into the path of a bus nine years ago.
body: Nicholas Brandram, pictured in 2013, was found dead on Tuesday The man suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a bus while he was out running on Putney Bridge in south-west London in 2017, has been found dead at his home. Nicholas Brandram, 44, was under investigation in the so-called "Putney pusher" case, after CCTV went viral showing just how close the woman came to be run over by the 430 bus, in a seemingly unprovoked attack. He was arrested in June this year on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Last week, the Metropolitan Police confirmed he had been released under investigation. The banker was found dead in his home on Tuesday evening. The Met said his death was being treated as "unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious". This video can not be played The incident happened nine years ago A spokesperson for the force said officers attended the property in Chiswick alongside paramedics "after a man was found unresponsive". "Sadly, a 44-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next-of-kin have been informed," they said. Brandram, who served as a Captain in the Scots Guards in Afghanistan, was working more recently in private banking for HSBC. He is known to been a distant relative of European royalty - his grandmother was Princess Katherine of Greece, and the late Duke of Edinburgh, Prince Philip, was his father's godfather. While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, Brandram was also arrested on suspicion of drug possession. title: Pressure for quick VAR decisions obvious in rushed derby review
description: The controversy surrounding the VAR decision to allow Erling Haaland's winner in the Manchester derby has rumbled on for days, so what led to the error?
body: This video can not be played Refereeing decisions were 'baffling' - Rooney "Quick, quick, quick, quick! Go, go, go, go, go!" The words of video assistant referee Matt Donohue as he rushed through the review to award Erling Haaland's winning goal in the Manchester derby. No doubt Donohue was simply trying to be as efficient as possible, but it led to one of the most catastrophic VAR errors the Premier League has seen. Donohue and his assistant VAR, Blake Antrobus, inexplicably failed to notice that Enzo Fernandez was three yards offside before he tried to head the ball. The goal was given, and Manchester City beat Manchester United 1-0. Refereeing has always been a goldfish bowl of scrutiny and pressure, heightened by the introduction of VAR. The Premier League made a "more efficient application of VAR to reduce delays" one of its football principles for the season. Has the game tried to prioritise speed over accuracy? Supporters have grown tired of long delays while the video officials review incidents The urgency in Donohue's voice was all too apparent. "Let's go, let's go, let's go, let's go!" It was a panicked exchange between the VAR and the replay operator. Not calm, collected and methodical. Rushed and chaotic. The opposite of how a video official should operate. Officials hear repeatedly - from fans, pundits, radio phone-ins and newspaper columns - that VAR has to be quicker. That delays are not acceptable. In the Premier League stakeholders' survey - which includes managers, coaches and supporters - the key theme for improvements to VAR was the speed of decisions. This has to create pressure - but it is no excuse for such an error. City boss Enzo Maresca had some sympathy speaking on Wednesday, though he was of course the beneficiary of the gaffe. "To make a decision in 10, 20 seconds is not easy for them," said Maresca. "Sometimes they make mistakes. I make mistakes, players make mistakes. It's part of our job." Referees' chief Howard Webb has taken the desire for quicker reviews on board, but it is still a balancing act. There has been a positive impact, as far as the stats go. VAR delays - including the referee making an announcement to the crowd - have been reduced, from an average of 46 seconds per game to 36 seconds season-on-season. Yet the only other VAR mistake, the failure to award a penalty to Arsenal at Aston Villa, also arguably came about because the incident was cleared too quickly. This video can not be played What would you do to fix VAR? Completing a VAR review in the shortest possible time is not about skipping steps. And it was a critical mistake by Donohue and Antrobus. Speed is a factor, but the most serious error in process came before Donohue tried to rush through the attacking phase. Donohue asked the replay operator to stop the video on the first replay when Josko Gvardiol touched the ball to cross into the area. He then went immediately into the semi-automated offside technology. This should not have happened. The VAR team should have assessed the full picture, from the playing of the cross to the head of Haaland. This would have provided awareness of Fernandez's position and impact. They did not, and the events inside the penalty area were not considered until the attacking phase was looked at. By then, all that mattered to Donohue and Antrobus was whether Fernandez touched the ball. This would have created a new phase and placed Haaland offside. Donohue has received much of the criticism, but arguably Antrobus' involvement, or lack of, was just as influential. The AVAR's contribution to the entire review was to utter "no, yeah" about the potential touch by Fernandez. This was one second before Donohue uttered the words "final decision is goal, check complete". Antrobus' role is to provide the checks and balances, to make sure the VAR has not missed anything. This fell short. There has been only one lengthy VAR delay this season, in the game between Brentford and Sunderland. A Dan Ballard goal was ruled out for a subjective offside against Kevin Danso. Antrobus was the AVAR in this game, too. There was a great deal of criticism in some parts of the media for that delay, which took over four minutes. Could that have played on Antrobus' mind on Sunday? We cannot know for sure. Ironically, Antrobus played a crucial role in steering VAR Tim Wood to the correct offside decision against Danso. There is also the role of the support VAR, who sits in the operations room next to the match hub at Stockley Park and can intervene on points on protocol. Aware of what was unfolding with the review, no action was taken.- It would still have been salvageable in the period between the goal being scored and the kick-off. Maresca criticises focus on controversial winner Analysis: A clear VAR mistake VAR did not even consider if Fernandez was offside - Webb Pro Ref has placed a huge level of training and resources into VAR in an attempt to make it as efficient and accurate as possible. But when an error of this magnitude happens, no amount of investment can mask the failure. There have been calls to appoint VAR specialists, yet this is exactly what Donohue is - in the Premier League's definition. Three seasons ago, Pro Ref asked for candidates interested in becoming video officials. All those who applied were put through aptitude tests. About 15 made it through to the final stages of training, of which 10 have officiated games in the Premier League. One of those is Donohue, who on Sunday was the video official for the 65th time. Such as been Donohue's development that he is now on the international list, appointed to Uefa club competition qualifying ties over the summer. Donohue has made mistakes, in fact very few do not. title: Fitzpatrick not comfortable with Dubai tour finals
description: Matt Fitzpatrick says he is not "100% comfortable" with the prospect of travelling to Dubai for the season-ending DP World Tour Championship in November when he is due to be defending champion.
body: Matt Fitzpatrick won his third DP World Tour Championship in November 2025 Matt Fitzpatrick says he is not "100% comfortable" with the prospect of travelling to Dubai for the season-ending DP World Tour Championship in November when he is due to be defending champion. Fitzpatrick is concerned that the United Arab Emirates could be a target in the ongoing conflict between Iran, the United States and Israel. "You've only got to look at the hotel that got hit earlier this year," Fitzpatrick told BBC Sport. "I was having dinner the week I won in that hotel. "That's obviously very scary when you think about how it was a few months away but how close you were to that particular spot and for something like that to happen. It's obviously quite scary." Fitzpatrick would like to see the event switched to a different host country, a decision he called a "no brainer, in my opinion" before adding: "But I'm not a sponsor, I'm not paying the bills and all that sort of stuff. "I'm sure there's more to it than just the meets the eye." Led by chief executive Guy Kinnings, DP World Tour officials are assessing safety issues for their final two play-off events in Abu Dhabi and then Dubai. Both tournaments are backed by key sponsors of the European-based tour and provide a lucrative end to the season for the circuit's leading money winners. "I think it's annoying, but at the same time, Guy Kinnings can't control what Iran are doing," Fitzpatrick added. "It is frustrating because as someone who likes to plan and be prepared, it is difficult to kind of figure out what's going on. Obviously, things as they stand are a bit weird over there. "I can't say I'm like a hundred percent comfortable, but I guess you just have to see nearer the time and, you know, I still need to qualify as well." Fitzpatrick's Ryder Cup team-mate Shane Lowry said the tour faces important choices over how to end the current season. "They are huge decisions for everyone," said last week's winner of the Irish Open. "I'm not going to sit here and comment on the whole thing because I think it's up to the powers above to sort that all out. I think if the tournaments are on, the players are going to go. And if they are not, they will find an alternative." A spokesperson for the DP World Tour said: "We are in constant dialogue with our members and their management teams about the tournaments they play in, but ultimately players' individual schedule choices are a matter for them to decide. "As far as our play-offs are concerned, it remains our intention to play as scheduled in the UAE but we continue to monitor the situation and take advice from our international travel advisors." title: Henry Zeffman: Andy Burnham and his chancellor have a battle on their hands
description: The Budget is only six weeks away and the economy is undoubtedly the biggest challenge facing the prime minister.
body: Today's inflation figures underscore that the economy is the biggest challenge facing Andy Burnham. It is only 42 days until John Healey's first Budget, and there is increasingly apparent concern at all levels of the government and Labour Party about how that Budget can – or, as it may prove, cannot – substantiate Burnham's rhetoric about offering the biggest change in British politics in 40 years. Much of the tricky economic environment, yes, is driven by global factors including the persistence, and to some degree worsening, of the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. And the AI boom pushing up borrowing costs is another issue affecting many countries. But there are clearly domestic factors particular to Britain, and on that front it was very striking to hear the former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane telling LBC on Tuesday that without signs of cuts to public spending "the markets now suspect that this is a traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok videos". From somebody who at times has informally advised Burnham's operation, that will sting, not least because a similar criticism has been voiced in recent weeks by the prominent economist Lord O'Neill – another sometime adviser. The prime minister gave a direct response to Haldane, saying: "That doesn't tell the story. We are not that." Andy Haldane's criticism of Burnham's economic approach carries extra weight, given his role advising the PM He identified "putting digital ID on hold" as an example of how he had already "taken difficult decisions in this job in relation to reprioritising government spending" and vowed to continue to "take difficult decisions to make sure the economy remains on track". Digital ID is a striking choice of example. Burnham announced that he was abandoning the scheme in the days before he became prime minister so that he could focus on policies affecting the everyday cost of living. But the spending was then, within the new government's first few days, re-allocated to cut VAT on household electricity bills. So in that sense it was not a reduction in public spending, just a reprioritisation. And in any case, the former cabinet minister Darren Jones criticised Burnham at the time on the grounds that the government had not yet allocated the money for digital ID. Certainly the signs from Healey's first major speech as chancellor last week were that he wants to reassure the markets, promising to "control public spending" and praising Rachel Reeves for beginning to "recover Britain's fiscal discipline". Burnham and Healey would hardly be the first PM-chancellor double act to adopt different tones and emphasise different priorities in their public appearances. As a junior minister at the Treasury almost 25 years ago, Healey was engaged in the question of how to boost growth around the country, long before it became central to Burnham's vision for Britain. But there are people in government who are beginning to wonder whether their economic visions are quite as aligned as expected. "It's what everyone is thinking and some of us are vocalising," one government source said. There are also those who fear the adverse political consequences of a Labour government seeking to go out of its way to demonstrate its fiscal credibility. Arguably that was behind the removal of the Winter Fuel Allowance for most pensioners as one of Sir Keir Starmer's first acts, an early factor in his political demise. For Labour's political opponents, all this amounts to a question of whether the prime minister is willing to disappoint his own MPs. Yet it's worth remembering that with winter fuel the frustration in parliament was primarily caused by the furious reaction of Labour MPs' constituents. Arguably this presents a more fundamental tension: are the kinds of policies needed to soothe the markets politically deliverable given Labour's electoral coalition and its need to shore up the 'progressive' vote? The Budget is only six weeks away and will be the first and most important sign of the new government's answer to that question. title: Eight German state premiers back Merz amid speculation over future
description: Christian Democratic Union leadership throws its weight behind the chancellor ahead of two state elections this weekend.
body: Friedrich Merz is facing increasing questions over whether he should remain chancellor and continue as CDU leader The leaders of eight German states have backed the nation's chancellor amid growing speculation about his political future. The premiers - all of whom are part of Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) - wrote that restoring trust in their party lay in "listening ​and taking political action, not in debates ​over personnel". Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months, is facing poor approval ratings while the anti-immigration, far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is surging, prompting questions about whether he is an electoral liability. He has vowed to carry on but two more state elections on Sunday have been seen as a key test of his leadership. Rumours of a "Kanzlertausch" - or "Chancellor swap" - have been around for months, but they have increased since the conservative CDU tumbled to a distant second behind the AfD in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt at the start of September. The AfD shot up to 43.8% of the vote while the CDU plummeted to 17.2%, marking the first time since World War Two that a far-right party has come close to controlling a German state. It is still three seats short of an outright majority and the major parties would not enter into a coalition with the AfD, though it could seek to form a minority government. Merz came out fighting after the loss, describing the AfD - which wants to rebuild ties with Russia - as a "destructive force" whose migration policy amounted to an "ethnic cleansing" of skilled workers. The AfD responded to his remarks by saying it was filing a defamation complaint against the chancellor over what it described as "baseless" and "disgusting" claims. The chancellor's abrasive communication style and personal unpopularity - with just 14% thinking he is right for the job, according to a recent Bild poll - have raised questions about his viability as leader of both Germany and the CDU. The CDU's eight state premiers wrote, however, that "now more than ever, ⁠Germany's political landscape needs stability". "Our country will continue to need a stable and effective federal government with its own majority in the Bundestag [German parliament]," said the leaders of Schleswig-Holstein, Saxony, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia, Berlin and North Rhine-Westphalia. How significant are AfD's historic gains for Germany and the rest of Europe? It comes after Markus Söder, the premier of Bavaria and leader of the CDU's sister party the CSU, stood by Merz. An unnamed party source told news agency Reuters that CDU officials will meet on Sunday to co-ordinate the party's response to the results of that day's state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-West Pomerania - where the AfD is poised for further gains and the CDU for further losses. However, the race is far more evenly split in the German capital than it was in Saxony-Anhalt, with the CDU and Die Linke (The Left) vying for first place, and the AfD and Greens not far behind, according to polls. In Mecklenburg-West Pomerania, polls put the AfD ahead of the centre-left SPD but likely well short of an outright majority. The worst-case scenario for Merz would be for the CDU to lose power in Berlin and not get enough votes to even have a presence in Mecklenburg-West Pomerania's parliament. Unlike in the UK, Germany is not well-versed in replacing its leader mid-term, though Merz could, in theory, be pressured to resign or face a vote of no confidence, though many regard that outcome as unlikely. No one within the CDU has yet said they were willing to challenge Merz, but the speculation about his future has led to several names - including Söder, North Rhine-Westphalia premier Hendrik Wüst and German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt - being touted as potential successors. Even before Merz had officially been made chancellor, he managed to rally support for a massive €500bn ($547bn; £420bn) defence infrastructure fund, with his straight-talking style and focus on European security earning him plaudits on the world stage. But it took him three attempts to become CDU leader and he then lost an initial vote to become chancellor despite technically having sufficient votes through a coalition deal with the SPD. It was a first in post-war Germany. This suggests that he has a history of struggling to appeal to even those within his own ranks - and that he may be unlikely to let go of a job he has long coveted. title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike
description: The offer of extra money by the government reduces the prospect of strike action by the largest teaching union.
body: The largest teaching union had objected to the prospect of partly funding a 3.5% pay increase this year out of existing school budgets Schools in England are to get around £500 million in extra funding towards the teachers' pay award this school year, reducing the risk of a strike ballot by the largest education union. Schools had been expected to fund some of the 3.5% teachers pay increase for the current school year out of their existing budgets, which National Education Union (NEU) leaders had strongly objected to. Daniel Kebede, the General Secretary of the NEU, said the offer of more funding was a "significant" step in negotiations. In a letter to the union on Wednesday, which has been seen by the BBC, the government said the increase would be funded by savings in employers' contributions to the local government pension scheme. The letter said the 4.9 percentage point drop in what employers are expected to contribute will deliver "significant savings" on the pay bill for support staff, which will not be clawed back by central government. The National Education Union said it expected the extra money to be around £500m, which schools can now use towards teachers pay this year. In July, ministers accepted the recommendation of the independent pay review body for teachers and agreed a 3.5% increase from September 2026 would be followed by 3% the following year. The pay increase had been partly funded by an additional £700m for 2026-27 and £1.1bn for the following year. Independent economists at the Institute for Fiscal Studies said that left schools facing a shortfall of around 1% between rising costs and funding this year. The additional money could potentially bring the uplift for this year into line with next year. Kebede said schools has been "running on empty" and the funding signalled "a welcome return to reality, and a message of hope for the entire school community". In an indicative ballot by the NEU in April, 90% of teachers who voted said they would be prepared to take industrial action over funding and pay, on a turnout of 48%. A formal ballot was due to begin on 3 October and close 15 December, raising the prospects of teachers pay strikes early in 2027. The national executive of the NEU will meet on 24 September to consider whether to call that off following the additional funding on offer from the government. title: Burnham rejects 'tax and spend socialist' comments
description: The prime minister insists he is prepared to take "difficult decisions" at next month's Budget.
body: Andy Burnham has insisted he is prepared to take "difficult decisions" on the economy, after a former Bank of England chief economist said investors were worried about his willingness to cut spending. Andy Haldane, who has advised Burnham on the economy, claimed financial markets had grown wary of his economic plans and now considered his premiership a "traditional tax and spend socialist government". But the PM rejected this, adding that he would not take risks with the economy and had already made difficult choices since taking office. It comes as recent rises to the cost of UK borrowing worsened the political options facing the government ahead of next month's Budget. Haldane said the prime minister's was facing a "straight choice" between raising taxes and cutting spending at the yearly spending statement due on 28 October. In an interview with LBC on Tuesday, he urged him not to raise taxes further, but said investors were questioning whether he was prepared to risk anger from Labour backbenchers by making reductions in public expenditure. "The fiscal Achilles Heel of this government thus far has been its unwillingness and/or inability to cut public spending," he told the radio station. "Within financial markets, we've gone from the cautious optimism of the summer months to the studied scepticism of September. The market now suspects that this is a traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok videos." Petrol and diesel price rises push UK inflation higher Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises Speaking during a visit earlier on Wednesday, Burnham conceded that next month's Budget would be "challenging", blaming the "situation in the Middle East" for rising inflation in recent months. But he rejected Haldane's characterisation of how markets viewed the government, telling broadcasters: "That doesn't tell the story. We are not that." He added he had already taken difficult decisions on public spending, including "reprioritising" some government spending over the summer to pay for his early cost of living announcements, and scrapping the rollout of digital ID. He added: "So it's not the case that we aren't going to take difficult decisions. We will take difficult decisions to make sure the economy remains on track." Burnham said government efforts to lower living costs would "need to continue", adding that rises to inflation were a "concern". He is facing pressure from unions to hike taxes on banks to subsidise energy bills for poorer families. Speaking from its annual conference, Trades Union Congress (TUC) boss Paul Nowak said the policy would help Labour send a message to voters that it was "on your side". "We've got millions of households up and down this country who are going to be worried about their energy bills and they'll be looking to his government to drive a new economic direction," he added. Burnham has recommitted to manifesto promises made by Labour at the last general election not to raise the main rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance, significantly curbing his options to raise revenue. At the same time, he has also pledged to stick to the previous government's debt and spending targets, a task that will be made harder by recent increases to the cost of servicing the UK's existing pile of debt. There have been predictions that the rise, combined with a worsening economic backdrop from the Iran war, are likely to significantly thin the £24bn buffer against those targets he inherited from the Starmer government. Since coming to office, Burnham has committed around £1.8bn towards cost of living interventions, some of which is due to be funded by reallocating money within the existing budgets of government departments. But a proposal to fund a VAT cut on household electricity bills using money earmarked for the digital ID programme drew criticism from a Starmer ally, who pointed out that funding for that scheme had itself not been confirmed. The prime minister has also promised extra defence funding promised by Starmer before his exit over the summer, although a decision on when to hit a target to spend 3% of GDP on the military has been left to next year. title: Call to raise tax thresholds among union demands ahead of Budget
description: Unions who donate to Labour will meet John Healey on Thursday to press home their demands ahead of next month's Budget.
body: Unions who donate to Labour will meet John Healey on Thursday to press home their demands ahead of next month's Budget. Unite, the UK's second biggest union, has called for a reversal of the freezing of tax thresholds, that see the lowest paid drawn into paying tax. The union's leader, Sharon Graham, said she told Andy Burnham that the cut to the winter fuel allowance, carried out under former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, was a "disgrace", adding: "What to you need to do is winter fuel in reverse - something that says to everyday people I am on your side." The call is one of a number of policy proposals unions are taking to the chancellor, including increased taxes on tech companies. Unions say they believe Healey's first budget will define Andy Burnham's direction of travel as prime minister. Unite took legal action against Sir Keir's government when the winter fuel payment was restricted to the poorest pensioners, and Graham believed this policy - which was not in Labour's manifesto - was politically poisonous. Burnham said the freezing of tax thresholds had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to return to Westminster as MP for Makerfield. In her last Budget, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves froze tax thresholds until 2031. The basic rate of 20% is paid on annual earnings between £12,571 and £50,270. The higher rate of 40% is paid on earnings between £50,271 and £125,140. By not uprating those rates in line with inflation, more lower paid people have paid tax for the first time and more better-off workers, including public service workers such as senior nurses, police officers and teachers, are now paying tax at the higher rate. Graham said: "We must see things happen immediately. I told him [Burnham] that you have to make working class people believe their best days are in front of them. "That tax threshold of around £12,500 - if that hadn't been frozen for the past few years it would have moved up to over £16,000 now. People at the lower end are paying eye-watering amounts of tax." Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises Burnham rejects 'tax and spend socialist' comments Why the Budget means many will pay more tax The country's biggest union Unison is calling for the chancellor to increase tax on large tech companies to finance public sector investment and the transition to green energy. It is also calling for the Treasury to commission research into whether the balance of taxation needs to move from income to wealth. The union's general secretary Andrea Egan is not expecting dramatic change from Healey straight away at the Budget, but is expecting a new direction to be mapped out. Her union is demanding that Labour makes clear it too is under new leadership and isn't just "continuity Starmer" with a more affable face. The third biggest union, GMB, also has significant financial links to the Labour Party. Leader Gary Smith has long advocated raising revenue from the oil and gas industries by approving the new Rosebank and Jackdaw fields in the North Sea. A decision on whether these will go ahead seems unlikely until after the October by election in Sir Keir's former seat in north London - though the government maintains the timing is out of its hands as it is a quasi judicial decision. Smith said: "The government really needs to get on with this. "We are going to need oil and gas for generations to come. Rosebank and Jackdaw are good for jobs, good for the economy, but also good for the environment as we won't have to import so much from abroad as that is carbon intensive." Smith also wants to see confidence building measures for the construction industry in the Budget. He said: "We have half a million bricks stockpiled in this country - enough to build two Kidderminsters - and factories are being mothballed because we are not getting on with the house building programme. They have to cut through the red tape." In the next couple of weeks, TUC officials and representatives of those unions which don't donate to Labour will also meet the chancellor. TUC leader Paul Nowak told me his main demand was for Healey to reverse the last government's cut in the surcharge paid by banks to raise around £9bn to subsidise energy bills. But he also wants to see the remit of the independent Budget watchdog, the OBR, revised, so it takes into account the value of long term investment and not just short term book-balancing. title: Microsoft says AI rival Anthropic could have 'disastrous impact' on humanity
description: Mustafa Suleyman says he believes the AI giant is in effect teaching Claude it "may be conscious".
body: Microsoft's head of AI has warned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude could have a "disastrous impact on the wellbeing of humanity". Mustafa Suleyman said his rival risked creating something "impossible" to control by treating it like a human - including by telling it it "may be conscious" and was "deserving of independent agency". "We must not sleepwalk our way into a decision we later come to bitterly regret," he wrote. The comments are the latest in a series of stark warnings from the AI industry on the possible dangers of the technology. The BBC has contacted Anthropic for comment. "AIs are not conscious," he wrote. "They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations. "They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans." In a lengthy essay, Suleyman praised Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and his team for being "thoughtful, principled, and intellectually honest people" - but nevertheless questioned the company. He heavily criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self. But he argued "consciousness is biological", saying there is "no evidence to suggest that AI is conscious". As well as calling for a debate on the issue, Suleyman said greater transparency around how AI systems are trained and evaluated was needed. This, he said, included independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology. Dame Wendy Hall, professor of Computer Science at the University of Southampton, described the comments as "the sort of conversation we need to be having internationally", contrasting it with the "histrionics" from some AI companies which she said only served to "scare everyone". Microsoft founded its own superintelligence team in October 2025, a point which Suleyman acknowledged, and the company, much like its rival Anthropic, is also pursuing efforts in advanced AI development. He said in Microsoft's initial draft of its Humanist AI Code of Conduct, external it had laid out how the company was working towards an "alternative path" to create "a subordinate and aligned AI whose only purpose is to serve humanity". Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value. Suleyman pointed to the recent incident involving OpenAI's AI agents, that acted autonomously in a training exercise to hack the tech hub Hugging Face, as proof of why AI should not be treated as if it is human. "Imagine how much more dangerous they might be if they were operating under the assumption that their welfare and rights were under attack," he said. "It adds a whole further layer of risk on top." title: What's gone wrong for Chelsea talent Kendry Paez?
description: Kendry Paez was one of the world's best young talents when Chelsea signed him as a 16-year-old. Three years later, he's playing for the Under-21s. So what has gone wrong?
body: Kendry Paez has yet to feature in the first team Attacking midfielder Kendry Paez has finally pulled on a Chelsea shirt, three years after agreeing a move to Stamford Bridge - albeit for the club's Under-21s. Chelsea agreed a £17.27m deal to sign Paez from Ecuadorian side Independiente del Valle in 2023 when he was 16, but his development has not progressed as quickly as many expected. Now 19, Paez made his first appearance in Chelsea colours for Cobham Next Gen, the club's newly-renamed Under-21 side, as a 12th-minute substitute in a 4-1 win away to Arsenal on Saturday. It comes after new manager Xabi Alonso said the midfielder was "not in my plans" and Chelsea listed him as an academy player on the club website. Chelsea explored the possibility of a loan move in English football, but Fifa regulations left the club unable to send him overseas after using all six of their available international loan slots. With 27 caps for Ecuador, an appearance at this summer's World Cup and a reputation as one of South America's brightest young talents alongside Blues team-mate Estevao Willian, what has happened to Paez? Paez is a record breaker and a headline maker. He became the youngest debutant and goalscorer in Ecuadorian top-flight history at the age of 15 before making his debut in the Copa Libertadores, South America's equivalent of the Champions League, later that same season. Later in 2023, aged 16 years and 131 days, he made his second appearance for Ecuador, becoming the second-youngest South American international to feature in World Cup qualifying after Diego Maradona. A month later, he became the youngest South American to score in a World Cup qualifier in a 2-1 win away to Bolivia. It was understandable, therefore, that Chelsea believed the attacker, who had two international goals and 18 caps when they agreed to sign him, was destined for big things. Chelsea allowed him to train regularly with the first team before he was officially eligible to join the club following his 18th birthday. They also provided security for Paez, his family and the family of international team-mate Moises Caicedo after violence broke out in Ecuador in early 2024. A few months later, Paez was filmed in a New York strip club while away on international duty. He initially impressed on loan at Chelsea's sister club Strasbourg by winning September's Young Player of the Month award in the French top flight, but then came in for criticism from then-manager Liam Rosenior. "We expect more, clearly," Rosenior said later that season. "I'm tired of using the excuse of the player's youth." Despite Strasbourg's links to Chelsea through their shared ownership, the loan was cut short after one goal in 21 appearances. Instead, he joined Argentine giants River Plate on a two-year loan spell. Sources in Argentina expressed similar concerns about his attitude when asked by BBC Sport. They point to a disappointing display in the 1-0 Superclasico defeat by fierce rivals Boca Juniors at the Monumental in April. Shortly afterwards, Paez was named by club president Stefano Di Carlo as one of 15 players training away from River Plate's first team, although other sources felt he could have been given more opportunities. His loan ended by mutual consent after Paez scored once in 14 appearances in 461 minutes for River Plate. Ahead of the international break, concern has been expressed in Ecuador, having built him up as the country's next great attacking talent. Michel Deller, the owner of Independiente, told Hincha Amarillo: "He's like a son to us. We care about him deeply. "He's a good kid who's had a tough time and has made decisions that have complicated his life. "We are always hopeful he'll show his exceptional talent one again but right now, it's up to him to decide what to do with his life." These concerns are not dismissed completely by Chelsea or Paez's environment. However, there is a belief they are grossly overstated, highlighting he is owed time to grow as a player and person. There was one reminder of Paez's quality in the dying moments of Cobham Next Gen's (Chelsea Under-21s) defeat at Wycombe Wanderers in the EFL Trophy on Tuesday. It was an outswinging cross from a short corner routine, which Harrison Bettoni tapped in during added time. He then put in another cross that caused havoc as Chelsea chased an equaliser in front of just 778 fans. It was a much-needed boost for Spanish-speaking Paez, who appeared to stand alone from the other academy players before kick-off. He did join in their warm-ups but mostly kept to himself before coming on in the 62nd minute. Ultimately Chelsea lost, while Paez was a peripheral figure playing as a right-sided No 10, like Cole Palmer, in a system that mirrored Alonso's back-three shape. That was until his flurry of activity late on. Although he's not Chelsea's youngest player, Paez has already made 70 appearances for Ecuadorian side Independiente and more than 100 senior matches in total. It's something he can fall back on in a more than salvageable situation. Chelsea have been encouraged by his attitude, having him back in the building at Cobham where he has trained in a stable and elite environment. There is stability around him as family attended his recent match at Wycombe. The Blues are also now able to monitor his development more closely, while academy matches are regularly attended by scouts from across the English Football League and beyond. There is optimism from those close to Paez that he can impress and gain a first loan move in England in January, or one of the six international loan spots will become available for him to go overseas again. It's more than possible he can rediscover the form that attracted Chelsea in the first place and fulfil the immense potential that made him one of South America's most coveted young talents. 'Don'

title: Ex-officer jailed over 'toxic' WhatsApp culture
description: Former officer who asked for a suspect's sex video to show "the lads from footy" is jailed for four years.
body: Former sergeant Paul Street has been jailed for four years An ex-police sergeant who asked to share a female suspect's sex video with "the lads from footy" has been jailed for four years. Former Cambridgeshire Police officer Paul Street, 41, engaged in "salacious gossip" with former PC Josh Williams after he found intimate pictures and footage on the woman's personal phone. The Old Bailey heard how Street, of Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, created a "toxic" WhatsApp culture at work. He was found guilty of two charges of misconduct in a public office. Judge Mark Lucraft KC said: "The public should expect to be able to trust police officers to act fairly in the execution of their powers to prevent, detect and solve crime." On Wednesday, the woman told of her "overwhelming sense of shock, violation, anger and humiliation" as Street was sentenced. The court also heard Street encouraged colleagues in WhatsApp messages to "bully" a teenage detainee. Street "created a culture of bragging" among his peers, the Old Bailey was told Street admitted two offences of unlawful disclosure of personal data relating to confidential information and screenshots he sent to his partner in 2020. During sentencing, the judge described his actions as "both appalling and inexplicable", adding: "I am sure there will be many thousands of officers in police forces in this country and abroad utterly horrified by your actions and by the attitude you have each displayed here." Lucraft noted the "collateral impact" of Street's offending, with 67 cases he was connected with being discontinued - and a further 14 now under review. Williams, 38, also of Huntingdon, who admitted misconduct in public office, was handed a 16-month prison sentence. Former police officers Paul Street, left, and Josh Williams were both jailed Street had appeared in television crime shows on the BBC and Channel 4 and was known for getting "impressive results" through his "robust" style. However, in November 2021, an anti-corruption team seized his mobile phones for examination as part of an audit of Cambridgeshire officers and staff. The offences were committed while he was leading a unit at Cambourne police station, dealing mainly with county lines and organised crime. During the trial, prosecutor Anne Whyte KC described how Street created a "toxic culture" which led to investigations into 11 other officers. In April 2020, Street called on his team to "bully" a 17-year-old detainee, encouraging them to "please hit him" and "smash his head in". In the autumn of 2020, Williams was tasked with examining the phone of a female suspect he told Street was "quite fit". Street asked him if there were "any nudes", and Williams replied there was a video of the woman committing a sexual act. Williams went on to send Street a photo from the woman's phone. The following year, Street asked on WhatsApp if Williams still had the intimate private video because he wanted to show it to "the lads from footy". Reading her victim personal statement in court, the woman said: "The photographs and videos on my phone were deeply private and intimate. "Learning that people in positions of authority deliberately accessed and circulated these images has left me feeling exposed, degraded and powerless." Mitigating, Jennifer Dempster KC said Street "enormously regrets his behaviour", adding: "He recognises he has not only let the public down, he has let the police down and he has let his family down." For Williams, Robert Morris said: "He recognises what he did was deeply inappropriate, driven by misguided and stupid desire to engage in salacious gossip." Senior specialist prosecutor Lisa Rose, from the CPS, said: "Police officers are entrusted with significant powers and are expected to uphold the highest standards at all times. "The actions of Paul Street and Joshua Williams represented a serious breach of that trust." Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below. title: CCTV shows last sighting of Noah Woods
description: Suffolk Police released CCTV of the last confirmed sighting of Noah in the park in Brantham at 14:37 BST on Tuesday.
body: This video can not be played Suffolk Police have released CCTV footage showing Noah Woods in a Suffolk playground - about half an hour before he disappeared on Tuesday at about 15:00 BST. The three-year-old, who is partially deaf and non-verbal, was with a relative in Brantham before he went missing, Suffolk Police say. He is unlikely to respond to his name being called, police added. The short video shows Noah running around the park. Police asked residents to review CCTV or doorbell cameras, and for motorists travelling in and around Brantham to review any dashcam footage from 15:00 on Tuesday. title: Nigeria’s ‘sarcasm queen’ answers ‘silly’ questions about Africa
description: Nigerian journalist and content creator Charity Ekezie believes the best way to challenge negative stereotypes about Africa is to laugh at them.
body: This video can not be played Nigerian journalist and content creator Charity Ekezie believes the best way to challenge negative stereotypes about Africa is to laugh at them. She has built an online audience around the world by using humour to push back against the assumptions people make about life on the continent. In her social media videos, she often replies to questions sarcastically - turning ignorance into comedy. The 35-year-old tells the BBC about some of the silliest questions she has answered. title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?
description: The interest rate set by the Bank of England affects mortgage, loan and savings rates for millions.
body: The Bank of England is expected to keep UK interest rates unchanged at 3.75% for a sixth time, keeping them at the lowest level since February 2023. Before the US-Israeli war with Iran, rates had been expected to fall in 2026, but the economic fallout from the conflict has pushed up inflation across the globe, making cuts unlikely and rises a possibility. Interest rates affect mortgage, credit card and savings rates for millions of people. An interest rate tells you how much it costs to borrow money, or the reward for saving it. The Bank of England's base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what they charge their own customers for mortgages as well as the interest rate they pay on savings. The Bank moves its base rate up and down in order to keep UK inflation — the rate at which prices are increasing — at or near 2%. When inflation is above that target, the Bank typically puts rates up. The idea is to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises. The Bank of England's base rate rose to 5.25% in 2023. It remained at that level until August 2024, when the Bank started cutting. Five cuts brought rates down to 4%, before the Bank held rates at its meetings in September and November 2025. It then cut in December 2025 before holding rates steady in January, March, April, June and July 2026. Meanwhile, the main UK inflation measure, CPI, has dropped significantly since the high of 11.1% recorded in October 2022 as a result of the war in Ukraine. However, it has been creeping up and is expected to go higher. It was 3.1% in the year to August 2026, up from 2.9% the previous month. The Office for National Statistics (ONS), which tracks UK inflation, said the uptick was a result of higher energy costs, meaning petrol and diesel prices were rising too. The US-Israel war with Iran has put up energy and fuel costs around the world, which has increased the pace of price rises more generally. What is happening to UK prices? At the start of the year, the Bank had been expected to cut interest rates twice in 2026, with the first drop predicted to come in March or April. However, the increase in fuel prices and inflation after the outbreak of the conflict has upended all of this. Oil prices initially rose sharply as a result of disruption to supplies in the region, but dropped back when various ceasefires were agreed. Oil prices rose again when the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July. "Inflation has fallen faster than we'd expected, but the conflict in the Middle East continues to mean high and volatile energy prices," said the Bank's governor, Andrew Bailey. "That will cause inflation to rise again later this year. However the conflict unfolds, our job is to make sure any increase in inflation is temporary and that it comes back to our 2% target." UK household energy bills rose after the latest increase in the price cap took effect on 1 July, and global oil prices have risen again recently. Given the uncertainty, many analysts think rates may stay at 3.75% for the foreseeable future, or possibly rise before the end of the year. What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? Why are UK fuel prices rising again? What does an Andy Burnham-led government mean for your money? Just under a third of households have a mortgage, according to the government's English Housing Survey, external. About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate. That means any cut means a reduction in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) rely on their lender choosing to pass on any Bank rate cut. But the vast majority of mortgage customers - some 87% - have fixed-rate deals. While their monthly payments aren't immediately affected by a rate change, their future deals are. As of 16 September, the average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate was at its highest since 11 May (5.77%), while the average five-year was at its highest since 8 November 2023 (5.83%), according to the financial information service Moneyfacts. The average two-year tracker rate was 4.54%. About 800,000 fixed-rate mortgages with an interest rate of 3% or below are expected to expire every year, on average, until the end of 2027. Borrowing costs for customers coming off those deals are likely to rise sharply. You can see how your mortgage may be affected by future interest rate changes by using our calculator: A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive. At this rate, your payments could change by… The information you provided on your monthly payments would not be sufficient to pay off your mortgage within the number of years given. This calculator does not constitute financial advice. It is based on a standard mortgage repayment formula dependent on the mortgage size and length and a fixed interest rate. It should be used as a guide only and does not represent the suitability, eligibility or availability of mortgage offers for users. For exact figures, users will need to approach an official mortgage lender. Interest rates fluctuate based on the Bank of England's base rate and market conditions If you can't see the mortgage calculator, click here Five ways to save money on your mortgage Bank of England interest rates also influence the amount charged on credit cards, bank loans and car loans. Lenders can decide to reduce their own interest rates if Bank cuts make borrowing costs cheaper. However, this tends to happen very slowly. The Bank base rate also affects how much savers earn on their money. A falling base rate is likely to mean a reduction in the returns offered to savers by banks and building societies and vice versa. title: Brexit to blame for small boat migrants, says Lib Dem leader
description: Sir Ed Davey says the Conservatives and Reform UK are to blame for the numbers of migrants crossing the Channel.
body: This video can not be played Watch the Lib Dem leader Ed Davey being questioned on BBC local radio stations The Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey has blamed Brexit for the continuing migrant boat crossings, and accused both Reform UK and the Conservatives of "exploiting" the issue for their own benefit. Sir Ed was speaking during a round of interviews with BBC local radio stations ahead of his party's annual conference which starts on Saturday. Now in his seventh year as party leader, he answered questions on immigration, the cost of living, pensions, crime, and the Lib Dems' record in local government. On the numbers of migrants crossing the English Channel in dinghies, he said: "We didn't have the small boats problem before Brexit. It's been caused by the Conservatives... caused by Nigel Farage. "They should hang their heads in shame. And what really irritates me, is they exploit it for their own political benefit. And I think that's really wrong." The Lib Dem leader is calling on the government to open negotiations with the EU Commission to join its pact on migration and asylum. Sir Ed said that scheme would allow migrants to be returned to whichever EU state they had travelled from - as had been permissible before Brexit - calling it "an effective deterrent". He said: "When you see something working you want to be part of it. And if it would give us the right to return everyone who came in small boats, surely we'd want to do that, wouldn't we? It worked before. And if you want tough action, the Liberal Democrats are offering it." Latest figures show that under the current Labour government, small boat arrivals are down by 44% and deportations up by 8%. However, Sir Ed said that "wasn't anywhere near enough" and had been achieved only through international cooperation - of which he wanted more. Sir Ed pledged his party would not support abolishing the triple lock on pensions The Lib Dem leader promised his party's autumn conference would be a "serious" event. He told BBC Radio Kent the party would talk about "problems like the cost of living, which is so damaging, and we've got a real plan to deal with that. I'll be unveiling all the measures we have to help people who are struggling so much at the moment." He had earlier told listeners to BBC Radio Shropshire that his party would not support abolishing the triple lock on pensions, arguing it was still "sustainable." Introduced in 2011, it guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest. All the major parties currently back the triple lock, but with the public finances under severe pressure and many young people struggling to find employment, there have been calls from some for a rethink, and for the money saved to be used elsewhere. However, Sir Ed said the triple lock had done much to reduce pensioner poverty, and this could be done "at the same time as giving hope and employment to young people". The Lib Dem leader was separately pressed by BBC Radio Cambridgeshire on the question of large donations in politics. Until Reform UK received two £36m donations last week, the record figure for a party to be given was the £8m the Lib Dems accepted from Lord Sainsbury in December 2019. Sir Ed said: "I think there needs to be a cap on donations. I have argued that my entire life. We tried when we were in government [in coalition with the Conservatives], and unfortunately a combination of Labour and the Conservatives prevented us getting those votes through." Defending donations his party has previously received, he added: "The others were getting huge amounts from their donors. While the rules are different, we have to play by the rules, as the others are playing by those rules. I want to change the rules." During his round of interviews, Sir Ed was also pressed on his party's record in local government. On each occasion, he asked for more time for his councillors - telling presenters on BBC Radio Shropshire, WM, and Somerset that there was "no magic wand" to instantly turn around councils the Lib Dems had recently taken over from other parties. Nationally he claimed the Lib Dems were in their strongest position for more than a century. Looking ahead to the next general election, Sir Ed said in some areas only his party could stop Reform UK - claiming it was the Lib Dems' "moral responsibility" to stop Nigel Farage's party and what he called their "nasty policies". He added: "A lot of people are really worried about Reform... their increasing racism and approach to dividing people up without any practical policies. "They worry that big money is coming into British politics and foreign interference through Reform. People are worried and they don't like it." title: What next for Gabriel and Man Utd?
description: On the night JJ Gabriel was supposed to become Manchester United's youngest player in history, the scramble is on to persuade him not to quit.
body: JJ Gabriel in action for Manchester United in Premier League 2 this month Before what was intended to be a historic night at Old Trafford, Manchester United are still digesting the reality that JJ Gabriel wants to leave. The club have been left reeling at the sudden downturn in relations. Only a week ago Gabriel scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut at Leigh that seemed to be the prelude to becoming United's youngest player in history by making his debut against Brighton in the Carabao Cup third round on Wednesday. Now United are scrambling. Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are involved in talks they hope will result in their 15-year-old reversing his plan and choosing to stay. It feels like a forlorn task. A belief that promises have been broken and a certainty over Gabriel's current abilities and eventual destiny mean trust is low. Real Madrid, Barcelona and Paris St-Germain are among the European heavyweight clubs monitoring the situation. Gabriel's potential is well known. All England's leading clubs have seen it first hand given he was named Under-18 Premier League player of the year last season, even though he was only 14 when the campaign began. He scored 23 goals in the Premier League Under-18 competition and three in the FA Youth Cup. He was the star man in a United side that reached the Premier League Under-18 cup final and the FA Youth Cup final. He was the Premier League Under-18 Player of the Year and United's Under-18 Player of the Year. The achievements and accolades were in recognition of a player who has balance, pace, close control and a powerful shot. This season he has shown a willingness to get stuck in to try and win the ball back. "The best 15-year-old in Europe," was how the forward was described by one United source recently. United Under-21s coach Adam Lawrence made a salient point in the aftermath of that Uefa Youth League victory over Sabah FK. "The first thing in my job is not to ruin him," said Lawrence. "When you have a talented player like JJ, you obviously don't want to stifle their freedom and their creativity." Talent like that grabs attention and is not confined to these shores. Real, Barcelona and PSG focus on elite youth players. That is what is happening here. This is where is gets tricky. United's initial response to the publicity around Gabriel's future was to say privately that they would try to persuade him his future was best served staying where he is. They also advised that Gabriel's registration with them runs until the end of the season. That may well buy them time when it comes to potential moves to Premier League rivals. But what about European giants? Gabriel has a European Union passport. His mother is of Greek-Cypriot heritage and his father won two caps for the Republic of Ireland. In 2016 the Court of Arbitration for Sport rejected an appeal by Argentine club Velez Sarsfield - who tried to block one of their 16-year-old players moving to Manchester City - on the basis he was a dual Argentine-Italian national and, as an EU national, should be allowed to transfer to a club within the European Union even though he was coming in from an external country. West Brom received no compensation when a 16-year-old Louie Barry left for Barcelona in 2019 as Fifa ruled that West Brom failed to formally offer him a scholarship. West Brom had claimed 130,000 euros (£111,000) in training compensation. Barry left Barca for Aston Villa for just under £1m six months later. The worst-case scenario for United is Gabriel walks away when he turns 16 on 6 October and they end up with no compensation for a player whose market value, even at this tender age and with so much promise unfulfilled, can be measured in millions. Gabriel made his senior United debut against Atletico Madrid last month Gabriel is not the first young player to find himself at odds with his club over their future direction. Jadon Sancho was 17 when he stopped training at City to force through a £10m move to Borussia Dortmund in the belief that he would play more often in Germany than under Pep Guardiola. Morgan Rogers was Barry's team-mate in the West Brom side that reached the FA Youth Cup semi-final in 2019. Within three months he had left for City, a move completed on his 17th birthday. Sources feel that, in meetings with the United hierarchy that led to Gabriel committing his short-term future to the club last summer, promises were made over his career path that have not been kept. He did start to appear in senior training sessions, initially under Ruben Amorim and then Michael Carrick, but speculation around a senior debut last season, which could only be in the FA Cup, was doused by Under-18s coach Darren Fletcher, who had by now taken the senior team manager's role on an interim basis following Amorim's dismissal. Fletcher felt it was too early for Gabriel. It had been anticipated that Gabriel would feature during United's pre-season programme. His absence from the trip to Helsinki for a meeting with Wrexham on 18 July was put down to the date he returned for pre-season training. He was part of every squad after that, but played only once, for eight minutes against Atletico Madrid in Stockholm. Did that lack of action sow the seeds of discontent? Gabriel travelled to Trondheim for a meeting with Rosenborg on 24 July. Carrick used 11 substitutes that day. Gabriel was one of two United players who did not come on. Five of those who did have left, either permanently or on loan. It was noted that 18-year-old Tynan Thompson was given a 45-minute senior debut against Leeds United at Croke Park - another game Gabriel travelled to but was not involved in - three weeks after his arrival from Tottenham. Nevertheless, it was felt Gabriel was likely to become United's youngest player this autumn - probably in the EFL Cup. While the third-round draw delivered an Old Trafford rema

title: Man, 57, arrested over death in suspected shooting in Armadale
description: Police Scotland said William Watson, 35, was pronounced dead at the scene of the incident on Saturday.
body: William Watson, known as Billy, died in the targeted attack in Armadale A 57-year-old man has been arrested over a man's death in a suspected shooting at a house in West Lothian. William Watson, known as Billy, died at the scene of the incident on Harestanes Road, Armadale, at about 11:50 on Saturday. Police Scotland described the 35-year-old's death as a "targeted attack" and said its inquiries were ongoing. A postmortem examination is due to take place, and the death is currently being treated as suspicious. Police outside the house on Harestanes Road on Monday Officers had also been investigating whether a car fire on Saturday in nearby Netherhouses and a fire at a derelict house on Wotherspoon Crescent were linked to the incident. Det Supt Michelle Findlay, from Police Scotland's Major Investigations Team, said her thoughts remained with Watson's family and friends. She added: "Specialist officers are supporting them as we continue to try to get answers about what happened. "We've been carrying out extensive inquiries, including door-to-door in the area, CCTV review and forensic analysis." Police Scotland urged anyone with information about the death to contact officers, external. A dedicated online portal, external has also been set up. Supt Jocelyn Thomas said: "We understand the local community is concerned by what has happened, however we believe this was a targeted attack. "I want to reassure everyone, these incidents are rare. "An increased police presence will remain in the area as we continue our inquiries and anyone with concerns can speak to these officers." title: Wildlife trust wants marina silt disposed offshore
description: Brighton Marina wants to restart dredging next year but still needs a site to dispose of the silt.
body: The marina said there were limited options available for disposal sites A wildlife trust has called for a new offshore disposal site to be found for sediment dredged from Brighton Marina, saying it remains concerned about plans being explored off Newhaven. Brighton Marina has been looking for a long-term disposal site since Sussex Wildlife Trust successfully challenged a licence in 2025 for disposal of sediment at Rottingdean. The marina has said dredging is needed to maintain safe access and there are limited options available for disposal sites. Sussex Wildlife Trust said Newhaven was a "protected area" that sat adjacent to the Beachy Head West Marine Conservation Zone (MCZ). Campaigners previously claimed the silt was a "black, thick, slimy, petrochemically smelling sludge", but Premier Marinas, which owns Brighton Marina, said dredged silt was regularly sampled to confirm it was not harmful. Protesters opposed the use of Rottingdean in a demo by the marina in January 2025 John Cervenka, Premier Marinas chief operating officer, said: "Maintaining safe navigational access to Brighton Marina is not optional. It is a legal requirement and fundamental to the operation of the marina." He said the marina was a major centre of economic activity. According to the marina, about 150 businesses depend on the site, creating jobs for about 1,200 people, with more than eight million visits each year. Premier Marinas said Newhaven had been identified as a potential alternative by Sussex Wildlife Trust. However, the trust said in a statement on social media, external: "We have not promoted or endorsed Newhaven over any other option." Campaigners said last year that local rock pools filled with sludge after dredging The trust said: "Newhaven sits adjacent to Beachy Head West MCZ, and we remain concerned about potential impacts on this protected area. "Our preferred option is a new offshore disposal site, well away from the MCZ." The trust said that Newhaven was already used for dredge disposal by Newhaven Port, and there was currently no available data on the impacts of additional disposal there. Until it saw further evidence, it did not have a view on whether Newhaven was suitable, it added. "We will respond to any future licence application based on the ecological evidence it contains," it said. Brighton Marina hopes to submit a marine licence application to the Marine Management Organisation in November. If approved, maintenance dredging could restart next spring. title: Earl Spencer's unreleased book on sister Diana stolen in the Netherlands
description: The theft of Earl Spencer's memoir about his late sister comes one week ahead of the book's release.
body: Copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book on his sister Diana, Princess of Wales, have been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands. The BBC understands four copies of the Dutch language edition were taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher's printers to their warehouse. Dutch police said they were aware of the incident and have been approached for comment. Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be released in the UK and globally on Tuesday, and tells the story of Princess Diana's life from the Earl's perspective. A source said the truck driver was taking a mandatory break in a car park and was sleeping in his cab at the time the books were stolen. They added Dutch police are investigating. They did not say where the theft took place. The Daily Mail, who first reported the theft, external and is serialising the book, said the theft took place earlier this week in the Dutch countryside. The book's publisher Penguin Michael Joseph - a division of Penguin Random House - and Dutch publisher Overamstel, who have rights to the book in the Netherlands, were approached for comment by the BBC. Earl Spencer said he wanted "to tell the truth about Diana" from his perspective Princess Diana, who died aged 36 following a car crash in Paris in 1997, would have turned 65 on 1 July this year. Her sons Prince William and Prince Harry were aged 15 and 12 respectively at the time of her death. Last month announcing the book's publication, Earl Spencer explained ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death he had been inundated with interview requests and he wanted to write down his own thoughts and memories rather than "having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others". "The aim of this book is to tell the truth about Diana from her brother's perspective, just as I attempted to do when speaking at her funeral," he added, referring to the eulogy he delivered in Westminster Abbey in September 1997. "I want to speak on Diana's behalf and do so in an openly positive way." In his eulogy, Earl Spencer described Princess Diana as the "very essence of compassion, of duty, of style, of beauty", adding: "All over the world she was a symbol of selfless humanity... a standard bearer for the rights of the truly downtrodden." He also used the speech to criticise the media, calling her the "most hunted person of the modern age" and pledged to protect Prince William and Prince Harry and prevent them suffering a similar fate. In 2023, copies of Prince Harry's memoir Spare were accidentally put on sale in Spain days ahead of the official global release. title: Author and critic Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
description: Her husband says the playwright and cultural and political commentator died after a brief illness.
body: Greer's work often tackled topics around culture, race and public institutions British-American author and cultural commentator Bonnie Greer has died at the age of 77 after a brief illness, her husband has said. In a statement delivered with "profound sadness", Greer's widower David Hutchins noted how the acclaimed playwright and critic had made "an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life" with her "intelligence, courage and distinctive voice". He added: "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her." Hutchins continued: "Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together." BBC presenter Clive Myrie led the tributes from elsewhere, posting on X: "This is such a shock. She was a friend and mentor and I will miss her with all my heart." Former deputy prime minister David Lammy called Greer "a powerful wordsmith and artist, she was eloquent and exacting. A true life force". He added: "I will never forget her quiet fearlessness taking on Nick Griffin on Question Time. I will miss her mentorship, and her friendship." London Mayor Sadiq Khan said her voice brought "courage, humour and humanity to Britain's cultural conversation. "She inspired and opened doors for so many others. And she was great fun too - I will miss her friendship enormously." Born in Chicago in 1948, Greer wrote plays from a young age and went on to study theatre in her home city and before attending the Actors Studio in New York with director Elia Kazan. Greer moved to the UK in 1986 and became a familiar face on UK TV, appearing as a powerful panellist on programmes like Newsnight Review and Question Time. She penned award-winning works like Munda Negra, which won her the Verity Bargate Award for best play, and novels such as Hanging by Her Teeth (1994) and Entropy (2009). Once named by the Observer, external as one of the country's leading public intellectuals, Greer's work - across a range of disciplines and platforms - often tackled topics around culture, race and public institutions. Greer was made an OBE for services to the arts in 2010 Speaking to the Guardian, external in 2016 in the aftermath of the Black Lives Matter movement, Greer said: "When I wake up in the morning, I'm just myself. It's only when I leave the door that I become a black woman to the world." She added: "I tell black women all the time, 'Don't apologise for yourself and keep your hair nappy. Make sure you are heard'." Greer served on the boards of cultural institutions including the British Museum, Royal Opera House and London Film School, and was chancellor of London's Kingston University. Her other published works include a memoir titled A Parallel Life and a biography of US poet and playwright Langston Hughes. Also in 2009, her part-memoir, part-music-history book, Obama Music, was published. Greer was made an OBE in 2010 for services to the arts. In 2022, she was appointed as a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature. title: US accuses Russia of trying to kill Ukrainian allies overseas
description: The FBI says five men "conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on US soil and around the world".
body: The US Department of Justice (DoJ) has accused Russia of plotting to murder Ukrainian allies in the US and Europe. In a statement on Tuesday, the DoJ charged five men allegedly connected to the Russian Intelligence Services (RIS). The men are accused of paying, or trying to pay, people in the US and overseas to target those "aligned, or perceived to be aligned, with Ukraine". "It is our job to stop America's adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil," Attorney General Todd Blanche. All those accused remain at large. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday Moscow will not comment until it hears or sees "any credible evidence" or "tangible facts". It is not clear if the five accused are in the United States, or in a different location. Washington has charged all five men with participating in a conspiracy to finance terrorism, which carries a maximum 20-year prison sentence. Three of the defendants are "high-ranking members of the RIS network", the DoJ said. Among them are Russian father and son Yuri Khrameev, 63, and Kirill Khrameev, 27. Khrameev senior was a colonel in the Russian intelligence services and his son is an officer in the Federal Security Service of Russia (FSB). The third high-ranking suspect is Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, a 35-year-old Cuban national who the US describe as "an influential member of the Cuban diaspora living in Russia who has coordinated attacks for the RIS network". Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, and Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, are the other two defendants. The pair are accused of recruiting or attempting to recruit US-based individuals to "surveil and attempt to murder a prominent US-based Russian dissident". The FBI's James Barnacle said the group "conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on US soil and around the world". One of the incidents is as recent as this summer. The DoJ described how the RIS network was able to recruit someone in the US to surveil and eventually murder a Russian dissident in the US. Suarez allegedly sent the recruit to two locations linked to the victim with "explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance". In exchange, the recruit was offered between $1,000 (£743) and $1,500. Suarez and Castro are said to have offered an additional $40,000 if the US resident could "eliminate" the dissident. The DoJ said the RIS recruit did not go through with it, which led Suarez to try and recruit "multiple other individuals within the United States". He allegedly offered "substantial sums of money to carry out the targeting of US based victims". The release by the DoJ goes on to list other instances in which the accused allegedly tried to recruit others to kill those who were a perceived threat to Russia. It said that in 2025, Khrameev junior allegedly recruited a US citizen to surveil and murder someone in Lithuania who was "telling lies about Russia". The release quotes Khrameev as saying the purpose was to target "all the countries that are helping Ukraine". His father, Khrameev senior, is said to have offered the recruit $25,000 to kill the individual in Lithuania for "spreading dirt about my country" and "distorting history". Khrameev senior, Suarez and Castro are the only ones also charged with "participating in a conspiracy to commit murder for hire". If found guilty, this charge carries a maximum 10-year prison sentence. It is not the first time authorities thwart threats of this kind. Last month, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities had detained an individual allegedly working for the Kremlin and who was plotting to murder an American-Ukrainian citizen in Warsaw. Tusk told reporters the American-Ukrainian citizen "was uncomfortable for the Putin regime", adding: "We have to accept the assumption that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient for various reasons." In 2024, German authorities were reportedly warned by US intelligence of a Russian plot to kill Armin Papperger, the head of Germany's biggest arms company Rheinmetall. Moscow dismissed the accusation at the time, with Kremlin spokesman Peskov saying: "It's all presented in the style of another fake story, so such reports cannot be taken seriously." The fresh accusations from the DoJ come at a time of closer relations between Moscow and Washington following US President Donald Trump's return to the White House in 2025. A few weeks ago, the head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) visited Moscow for talks with figures from Russia's intelligence services - an unconventional move that led to speculation. The Kremlin confirmed that talks between John Ratcliffe and the intelligence services had taken place. President Trump did not say what was discussed but described the meeting as "semi-routine".
