title: Complaints to watchdog about water firms jump 84%
description: Many complaints were about affordability, after customers saw steep hikes to bills.
body: Many water customers in England and Wales saw steep bill hikes this year The number of complaints made by households about water companies to the industry watchdog has risen by a record 84% in a year, driven by customer concern and confusion over rising bills. The Consumer Council for Water (CCW) said the year-on-year increase was the highest in its 20-year history and showed "just how dissatisfied" many people were. Water customers in England and Wales have been hit with steep price hikes in recent years. The regulator Ofwat has also allowed firms to put up bills by 36% between 2025 and 2030. Water UK, which represents firms, said it understood that higher bills was never welcome, but the money was needed "to fund vital upgrades". The total number of complaints to the watchdog rose to 15,115 in 2025-26, from 8,235 in the previous year. Meanwhile, complaints made by households directly to water companies, which is required before complaining to the CCW, rose by 56% to 321,347. The top three subjects of complaints to the CCW were measured billing, affordability and billing admin. Mike Keil, the chief executive of the CCW, said the figures "reflect just how dissatisfied many people still are with the state of the water sector". He said customers are "impatient to see the benefits" of higher bills. "Companies need to be clear and open with their customers about how they are investing people's money to deliver real improvements." The CCW assessed each water company's performance on the number of complaints it received for every 10,000 households it serves, and the amount of effort customers have to put in to get their complaint resolved. Thames Water and South West Water rated "poor" for both performance measures. David Bird, retail director at Thames, apologised to customers who "have not received the service they should expect". "We know bill clarity has been a particular source of frustration, which is why we have launched a programme to redesign them, so they are easier to understand," he said. Bills for the average Thames customer rose by 31% in 2024, but were a lot smaller this year at 3.4%. South West Water said: "We know there is more to do to improve our customers' experience. We are taking action by reducing repeat contacts, resolving issues when people contact us for the first time, and ensuring they receive clear, timely communication." Portsmouth Water and Bristol Water were the only companies to score "good" in both metrics, retaining their position at the top of the rankings as the sector's best performers. Last month, Ofwat approved bill increases for 13 companies to meet increased pressures on infrastructure and the environment. Five of those companies — Thames, Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, Wessex Water and South East Water — were already permitted to hike bills in 2024. A spokesperson for industry body Water UK said: "We understand increasing bills is never welcome, but the money is needed to fund vital upgrades to secure our water supplies, support economic growth and end sewage entering our rivers and seas. The spokesperson said that 94% of complaints are "being dealt with at the earliest possible stage without the need for further involvement from the consumer body". "The industry remains committed to improving communication with customers and showing clearly how their money is being used to deliver the improvements they expect," the spokesperson added. title: 'My sex offender ex is fighting for access to our child'
description: The woman, who is "sick" at the thought of her sex offender ex having access to their child, is calling for laws to change.
body: 'Lucy' is calling for a change in the law to strip people convicted of child-related sex offences of their parental responsibility (stock image) A woman who is fighting to stop her sex offender ex-husband having contact with their child has said the thought of it makes her "feel sick". Lucy - not her real name - described how her "world was blown apart" when her then husband was convicted of possessing indecent images of children, including videos of children being sexually abused. She told BBC News NI she was further "horrified" to discover he was taking her to family court for supervised access to their child. She is now calling for a change in Northern Ireland's laws to strip people convicted of child-related sex offences of their parental responsibility. Commissioner for victims of crime, Geraldine Hanna, said courts had discretion in individual cases but she believed they should be given "all the powers they need" to address concerns on this issue. "When I think of my husband, who I believed him to be, compared to this person, this person's a complete stranger to me," Lucy told the BBC. "It makes me feel sick to think that he would be even near my child. So I really do not want to put my child in a room with a stranger, supervised or not. "As a mother all I want to do is protect my child and I'm not doing that if I'm letting [them] in a room with a stranger." Lucy said she recognised her call for the law to change was a "huge" demand, but that it was aimed at protecting children and families. Earlier this year, Finance Minister John O'Dowd committed to changing family law to automatically remove the parental responsibility of anyone convicted of murdering someone with whom they shared a child. Lucy said she believed that should be extended to anyone on the sex offenders register – which includes her ex-husband. She said it was a move she thought could also help deter people from offending. A spokesperson for the Department of Finance confirmed O'Dowd was committed to developing legislation that would provide "stronger protections for children and families". In England and Wales, Jade's Law automatically suspends parental responsibility for a parent convicted of murdering or committing voluntary manslaughter against a partner or ex-partner with whom they share children It is named after Jade Ward, who was 27 when she was murdered by ex-partner Russell Marsh in 2021. However, Jade's Law does not apply to Northern Ireland. The spokesperson for the Department of Finance said a consultation would be launched this autumn, which would set out proposals for reform in cases involving homicide and "on whether comparable protections should be extended to other forms of serious offending". Safeguarding expert Marcella Leonard told the BBC that when it comes to people convicted of child-related sex offences, their "right to family life" should be explored by the courts. This should also be the case, she said, in regards to the child's right to have a relationship with that parent. However, she said that process should be "bespoke" and based on strict criteria. "The person must have undergone specialist risk assessment that looks at why they did what they did and the particular risk to the child," she said. "They must also engage with therapeutic interventions which are tailored for the individualised risk that the person poses – not general programmes which are not specific to the individual. Then and only then should contact be considered to be supervised." She added that the person doing the potential supervising must also undergo "protective assessments" that identify any education they may need to in order to properly hold the parent to account and ensure the child in question was protected. 'Lucy' is calling for a change in the law to strip people convicted of child-related sex offences of their parental responsibility Lucy said she had had no idea of her ex-husband's offending until police knocked on their door with a search warrant to seize his devices and arrested him. She described feeling like an "indirect victim" of his crimes and has called for greater support for family members of sex offenders who experience their own kind of trauma. "Whilst I can't imagine what the children in the [indecent] pictures have gone through, and there's a part of me that almost doesn't let my brain go there, what happened from the door knock completely broke our lives," she said. "There's a before and there's an after. "And the before is this lovely time of innocence, of believing somebody at face value, of believing that people are safe. "Since the door knock, nobody is safe and I struggle with that. "Our whole lives have being totally and utterly upended and still continue to be so, that whilst we're not direct victims, we're certainly indirect victims." She said she and her child had to leave the family home and relocate to another area – to protect the child from the "horror of the truth" about their father. Despite initial contact with social services, in which Lucy said she had to be deemed fit to parent her own child, there was no further support – particularly around the time of her ex-husband's court case. "Why isn't there a system in place to tell family members ahead of that to prepare us or to make sure that we're safe?" she said. "You're totally on your own. There are no organisations in Northern Ireland, there's no local support to help family members deal with this, so where do I go to next to get the help for what happens next?" Geraldine Hanna said crimes of the type Lucy's husband was convicted of were "devastating" and "land like a bomb" in people's lives. "This case really highlights the broader ripple impact of crime," she said. "We don't often think about the wider impact... that it has on those who are associated with the accused in such

title: Let them ref the games and be humans - Andrews
description: After Brentford overcame Reading to reach the Carabao Cup fourth round, head coach Keith Andrews believes the video assistant referee (VAR) is preventing referees from making decisions in matches.
body: Brentford are unbeaten in the Premier League this season with one win and three draws Brentford head coach Keith Andrews believes the video assistant referee (VAR) is preventing referees from making decisions in matches. As his Bees progressed to the Carabao Cup fourth round with a battling 2-1 win at League One side Reading, Andrews said he was not happy with the officiating. Reading defender Paudie O'Connor had a goal for a first-half overhead kick ruled out by referee Tom Nield for a high boot, prompting Royals boss Leam Richardson to say it was "possibly in the top three [wrong] decisions that I've seen in my career - and I've seen thousands of games and played in hundreds". With no VAR used at this stage of the EFL Cup, Andrews added: "It's been a tough week for officials as everybody is probably aware. "I think we just need to let them ref the game and be human beings and make decisions. "We have gone through a period in the game where I feel like they weren't actually making decisions in both boxes because of the technology we have in the game and I feel like that is a real shame." His comments followed the admission of Pro Ref to an "error of judgement" in awarding Erling Haaland's winning goal for Manchester City in their Premier League encounter at Manchester United on Sunday. There was intense debate over whether the goal should have been disallowed for City midfielder Enzo Fernandez - who was in an offside position - interfering with play as he dived, attempting to head the ball in a central position before Haaland's finish. Andrews, whose Brentford side are seventh in the Premier League, said referees were no longer allowed to "make mistakes". "I always felt as a player, when there was a relationship with an official that was built on respect and being able to speak to each other in a certain way," he added. "We've gone away from allowing them to officiate and allowing them to make mistakes and I think it is a real shame. "Now they are having to go back to that and it's not the habits they have had in recent years." On Sunday's refereeing error in the Manchester derby, Andrews said it was "pretty alarming" Haaland's goal was allowed to stand. "The first thing was whether [Erling] Haaland was offside and then obviously [Enzo] Fernandez was. It's a shame," he admitted. title: 'Superstar' Dowman shows his class - but Arsenal know caution is needed
description: Max Dowman shines with two goals against Ipswich Town - but boss Mikel Arteta warns Arsenal cannot rush his development.
body: Max Dowman is the third 16-year-old to score for Arsenal in a League Cup game Arsenal teenager Max Dowman shone with two goals in the 4-2 Carabao Cup win over Ipswich Town - but boss Mikel Arteta warned they cannot rush his development. The 16-year-old played 13 times last season, but has had to settle for a place on the bench so far this campaign - until now. He scored two lovely goals at Portman Road to stake his claim for more minutes in the Premier League. But Arteta warned: "He is 16 years old and we have to be really cautious. "We don't want to stop him, we don't want to put the brakes on him, we need to develop him and we are fully aware what he needs. He will have opportunities." His first was a fine solo goal as he ran through, leaving defenders on the floor before slotting in. "Unbelievable, he's unpredictable, he can go either way, so fluid, so nice to watch," said Arteta. And for his second goal, Dowman showed good composure to place the ball in the bottom corner. He is just the second 16-year-old to score two goals in a game for a Premier League side in any competition, after Wayne Rooney for Everton against Wrexham in 2002 - which was also in the League Cup. "With the demands that we put in them, to be able to do that is extremely difficult and he's coping better and better and better," Arteta added. "He's an unbelievable player because of the character that he has and how much he loves to play at the biggest stage. "It's not easy [to contain the hype], I understand, but what we have to do is look after him. He's 16 years old. You don't see that in this league. "In other leagues in Europe, that's a totally different context, but in this league, with the demands that the league has, the players and everything put on you, we really need to make sure every time we throw him in, he's in the right context with the right preparation." Perhaps Dowman might have expected to have more minutes this season. His breakthrough came last season as he broke several records. He became the youngest Champions League player ever, aged 15, Arsenal's youngest ever starter as well as the Premier League's youngest starter, goalscorer and title winner. In 13 appearances in all competitions, he scored once - against Everton to make a win safe during the title run-in. In fact his strike, where he ran the ball halfway down the pitch before scoring into an empty net - with Jordan Pickford upfield - was voted Arsenal's goal of the season. And all of this while he was studying for school exams. He received his GCSEs from Brentwood School in the summer and left school to focus on his football career. Sky Sports pundit Jamie Redknapp said: "He is a wonderful player who will be able to do everything in the game. "But just give him time and how they are handling him is perfect. What you don't want to do is not give him the amount of game time he needs. He is an elite player." Breaking into the Arsenal first team will be a tough task for Dowman especially when the Premier League champions are in such fine form. Arsenal have won all seven games this season, across four competitions. Dowman was an unused substitute in four of those games, and not involved for the other two, before playing all 90 minutes against Ipswich Town. The Gunners have played the same attackers in each league game so far - Bukayo Saka, Christos Tzolis, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz. But Dowman, especially considering Arteta turned to him in key moments in last season's title race, will hope to gain more of a supporting role. "He's an unbelievable talent," team-mate Mikel Merino told BBC Radio 5 Live. "He will be a star in the future if he keeps his eyes and ears open and keeps learning. "He's just 16 so he needs a lot of coaching, especially tactically. But I can't take anything away from him. He's always keen to learn. We'll keep helping him." Quite possibly the best 16-year-old in the world, it is not unthinkable that he could earn his way into England's Euro 2028 thinking. In fact there was even a debate about whether he should be going to the World Cup earlier this year. "He is a real superstar," said former England defender Conor Coady on Sky Sports. "A 16-year-old boy should not be doing this. He has got no better manager than Arteta to look after him. You want him to be looked after properly. If he plays every game at this age, he won't be scoring goals like this." And it comes on the day it emerged highly rated 15-year-old striker JJ Gabriel is on the verge of leaving Manchester United. Gabriel had been expected to make his debut in Wednesday's Carabao Cup tie with Brighton. That will probably deny him the opportunity to break up the stat that the three youngest players to score in the League Cup for a Premier League side all did so for Arsenal. They are Cesc Fabregas (16y 212d v Wolves, 2003), Dowman (16y 258d v Ipswich) and Jack Wilshere (16y 266d v Sheffield United, 2008). title: Turkey arrests dozens in crackdown on LGBTQ+ activists
description: The arrests are an escalation in the Turkish government's campaign targeting LGBTQ+ community and activists.
body: Turkish police have arrested dozens of people as part of the government's recent crackdown on LGBTQ+ activists and venues. The protesters were detained as they gathered on Tuesday outside Istanbul's main courthouse. They were calling for the release of another group of LGBTQ+ activists, who were arrested over the weekend in a series of raids on gay bars and at the homes of activists. The Turkish government has detained members of the LGBTQ+ community and activists as part of a campaign dubbed "My Family is Safe", which the government says has been designed to protect family values. At Tuesday's protest, people chanted "Long live the struggle for freedom!" and called for the detained activists to be released, news agency AFP reported. Police made several arrests after some demonstrators unfurled a banner reading "Being LGBTQ is not a crime". "What we are seeing now is deeply disturbing," one protestor told AFP. Rights groups have described a widening campaign against the LGBTQ+ community. Over the past week the authorities raided association offices, blocked websites and made arrests across multiple provinces. The government has also blocked or restricted access to the social media accounts and websites of dozens of LGBT, media and rights organisations, according to a post from the NGO Human Rights Watch. Same-sex relations are not an offence in Turkey but homophobia is common, and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has described LGBTQ people as "perverts" responsible for the falling birth rate. The Commissioner for Human Rights at the Council of Europe, Michael O'Flaherty, has raised concerns about the arrests. "I am concerned by reports of a series arrests, raids and the blocking of websites and social media accounts targeting LGBTI civil society and human rights defenders across Turkey," he said. O'Flaherty's statement said that Turkey's Minister of Justice had said the operation was being conducted against 162 individuals, nine associations and 13 businesses across 15 provinces under the coordination of several Chief Public Prosecutors' Offices. title: 'Luck and timing': Matthew Rhys on his historic Emmy Awards double win
description: Speaking to the BBC, the Welsh actor described the "surreal" experience of becoming the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night.
body: This video can not be played Welsh actor Matthew Rhys described the "surreal and incredible feeling" after making history on Monday by becoming the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night. Rhys was recognised at the prestigious US ceremony for his roles in supernatural TV comedy Widow's Bay and psychological thriller The Beast In Me. Speaking to the BBC, Rhys said he wasn't expecting to win the first award for The Beast In Me. "I hadn't really prepared anything, as may be apparent from the vomit of a speech I came up with," he explained. Welsh actor Matthew Rhys makes Emmy Awards history with double win. title: MSPs asked to pause Scotland's AI data centre boom
description: The growth of AI is happening at lightning pace, so what are the advantages and disadvantages of Scotland being at the forefront?
body: Activists protested against data centres in their local area outside the Scottish Parliament earlier this month Scotland has a new boom industry, at least if planning applications are taken at face value. The term "hyperscale data centre", rarely heard a few years ago, is now dividing opinion across the country as a rush of applications are made to build them. A debate at Holyrood later, led by the Scottish Greens, will call for planning applications to be put on hold until promised new national guidelines are in force, with an emphasis on energy demand and the environment. The growth of AI is happening at lightning pace, so what are the advantages and disadvantages of Scotland being at the forefront? The single biggest reason why developers are interested in Scotland is because it allows them to say that their energy-hungry facility is being powered by green electricity. Scotland has an abundance of wind and much of the energy from it is currently wasted because the transmission infrastructure isn't large enough to carry it from where it is generated to the consumers. There are two ways of fixing that. Installing more, bigger pylons to ship the electricity to England, where the bulk of the UK's population is, or bring the largest consumers of that electricity closer to the generators. In fact, what's happening is both. Research by BBC Scotland News has identified, as of 24 June, at least 23 projects which are in the planning process, though most experts believe many of those are speculative applications and will never be built. But that doesn't allay the fears of people living in communities where potential sites have been identified because the faceless, warehouse-like buildings housing the servers can cover a massive footprint. Jamie Prentice is worried about the potential impact of data centres At Blackdog in Aberdeenshire, local resident Jamie Prentice spoke to me about the development planned for there which would stretch across several fields. His house looks out to the Aberdeen Bay wind farm and the sea beyond. But he says that if it's built there he'll effectively be living on an industrial estate. Local people have begun to mobilise their opposition to it through social media, but Jamie clearly feels it will ruin the area. He asks me whether I think the Blackdog project will ever happen and I have genuinely no idea. It is likely the site has been chosen because of its proximity to the offshore wind farm which could give the developer some "green" kudos. Scotland may have plenty of renewable power generation but experts have warned that does not necessarily mean data centres would run exclusively on renewable power. During periods of low wind or when clouds are blocking the sun, it may mean having to fire up fossil fuel power stations to provide the energy required to keep the servers blinking. Dr Callum MacIver warned MSPs this week that the additional demand could make climate change targets difficult to achieve because of the additional reliance on gas. A mechanism that requires data centre developers to match their projects, with new green generation capacity being commissioned, would be a neat way of mitigating the risks but that requires government or regulatory intervention. Political leaders across the globe have so far seemed reluctant to intervene, despite warnings. There are concerns about the unintended consequences of building data centres which have been pushing up bills in Ireland and some parts of the US. Last year, Irish data centres consumed 23% of the country's electricity and the demand for energy has pushed up the price for consumers. The electricity system operator here says it is delinking the price of electricity from the high wholesale cost of gas, which should prevent a similar outcome. But analysts are not yet convinced that is going to be fully effective. There has been much anger in recent years about how much water some of the larger data centres consume in trying to keep the equipment cool. Relatively speaking, Scotland has no shortage of water although recent summer heatwaves have resulted in the east of the country experiencing drought-like conditions. Technology, though, has improved rapidly in this area and more modern facilities use a closed loop of water, similar to that in domestic central heating systems. One of the reasons Scotland is favoured by developers is the relatively cool climate which means it generally requires less energy to bring down the temperature of that water. Currently the water consumed by existing data centres is relatively low. Colin Lindsay, a manager at a commercial subsidiary of Scottish Water, recently claimed the 97 cubic metres used daily is less than the amount consumed by Scotland's libraries., external However, the concern is about future growth and location specific impacts. Lindsay argues careful planning will be needed to avoid pressures on the drinking water supply. The Scottish government has said it wants to "harness the economic opportunities" which come from data centres as an emerging sector. The relative cheapness of land in Scotland makes it an attractive location for data centre developers. Supporters claim they can bring with them thousands of jobs but most of those are in the construction phase. Once operational, they can run with just a handful of people on site. While they might be energy hungry, there are ways in which electricity system operators can manage that hunger so that supply and demand are matched. title: Brook likened to Pietersen in SL win - how do they compare?
description: Harry Brook hits a brutal century and draws comparisons with Kevin Pietersen as England thrash Sri Lanka by 119 runs in the first T20 in Southampton.
body: This video can not be played Brook's brilliant 100 against Sri Lanka England 254-4 (20 overs): Brook 114* (49), Buttler 80 (44) Sri Lanka 135 (19 overs): Wellalage 33 (21); Baker 3-12 England won by 119 runs Harry Brook hit a brutal century and drew comparisons with Kevin Pietersen as England thrashed Sri Lanka by 119 runs in the first T20 in Southampton. The sensational Brook, after a summer without a Test hundred, crashed the ball to all parts in hitting 114 not out from 49 balls to power his side to 254-4. His 10 fours and six sixes were ferocious - reminiscent of former England batter Pietersen, the newest addition to this side's backroom staff. His intensity and running between the wickets was equally impressive. "I don't even think the genius of KP could come close to what Harry Brook has talent-wise," said Brook's former captain and team-mate Ben Stokes, who was watching on TV. "You are an absolute freak, Harry." Brook was six years old when Pietersen - a shock appointment as a mentor through to next year's World Cup - secured England the Ashes on the final day at The Oval in 2005. He was 14, now old enough to understand, when Pietersen was controversially dumped by England after the 2013-14 Ashes defeat. "I used to love watching him bat when I was younger," said Brook, external - then little more than a year into his international career. "He always looked to take the attack to bowlers and put them under pressure. In that aspect, I'm quite similar." Brook is, in many ways, the TikTok generation's Pietersen. Pietersen invented the switch hit - a shot Brook rarely plays. Brook's version is that tumbling scoop over his and the wicketkeeper's head, a shot which was absent here. They are most similar in the way they pick length, allowing them to pull, flat-bat or cut balls from spinners even in good areas. Brook did so throughout his partnership with Jos Buttler, who also played superbly for his 80 from 44 balls. They put on 128 after debutant Aneurin Donald made 12. And while Pietersen was educated in Pietermaritzburg, South Africa and Brook under the Cumbrian hills in Sedbergh, they come from the same cricketing school. "That's the way I play," Pietersen said after one aggressive shot too many during a Test in 2009. "I got to 97 playing that way so it obviously wasn't meant to be." Those words could easily have come from the mouth of Brook. Such words are why Pietersen and Brook have stirred opinion among England fans more than any other batters in the modern era. "Is it really that hard to just sit back and admire these players for what they are, on the good days and the bad days, and stop berating them for doing things that we would never, ever, ever even think of doing because we simply aren't on their level to think that way?" Stokes added on social media. Stokes, who backed Brook to succeed him as Test skipper, has always been a Brook fan. Picking between Brook and Pietersen may well be pub chat one day, should Brook's career turn out as many hope. For what it is worth, there is little to choose between their records at Brook's age of 27. Pietersen's Test average, which ended at 47.28 after his 104 Tests, stood at 49.55 at this stage. Brook's is 53.08, though Pietersen had two more centuries. Pietersen has the edge in one-day international cricket - an average of 47.87 and six centuries to Brook's 37.43 and three - but the Yorkshireman's second T20 century, hit on the south coast, is two more than Pietersen ever managed. Perhaps where Brook lags behind is those iconic moments. While Brook's Test best 317 on a road in Pakistan is a mark few can match, Pietersen's 158 at The Oval won England the 2005 Ashes in his fifth Test - the first of his four Ashes series wins. Eighteen months later he made the same score against Australia in Adelaide against Shane Warne and Glenn McGrath. Brook's best Ashes score remains 85. He is yet to win the urn. This video can not be played Brook & Baker shine as England crush Sri Lanka Still, Brook's latest T20 display showed the company he could one day keep. A more mature batting style in whites this summer has also been noted. Since being promoted to number three in England's T20 side at the World Cup earlier this year, Brook averages 95.20 at a strike-rate of 200.84. He has scored 288 runs in the format since he was last dismissed. "Harry Brook has today cemented himself as maybe the best all-format batter in the world," said former England bowler Steven Finn. "[Australia's] Travis Head would be up there and so would [India's] Shubman Gill. "Brook is lacking a Test century in the last year or so but he still averages 42 in that time. "When you see the versatility of what he did today and the tempo he has played, he's a mighty special player." Brook also has one clear advantage in any debate for the maverick position in a fantasy England XI. Overlooked for the Test captaincy, Brook has won 18 of his past 20 T20s as England captain. Pietersen's stint as England skipper lasted only five months. Sri Lanka's target was always likely to be beyond them but, even without Jofra Archer or Sam Curran, England ruthlessly dismissed their opponents for 135 in Southampton. Brook oversaw young seamer Sonny Baker's best performance in an England shirt. He took 3-12 in four overs. "I thought the performance tonight was near perfect," he said afterwards. England want Pietersen to help them win the 50-over World Cup next year. He will do well to improve on this. title: 'One in, one out' scheme costs £56,000 per person returned to France, home secretary says
description: Shabana Mahmood says the policy has been "difficult" to scale up and the numbers involved are still "relatively small".
body: The government's "one in, one out" scheme to send migrants who cross the Channel back to France costs on average £56,000 per person, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has said. That is higher than the Home Office's estimated average cost for enforced migrant returns of £48,800. The deal allows the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who are believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain. Mahmood told MPs the policy had been "difficult" to scale up and the numbers involved were still "relatively small". She said the total number deported under the scheme since it began in August 2025 was around 1,400. Asked by the Conservative MP Robbie Moore whether she thought the scheme had been a success, Mahmood said: "On its own terms, can you prove the concept that such a deal is viable, that you can get returns off and up and running - yes. "It's not been without its challenges, obviously. The numbers are still relatively small. "What has been more operationally difficult is to scale up very large numbers of removals every week into the French system." She said the UN and other agencies had reported that some migrants were not getting on small boats because they thought there was a chance they could be accepted under the "one in, one out" scheme. Fall in small boats down to law enforcement, agency says Fourteen go on trial over deadliest Channel small boats disaster Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats The agreement aims to deter people from making the dangerous journey across the Channel. It had been due to end in June 2026 but has now been extended into October. Asked how much the policy was costing, Mahmood said she thought it was "about £56,000" but added that she would write to the committee to confirm the figure. So far this year, 17,425 people have arrived in the UK by small boat, a 44% decrease compared to the same time last year. The National Crime Agency has said law enforcement had been a "key factor" in getting the numbers down. It also said supply chains for small boats had been disrupted by the war in the Middle East. Between 1 January and 14 September 2026, a total of 17,425 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 44% on the same period the previous year. These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020. Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered. Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026. Boats that arrived in the UK from 15 September 2025 to 14 September 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021. Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN). When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers. People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026. In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office. Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year. There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit. The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known. title: Search launched for boy, 3, missing at playground
description: Police carry out door-to-door inquiries in Brantham and a helicopter has been seen circling the area.
body: Noah was wearing a white Bluey T-shirt, shorts and white trainers at the time he went missing, police said Emergency services are looking for a three-year-old boy who went missing at a playground. The boy, named only as Noah, was with a relative at the small park at Merriam Close in Brantham, but "became separated" from them as they left at about 15:00 BST, Suffolk Police said. The toddler, described as white, with curly ginger hair, was reported to have run down a nearby alleyway towards a newbuild housing estate. Residents have been asked to check their gardens, sheds and outbuildings by the police. A helicopter has been pictured flying over the scene, which is near the estuary of the River Stour and close to the Essex border. Police have cordoned off the area surrounding the park Passengers on trains between Manningtree and Ipswich have been told their services must run at a reduced speed due to the searches. Rescue teams have been carrying out door-to-door inquiries in the area. Searches are continuing into the night in Brantham BBC reporter Zoie O'Brien, who is at the scene, says more than 100 people have joined the searches on Tuesday evening. She said the helicopter appeared to be circling above fields and a wooded area behind the housing estate. Posting on its Facebook page, Suffolk Police said: "It is overwhelming to read the support people are offering." A spokesperson for HM Coastguard said: "We are assisting Suffolk Constabulary with an incident at Brantham by sending an HM Coastguard helicopter and Coastguard Rescue Teams from Felixstowe and Holbrook." title: Letby hospital consultant says inquiry makes for grim reading
description: The Thirlwall Inquiry finds some babies could have been saved if action had been taken earlier.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Former consultant hopes Letby inquiry recommendations will prevent deaths happening again One of the senior doctors who tried to raise concerns about Lucy Letby with hospital managers has told the BBC the final inquiry report makes for "grim reading". Consultant paediatrician Dr John Gibbs worked at the Countess of Chester Hospital throughout the period in 2015 to 2016 when Letby murdered seven babies, and attempted to murder seven more, on the neonatal unit. He said that he accepted that consultants must bear "collective" responsibility for some of the failings identified in the report. "I wish we consultants had been brave enough to follow our suspicions and escalate things to the police earlier," he told the BBC. "When I say, 'we consultants', I am responsible as well and if my other consultant colleagues didn't go to the police, I should have." The Thirlwall Inquiry was launched after former nurse Letby was convicted in 2023, and the final report was published on Tuesday. In the 822-page document, Lady Justice Thirlwall described "a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital". The report found that the police "should have been notified earlier than they were" and that hospital managers had repeatedly dismissed consultants' concerns. Reflecting on the findings for the first time, Gibbs said: "I wasn't expecting it to be an easy read and it certainly isn't. I'd imagine it's an extremely difficult read for the parents of the babies concerned. "As I admitted when I appeared before the inquiry to give evidence, I feel we failed the babies and I apologise to the families for that." Gibbs, who began working in Chester in 1994 and is now retired, agreed with the report's finding that hospital executives had multiple opportunities to act and potentially save babies' lives while the deaths were happening. "But it was during that 11 months after Lucy Letby was moved off the unit, before the police got involved, that it was a very difficult atmosphere, very tense, very stressful dealing with the managers," he added. Managers "were determined to ensure that we accepted Lucy Letby had been wrongly suspected of doing any harm," the senior doctor explained. He also spoke of the failures of his and his wider team, specifically referencing a doctor who disregarded blood test results that suggested a baby had been poisoned with insulin in August 2015. While one of his colleagues had missed the relevance of the results when they came back from the lab, it had been a collective team failure, Dr Gibbs concluded. "Others of us were on call and covering the neonatal unit over the next week or two before the baby moved out of the unit. We all had the opportunity to review the notes." The inquiry looked into the actions of managers at the hospital where Lucy Letby worked Letby is serving 15 whole-life terms for the murders and has twice been denied permission to appeal against her convictions. The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), an independent body set up to examine potential miscarriages of justice, is currently reviewing her convictions. In the weeks and months after Letby was convicted, questions about the case arose in the form of online conspiracy theories and discourse from serious academics, including medical experts and statisticians. Gibbs said that the continuing support for Letby had taken a toll on him and other consultants, and that claims she had been wrongly convicted were "frustrating and difficult" to hear. "I particularly find the misinformation that's on the internet is difficult to deal with," he said. He added: "I haven't changed my mind that I think Lucy Letby is guilty." However, he emphasised that, because of the "calibre of some of the people who've raised concerns", it is "important" that the evidence used to convict Letby is being examined by the CCRC. title: Trump says Kennedy Center will shutter 'immediately', as judge rules his name must stay off building
description: The ruling came as the centre's Trump-appointed board was reportedly scheduled to vote on closing it for two years.
body: This video can not be played Watch: President Trump's name added to facade of Kennedy Center The Kennedy Center board has voted to close the performing arts centre for two years, just as a US judge blocked it from adding President Donald Trump's name back to the building. In May, the same judge ordered the removal of Trump's name and blocked its temporary closure for proposed renovations The board, which is chaired by Trump and comprises his cabinet members and allies, approved a resolution in August that called for the inscription "Renovated and Restored by President Donald J. Trump" to be added to the venue. Trump announced the addition of his name to the institution, among other rebranding measures across the nation's capital, last year. The judge's written order came less than an hour before the centre's board voted on the closure. This was the third time it has approved closing the centre since February, amid legal challenges to Trump's work to take greater control of the institution, and there is a chance the centre's doors could stay open despite Tuesday's vote. Trump wrote on Truth Social that the board voted "almost unanimously" to close the storied venue "for safety reasons" and to begin the process of reconstruction. While the closing "will take place immediately", Trump said renovations cannot begin until the court "rules on the Board's approved name" and vowed to take the case to the Supreme Court if it is a "negative" ruling. He added that the US Department of Justice will ask for an expedited appeal and that he had raised $17m for the centre to "keep it afloat". Also in August, the board approved a resolution to rename the campus the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza" if $100m was raised for the renovations. Congress approved more than $250m for renovations in Trump's massive spending legislation known as "The Big Beautiful Bill". However, the centre cannot close unless the federal judge, Christopher Cooper, lifts a temporary block that he put in place in May requiring it to stay open while a lawsuit brought by board member Joyce Beatty goes ahead. When he put the block in place, Cooper said the board could return and request it be lifted, provided it had come to the decision to close "in a prudent manner". The justice department is expected to make that request by Friday, CNN reported. Beatty, an Ohio congresswoman and Democrat, said on Tuesday that the centre had planned to undergo phased renovations for years while still putting on some performances, instead of fully shuttering. She blamed Trump's attempt to rename the centre for the departure of donors, patrons, and artists. "Donald Trump only cares about the Kennedy Center for his vanity," she said in a statement to the BBC. "That is wrong and it is a breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee. Congress established the Kennedy Center as a living memorial to President Kennedy, and I am proud to defend this cherished institution." In February 2025, Trump replaced several trustees on the board, which then decided in December to rename the institution. New lettering bearing Trump's full name was affixed to the centre's front portico the following day. The changes, including the re-naming, were followed by cancellations by artists booked at the venue and a drop in ticket sales. Most of the legal challenges to Trump's changes focus on the fact that Congress established the centre as a memorial to President John F Kennedy, who was assassinated in 1963. While detractors say that means Congress must approve changes to the memorial, Trump has argued that he has the power to act. "Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing," Judge Cooper said in a written order issued on Tuesday. The judge said the board's proposal to add language to the existing name of the centre and its surrounding campus "bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted". That statute was a decision by the US legislative body to memorialise Kennedy, "and no one else, at the Center bearing his name", the order said. On Sunday, the Kennedy Center administration told its board that the arts institution was on the brink of bankruptcy, the Washington Post, external reported. The administration said it was in a "precarious fiscal position" and would not be able to support its payroll obligations and routine maintenance contracts "within a matter of weeks". The current leadership at the centre has said the building is unsafe for continued occupancy, pointing to part of the ceiling falling in earlier this month. But others close to the centre dispute that it must be closed. The Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment. Earlier on Tuesday, Trump said on Truth Social that the Kennedy Center is "in a virtual state of collapse". He described dire conditions and railed against the "hostile and conflicted" judge for keeping it open despite not having performances scheduled or "people that would have the Courage to even go in". title: Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI?
description: The BBC's North America editor Sarah Smith looks at why the US president is contradicting AI leaders, who are calling for the technology's development to be slowed down.
body: This video can not be played The head of AI company Anthropic has called for the pace of development of artificial intelligence models to slow down and to be closely monitored, and other AI leaders have joined him. But US President Donald Trump is opposing calls to regulate the technology. The BBC's North America editor Sarah Smith explains the two reasons that are keeping the US president from regulating AI. title: Thirteenth Met Police officer sacked after Charing Cross Panorama film
description: PC Mason O'Connor is dismissed after a hearing found he had breached standards of professional behaviour, the Met said.
body: A Panorama journalist spent seven months filming undercover at the central London police station last year. Another Metropolitan Police officer has been dismissed following BBC Panorama's undercover investigation into the force's Charing Cross station. PC Mason O'Connor was sacked after a hearing found he had breached standards of professional behaviour, relating to a comment he made to a female colleague, the Met said. O'Connor was reported to a "proactive wider investigation" following the broadcast of the programme in October 2025 and he has become the 13th officer to be sacked since then, the force added. Other officers who were covertly filmed for the documentary were seen calling for immigrants to be shot, boasting about excessive use of force and joking about rape and sexual assault. Met Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said at the time that this behaviour was "totally unacceptable". A disciplinary panel on Tuesday heard that O'Connor had, while off-duty at a pub, told a female colleague that he hoped she would be raped on her way home. He was found to have breached standards of professional behaviour for authority, respect and courtesy, equality and diversity, and discreditable conduct, the Met said. As well as the 13 officers the Met has sacked, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said another two men, both former officers, had also been found to have committed gross misconduct. The policing watchdog added it was still investigating the conduct of a further 15 officers or police staff in the wake of the Panorama film. "This is one of our largest ever investigations in terms of the number of officers investigated," said the IOPC's Amanda Rowe. "The sheer number of fast-tracked disciplinary proceedings show how seriously the IOPC and the Met, who held the misconduct hearings, are treating this matter," she added. Panorama: Undercover in the Police Secret filming by Panorama reveals evidence of racism, misogyny and officers revelling in the use of force at one of London’s busiest police stations, Charing Cross. O'Connor's dismissal comes weeks after his colleague, PC Lloyd Hunter, was also dismissed from the force. In unaired footage from Panorama which was shared with the IOPC, Hunter was seen saying he enjoyed "Tasering people" and that he hated homeless people. Met Cmdr Simon Messinger said the pair had been fired for their "appalling comments and attitudes", adding that the force would continue to support the IOPC investigation. "I hope this sends a very clear message about the standards we expect from all our officers and the Met's determination to improve our culture across the organisation," he said. title: Southport attack victims, survivors and families hit by data breach
description: The Ministry of Justice says sensitive and personal data was accessed in a limited number of cases.
body: The MoJ says sensitive and personal data was accessed in a limited number of cases An investigation is under way after a data breach involving court files relating to victims, survivors and families of the Southport attack, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has said. The unauthorised access by courts staff was identified during a review of the department's digital systems. For a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data, but the MOJ did not state how many people were affected. An spokesperson said the MOJ was "appalled", but there was no evidence personal data had been shared with third parties and the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) had been told. The prime minister has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee the matter. An MOJ source said its independent Data Protection Officer had assessed the matter and found that, for a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms. Those affected are being notified directly, the department said. An MOJ spokesperson said: "We are appalled that this happened and recognise the distress it will have caused victims, survivors, and their families. "We apologise to those affected - unauthorised access to court files is completely unacceptable. "This is now being investigated urgently, and the prime minister has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee this. "All wrongdoing will be met with extremely firm action." The department said it was also reviewing policies and frameworks covering staff conduct, acceptable use and its fraud response plan. HM Courts and Tribunals Service and HM Prison and Probation Service are also investigating. Bebe King, six, Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, were murdered during the attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in Southport on 29 July 2024. Ten others were physically injured. The data breach disclosure follows separate cases involving inappropriate or potentially inappropriate access to the medical records of people involved in the attack. In May, a Liverpool hospital trust admitted nearly 50 staff had inappropriately accessed the records of some victims treated at Aintree Hospital. North West Ambulance Service later began investigating potential inappropriate access to patient records by some of its staff. title: US borrowing costs hit highest level since 2007
description: The effective interest rate on US government bonds over 10 years, known as the 10-year Treasury yield, has risen as high as 5.04% but has eased back since.
body: US government borrowing costs climbed to their highest level since 2007 after a jump in oil prices further fuelled concerns about inflation. The effective interest rate on US government bonds over 10 years, known as the 10-year Treasury yield, rose as high as 5.04% but has eased back since. Government bond yields have been rising globally for months, driven by worries that inflation caused by the oil price surge since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran will lead to higher interest rates. The US has been buying back bonds back in a bid to drive the Treasury yield down, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling the intervention "successful". The global benchmark wholesale oil price rose to over $109 a barrel on Tuesday, up from around $86 at the end of August, after renewed concerns about Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil following rising tensions in the region. Investors are anticipating the US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will raise interest rates to combat the inflation caused by higher oil prices. However, US President Donald Trump opposes a rate hike, having long argued lower rates are great for boosting the economy. He fell out with Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell over his decision not to cut rates. Higher interest rates and inflation tend to drive up the yields bond investors demand on government borrowing. Bond yields can also be a sign of how much faith investors have in a given government, with a higher yield reflecting less confidence. Competition for debt from artificial intelligence (AI) firms is also driving up yields. Tech giants are borrowing massive piles of cash to build huge data centres. This raises interest rates on tech firm's debt which increases government bond yields in response. Carol Schleif, chief market strategist at BMO Wealth Management, said bond markets had been signalling for weeks that higher interest rates may be needed. While the rise in borrowing costs has been "orderly" this year, rather than sudden, she said rates could remain elevated if geopolitical tensions and high energy prices remain "front and center". title: Tech Life
description: What should children learn in a world transformed by artificial intelligence?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·15 Sep 2026,·26 mins Available for over a year AI is developing rapidly. What should parents and children make of it all? And how can young people navigate school and future careers when AI is becoming increasingly important? We speak to an expert who has written a new book about these issues. Also this week: we find out how one piece of health tech is helping scientists uncover disease-fighting data in menstrual blood. And satellite imaging is used by conservationists in Indonesia to protect the habitat of a rare species of orangutan. title: Tuchel regrets not eating Azteca turf after win over Mexico
description: Thomas Tuchel regrets not eating any of the grass at the Azteca Stadium after England's epic World Cup win against Mexico.
body: Tuchel led England to the semi-finals in his first major tournament in charge Thomas Tuchel regrets not eating any of the grass at the Azteca Stadium after England's World Cup win against Mexico. His Three Lions beat the co-hosts 3-2 in the last-16 tie in July, despite playing much of the second half with 10 men following Jarell Quansah's red card. England went on to reach the semi-finals, where they lost to Argentina, before beating France in the Bronze medal match for third place. Tuchel, though, made a bizarre admission during an interview with Daniel Sturridge for the FA's forthcoming feature 'Reflections: England's World Cup Journey'. He said: "I texted a friend after the match and I just wrote, 'I regret that I didn't eat some grass after the match to keep something from this in my body forever'. That was the feeling. That was the moment. This video can not be played England win thriller against Mexico to reach quarter-finals England's victory was only the third time Mexico had tasted defeat at the stadium in 90 competitive matches. Tuchel described it as one of the highlights of the campaign and hailed the "huge bond" within the camp, especially the reaction to Jordan Henderson's tournament-ending injury after falling over an advertising hoarding while celebrating the Azteca success. "This game had so much of what you could wish for," added the German. "If you needed any proof of what it meant to these players and how they were with each other, it was the moment Jordan fell over and broke his arm. "Within a second, the players were there. Every single player was there stopping the celebrations, building a shield, protecting Jordan, not going anywhere, in full empathy. It was so special." England are next in action against World Cup winners Spain on 26 September in their 2026-27 Uefa Nations League opener, with the 2028 European Championships also on Tuchel's radar. Confident of ending England's wait for a first senior men's trophy since 1966, he believed their World Cup run not only cemented his relationship with the squad - "it feels like they are my players now" - but also represented "something to build on". Tuchel added: "I'm very excited. I think we got another step closer and I think we're there." title: Turner Prize winner's new vision for hometown
description: Keith Tyson said he hopes to create a space for exhibitions, education and community engagement.
body: The former Mercedes-Benz garage is to be converted into a space for exhibitions, education and community engagement A Turner Prize-winning artist has revealed plans to transform a former car showroom near where he grew up, into a centre for art and learning. Keith Tyson has bought the former Mercedes-Benz garage on Princes Street in Ulverston, where he said he hopes to create a space for exhibitions, education and community engagement. The privately funded project aims to give young people opportunities to experience art after Tyson's own artistic education was shaped by local libraries growing up. He said "there were no galleries for miles around" so he thought this could be a chance to "give young people in the community an opportunity to see and learn about art" in a way that he never had. Tyson said the project had potential to become an arts destination for the north Tyson said the project was still in its early stages but he was "excited by the building's potential to become an arts destination" for the north. The artist, who won the Turner Prize in 2002, said he hoped the centre would include exhibition space, a reference library and programmes for schools and the wider community. "We're still in the very early stages of the project, but I'm really excited about this beautiful building's potential to become an arts destination, celebrating creativity, especially in the north, and supporting learning and engagement through exhibitions, education, and other resources," he said. Among those pleased to see the plans come forward is Adrian Newnham, Tyson's former art teacher at George Romney School in Dalton. Newnham said: "I was Keith's art teacher when he was 10-years-old. I told him he had a talent and I kept his artwork. "When he won the Turner Prize I showed him the artwork I'd kept. He thanked me in the programme when he won. He was a highly talented lad." Newham said Ulverston already had a strong cultural identity and believed the project could strengthen it further. "Ulverston is a festival town with a cultural buzz. Hopefully, his venture will raise the artistic status of the town even more," he added. Tyson became known for work combining art, science and technology across a range of media, including painting, sculpture and installation. title: Nigeria arrests alleged Mexican drug kingpin at international airport
description: Arturo Carrera Loaiza denies allegations he was involved in meth production, the Nigerian authorities say.
body: Arturo Carrera Loaiza has denied allegations that he was involved in methamphetamine production, Nigeria's drugs control authority says An alleged Mexican drug kingpin was arrested in Nigeria last month as he tried to leave the country, the drug enforcement authority has just revealed. That arrest resulted in the discovery of a suspected industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory - the third such find allegedly linked to Mexicans in four months. When Arturo Carrera Loaiza, 40, was detained at Lagos international airport, officials allegedly found digital images of him wearing what they believed to be a laboratory coat alongside equipment consistent with meth production. The pictures' location data led officers to a property in Ebonyi state, where they said chemicals and drug-making equipment were found. Loaiza has denied involvement in methamphetamine production and said he had been invited to Nigeria by a local contact for a restaurant business venture, according to a statement from the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA). How Mexican drug cartels have outsourced meth labs to Nigeria The agency's investigators found a CCTV memory card at the suspected laboratory in Ebonyi with footage from the property showing someone who looked like Loaiza wearing a blue laboratory coat. A Nigerian man was also identified directing people as they removed chemicals and equipment from the site. NDLEA chairman Gen Mohamed Buba Marwa said further intelligence led officers to an isolated house in a neighbouring community, where they recovered chemicals, dehydrators, condensers, a reaction pot, weighing scales, mixers, drums, gas burners and a sieve containing traces of methamphetamine. No estimate has yet been given for how much methamphetamine the alleged laboratory was capable of producing. The NDLEA released pictures of some of the things investigators found after raiding a suspected laboratory Investigators have alleged that Loaiza had recruited and brought a fellow Mexican to work at another suspected methamphetamine laboratory hidden in a forest in Oyo state, which was raided in June. Four Nigerians were also arrested after the raid. A month earlier, NDLEA officers arrested three Mexican nationals and seven Nigerians at what the agency described as an industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory hidden in a forest in another part of the country. Marwa said the operations showed international criminal groups were attempting to establish drug-production facilities in Nigeria's forests and rural communities. "Nigeria will not be allowed to become a haven for transnational drug cartels seeking to relocate their laboratories from other jurisdictions into our forests and rural communities", he said. The NDLEA said its investigation into the network is ongoing, including into those it believes financed or helped facilitate the operations in Nigeria. Unlike plant-based drugs, such as cocaine or heroin, which can only be grown and processed in certain places, a synthetic drug like meth can be produced anywhere with the right chemicals and expertise, making it easier for organised crime groups to quickly scale up production. West Africa poses numerous attractive benefits to Mexican syndicates, starting with swathes of forested land which serves well for secluded production sites. title: South African president vows justice as more women's bodies found near Johannesburg
description: Police have not linked the deaths to a serial killer but are investigating this possibility.
body: Elizabeth Moselakgomo's body was found on Saturday three days after she went missing during a routine jog South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" in finding those behind the killings of several women in and around the town of Kempton Park, north-east of Johannesburg, over the last two months. Another body was discovered on Tuesday morning and police say their investigation now includes the deaths of seven women most of whom have been found either partially or fully naked. "These incidents are causing fear and uncertainty in our communities, and especially among women," the president said. Police say they are not linking the deaths to a serial killer at this stage, but are investigating the possibility that a group of people is behind the killings. "[It] could be that it's a copycat crime that is happening right here but so far, no linkages as yet," police spokesperson Brig Athlenda Mathe said. One arrest has been made in connection with the discovery of the first body. The person is still in police custody. So far only two of the seven women have been identified. South Africa calls gender violence a national disaster after protests I built this 'AI aunt' for women after family tragedy in South Africa On Monday, police said that one of them was Elizabeth Moselakgomo, a runner whose disappearance last week sparked a frantic and public search for her. President Ramaphosa said he had directed that the cases be prioritised: "Our law enforcement agencies are working urgently to establish the facts, keep communities safe and bring the perpetrator or perpetrators to justice." South Africa experiences some of the world's highest levels of gender-based violence (GBV), with the rate at which women are killed five times higher than the global average, according to UN Women. The discoveries of the bodies have sparked outrage and fear across the country, with many criticising the authorities for failing to adequately protect women. Moselakgomo was identified by her relatives on Monday after her body was discovered on Saturday. It was the 38-year-old's young daughter who raised the alarm about her disappearance after she failed to return from her daily run last Wednesday. The body of the first woman was found in mid-July, the second in late August - the others were discovered this month, two in the last two days. On Tuesday, police said that the body of woman found on 7 September in a town nearby Kempton Park was also being included - bringing the total number of bodies being investigated to seven. "After noticing that there are bodies being picked up, we went back to our police stations… and unfortunately it came to light that a body of a female in her late 20s was observed in a river next to a mall," Maj-Gen Fred Kekana, acting police chief for Gauteng province, said at a briefing. Police have urged women in the Kempton Park area - which is by South Africa's main international airport - to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas". South Africa's Commission for Gender Equality urged residents of Kempton Park to work with the police to find the perpetrators. "These deaths are indicative that women in South Africa continue to face environments in which their ordinary freedom of movement can become a matter of life and death," it said. "Women should be able to run, walk to work, use public transport, return home, visit friends and participate in community life without having to calculate whether an ordinary activity could place their lives at risk." title: Ministers could force phone companies to add 'anti-theft protections'
description: The government could legislate to force firms to act if there is not a drop in phone thefts, the policing minister says.
body: Purple pavement markings in Oxford Street in August 2025 warned pedestrians of mobile phone theives Policing minister Sarah Jones has said that unless there is a drop in the number of mobile phones being stolen, the government could force phone companies to add "anti-theft protections" to their products. Writing to the Science and Technology Committee,, external she said the Home Office had so far chosen to work collaboratively with the tech giants to reduce thefts, but would consider legislation if she did not see progress. Phone thefts have been particularly prevalent in London, but numbers are starting to fall. Samsung said it was "fully committed" to protecting its customers and had "worked quickly to make a significant amount of security enhancements to help address this issue". Apple said it had "led the industry in protections and features to deter theft". Jones' letter comes months after Met Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley urged the government to compel all phone companies to make stolen devices "unusable bricks". Speaking to the BBC in June, Sir Mark said the market for stolen phones relied "on the fact that security hasn't been good enough on these devices" allowing stolen phones to be reset using "dodgy software" and resold as new. However, he added that Apple - the biggest seller of mobile phones in the UK - had been able to "crack" the engineering problem and since then the "vast majority" of phones stolen in London had not been reset. "That shows they are right and their security is making a difference," he said. In her letter - published last week and first reported by The Times, external - Jones said: "My overriding objective remains to see that the proportion of stolen devices being reused/reactivated reducing, as this should support a reduction in the number of devices being stolen. "If there is no means to reactivate a stolen device, its value is significantly reduced, alongside the incentive to steal it." Make stolen phones unusable, Met Police urges tech giants Met gets more e-motorbikes to fight phone thefts Tech bosses could stop mobile phone theft, say MPs She acknowledged that work between the Met Police and phone companies had been "constructive" and that the results were "promising", pointing to data showing there were 14,700 mobile phone thefts in London in the past year - a fall of 18.7%. Jones said the fall was "welcome" but added that she wanted further reductions and that officials in her department were developing new laws that could introduce a "technical standard for anti-theft protections". She noted the government had so far opted for a collaborative approach with the companies but warned: "If at any point I am not satisfied about the pace of progress in the context of efforts being made, we will legislate." The Science and Technology Committee held an inquiry into mobile phone thefts last year. At one hearing, Conservative MP Kit Malthouse asked if companies were "dragging their feet" due to "a very strong commercial incentive". "The fact that £50m-worth of phones are stolen in London every year means that, if that stopped, £50m of sales would be depressed," he said. The companies giving evidence to the committee rejected the suggestion they were profiting from phone thefts. Responding to Jones' letter, a spokesperson for Samsung said: "We recognise how distressing phone theft can be and have worked quickly to make a significant amount of security enhancements to help address this issue, completing several requests from both the Home Office and the Met Police over the last 18 months to demonstrate how seriously we take this issue. "We have a number of features that would render phones unusable if stolen, including Factory Reset Protection, which restricts a device when a factory reset is attempted and requires authentication with the previous Google account. "Additional One UI anti-theft features include both Identity Check, which requires biometric authentication for any sensitive security setting changes, and Security Delay, which activates a one hour delay if there is an unauthorised attempt to reset biometric data." In a statement, Apple UK said: "We take all threats against our users very seriously and are in close contact with the Met Police and Home Office to ensure they are aware of our initiatives to combat phone theft and are dedicated to supporting their efforts to defeat the criminals targeting our users. "Apple has led the industry in protections and features to deter theft, including Find My, Lost Mode, Stolen Device Protection, Activation Lock, and Activation Lock for parts, which minimise the incentives for thieves to target Apple devices and help protect our users and their data even if their device is stolen, and we are committed to our innovation in this area."
