title: VAR did not even consider if Fernandez was offside - Webb
description: Referees' chief Howard Webb has admitted that the video assistant referee (VAR) did not even consider whether Enzo Fernandez was offside for Erling Haaland's controversial winner in Sunday's Manchester derby.
body: This video can not be played Refereeing decisions were 'baffling' - Rooney Referees' chief Howard Webb has admitted that the video assistant referee (VAR) did not even consider whether Enzo Fernandez was offside for Erling Haaland's controversial winner in Sunday's Manchester derby. Speaking on the first edition of 'Match Officials Mic'd Up' of the season, Webb said he was "really disappointed" with the error made by the VAR Matt Donohue and his assistant Blake Antrobus. Manchester City striker Haaland thought he had scored the only goal of the game at Old Trafford in the 60th minute, but it was disallowed on the field for offside. A VAR review found Haaland was just onside, and the goal was awarded. But it immediately became apparent that the video officials had made an error in failing to identify an offside offence by Fernandez, diving at the ball in a central position and interfering with opponents. "I was really disappointed with this outcome. We all are," said Webb, Premier League refereeing body Pro Ref's chief refereeing officer. "None more so than the officials themselves. They take a lot of personal pride in what they do and they're obviously hurting now, having fallen short in this situation. "They'll not be officiating again until after the international break." Manchester City won 1-0 at Old Trafford after a VAR mistake handed them the only goal of the game One of the questions which many supporters have asked is how the VAR team could possibly reach the conclusion that Fernandez did not commit an offside offence. Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez initially appeared to be marking Haaland, but then moved over to try and intercept the ball from Fernandez. This left Haaland free at the back post to finish. Former England striker and BBC Sport pundit Wayne Rooney said on Match of the Day that "to not see that and recognise that Enzo Fernandez was in an offside position...anyone who has played the game at any level understands that and to get it so wrong is baffling." The Mic'd Up audio revealed that at no stage did Donohue or Antrobus consider whether Fernandez was offside because, as Webb describes, they got "tunnel vision" over Haaland. The semi-automated offside technology told the VAR that Haaland was three centimetres onside from Josko Gvardiol's cross. But the video officials then only checked for a touch by Fernandez which would have created a new offside phase against the Norway international. This is the transcript, which was dominated by the VAR with the AVAR only making one minor contribution. At the start of the season, video officials were encouraged to be more efficient with their checks and not take an excessive amount of time. Comments made by the technical replay operator have been omitted. VAR: Checking the on-field decision of offside against Haaland. The VAR and the semi-automated offside operator then discuss the decision against Haaland and he is shown to be onside. VAR: Okay, so he's onside. So we now need to check the full APP (attacking phase). VAR speaking to referee Michael Oliver: Michael, Haaland's in an onside position, but I need to check the full APP now. Stand by. VAR: Haaland's clearly onside. Roll it all the way through. Roll it all the way through. VAR: Let's go, let's go, let's go, let's go. VAR: Go back just to check Ndiaye wasn't on offside. Sorry, my apologies. When it's flicked. Quick, quick, quick, quick. Yes, fine. Go, go, go, go, go. VAR: Let's go. It should be a goal. All the way into the back of the net now. VAR: Quick, quick, quick, quick! Go, go, go, go, go! This is the point at which Gvardiol crosses the ball into the box. VAR: Deflection. Onside. No touch there [by Fernandez]. Confirm, no touch. There wasn't. VAR: Just something [camera angle] tighter. Clear gap. VAR: There's not a touch, is there [by Fernandez]? There's no touch. VAR: Another angle. Roll it through, roll it through, roll it through. VAR to referee: Michael, confirming that you need to change your decision to goal. Haaland is in onside position. Final decision is goal. Check complete. Webb said that the VAR failed to assess how Fernandez found himself in that position, so did not consider the offside offence. "The VAR gets super-focused on Haaland," said Webb, who had already been in contact with Manchester United to share the VAR audio and video. "He establishes he's onside, he thinks that's a good goal. "He doesn't truly evaluate the full impact of Fernandez's position. He has a look to see if he touches the ball, because then that relates to potentially knocking it to Haaland, who goes on to score." Webb highlighted the lack of assistance from Antrobus as the assistant VAR, who did not offer a meaningful contribution during the review. "In that moment, he [Donohue] gets tunnel vision," Webb said. "It's down to the rest of his team to pull him out of that tunnel, and unfortunately, that didn't happen on this occasion. "What looks like a really clear subjective offside, because Fernandez doesn't touch the ball but still clearly impacts [the play but] doesn't get identified, and it's really disappointing. "This goal should've been disallowed. And highly unfortunately, it wasn't, and we'll review it, reflect upon it, and try to take the learning forward to prevent this unusual type of error from happening again." There was also much debate over the red card shown to Phil Foden in the 23th minute for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes, largely because there was no sanction against the Portuguese midfielder for a similar act. Webb backed the decision to dismiss Foden, but said the action by Fernandes did not meet the threshold for violent conduct. "I agree with the red card for Phil Foden," said Webb. title: Warning of space arms race as US confirms weapons in Earth's orbit
description: The US has confirmed it deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit, the first time it has acknowledged such offensive capabilities.
body: This video can not be played The US has confirmed it deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit, the first time it has acknowledged such offensive capabilities. Russia and China responded by warning of an arms race in space. However, according to the BBC's Defence correspondent Jonathan Beale, this is already happening. Details of how the weapon operates have not been disclosed by US officials. Warning of space arms race as US confirms weapons in Earth's orbit. title: 'My son was failed' - Noah Donohoe inquest finds tunnel errors possibly contributed to death
description: The nine jury members, who had 10 questions to answer, returned their verdict on Tuesday at the end of an inquest which began in January.
body: Noah Donohoe was found dead almost a week after he went missing in June 2020 The jury in the Noah Donohoe inquest has found it was possible, but not probable, that failings by the Department of Infrastructure (DfI) over the tunnel in which he was found dead contributed to his death. The jury found that the DfI had failed to identify a hazard at the site, which it maintains, and that there was no warning sign. They also found numerous failings in the Police Service of Northern Ireland's (PSNI's) investigation but that these did not contribute to the 14-year-old's death. Noah's mother, Fiona Donohoe, said he had been failed by both the department and police while the family's solicitor said she had suffered "indignity after indignity". Fiona Donohoe, Noah's mum, outside Belfast Coroner's Court on Tuesday The PSNI said it was a "complex and challenging investigation which garnered huge public and media interest, along with widespread speculation" and the eventual outcome was "devastating". Assistant Chief Constable Davy Beck said there was "no action that police could have taken" that would have prevented Noah Donohoe's death. He added it was important to reflect on any learnings and "ensure they are applied in the future". He said: "Noah was a child with his whole life ahead of him. His death is a tragedy, and our thoughts remain firmly with his family and those who loved him." Infrastructure Minister Liz Kimmins said Fiona and Noah's family are at the forefront of her mind. "As Minister, I will make sure the department does everything it needs to ensure all lessons are learned." As it happened: Noah Donohoe inquest jury finds failings by department officials possibly contributed to death Noah went missing on Sunday, 21 June 2020, after leaving his south Belfast home on his bicycle, sparking a huge search across the city. He was found dead six days later in the water tunnel in the north of the city, which leads into Belfast Lough, with the cause of death found to be drowning. Eyewitnesses, who were the last to see him in the vicinity of the tunnel, reported that he was naked. The incident sparked widespread speculation about what happened to Noah, with his family launching a high-profile campaign. There was no conclusive evidence at the inquest about why Noah was without his possessions and all the clothing he was wearing when he was last seen alive. There was also no evidence about any physical interaction between the schoolboy and anyone else during his journey from his south Belfast to the north. An inquest verdict at last - but many mysteries remain about Noah Donohoe's death Noah Donohoe inquest jury finds failings by department officials possibly contributed to death How the Noah Donohoe inquest came about after six years of delays The inquest began in January, five-and-a-half years after the death of the schoolboy and following numerous delays. Juries do not typically sit for inquests but can be summoned in certain circumstances. Noah's family had requested a jury be used, with a coroner, in 2022, agreeing that it was "desirable". The jury deliberated for five days in total - first, for three days in June and July before the case was adjourned due to the holiday plans of some jurors; and then on Monday and Tuesday when it resumed. The nine members - seven men and two women - had 10 questions to answer and delivered a unanimous verdict, as required by the coroners' court. Those questions included asking the jury to summarise the scenario in which Noah's death occurred; to explain why he behaved how he did after he left the house; to say when and where he died; and whether the Department of Infrastructure's management of the tunnel or the PSNI's investigation contributed to his death. In answering those findings, the jury found: That Noah died between 19:00 BST and midnight on 21 June 2020, the day he disappeared, in the lower reaches of a culvert That there was insufficient evidence to reach a conclusion as to explain why Noah behaved how he did when he left his home That it was possible, but not probable, that any error by the Department of Infrastructure in how it managed the tunnel contributed to his death That it was not possible any PSNI error contributed to his death But there were 13 failings related to the PSNI and DfI that impacted the inquest's ability to reach a conclusion on aspects relevant to his death The finding of the time period of Noah's death means that Noah could have died before his mother raised the alarm with the police at approximately 21.45 on 21 June 2020, or within an approximate two-hour period after he was reported missing. There was no indication at that stage of Noah's precise location, other than he had left his home off the Lower Ormeau Road to travel across the city to Cave Hill. The initial police searches that evening and night covered a wide area of Belfast based on the limed information available at that stage about Noah's intended journey from the south to the north of the city. Noah's presence in the Northwood Road area was not known until the following day. Why was the Noah Donohoe inquest held with a jury? During the inquest, the Department for Infrastructure was criticised about aspects of its maintenance of the tunnel in terms of public access and safety. The PSNI was also strongly criticised by the legal team representing Fiona Donohoe. During the inquest, the police chief in charge of the investigation apologised to the boy's mother for "missed" investigative opportunities. Before the jury resumed their deliberations on Monday 14 September, the coroner Mr Justice Rooney announced that one juror, who had taken part in the previous phase of the deliberations, had been discharged. No reason was given in public for the man's removal from the process. Fiona Donohoe has led a high-profile campaign for answers around her son's deat

title: Baby 'cot cams' plan after inquiry finds Lucy Letby crimes could have been prevented
description: Plans will be "urgently" developed for live-streaming cameras after an inquiry report into Lucy Letby's crimes.
body: Lucy Letby was convicted of the murders of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has said officials will "urgently develop plans" to introduce live-streaming cameras on England's baby wards after an inquiry into Lucy Letby's murders and attempted murders. Inquiry chair Lady Justice Thirlwall called for a series of urgent reforms to neonatal units, including CCTV for all cots and incubators, and restricting access to insulin. Thirlwall said some of the babies Letby killed could have been saved if managers at the Countess of Chester Hospital had taken action earlier. Her report criticises a "complete failure to protect babies" and a "profound failure of management, governance and safeguarding" at the hospital. Thirlwall said this was because "no one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt." She said it would never be possible to know exactly how many lives could have been saved if safeguarding procedures had been properly followed. This video can not be played Watch: The key findings and recommendations from the Lucy Letby report Thirlwall added her report described "dysfunctional management and governance, a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians, and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding". Letby was moved on to administrative duties in July 2016 after consultants expressed concerns about her to the hospital's executive team. But the inquiry has found that alarm bells should have been sounded earlier. There were several "missed opportunities" for hospital bosses to intervene, the report said, including when three babies died in one cluster in June 2015. Parents of the babies were "kept in the dark for years" over the concerns that their babies might have been deliberately harmed, the inquiry also found. Thirlwall described the lack of consideration shown to parents as "reprehensible". Repeatedly untruthful, callous and quiet - what we learned about Lucy Letby from inquiry report Key findings from Lucy Letby Thirlwall Inquiry As it happened: Read the live coverage from the Thirlwall Inquiry The report is highly critical of managers at the Countess of Chester Hospital. Hospital bosses carried out a number of internal reviews into increased infant mortality in 2015 and 2016, but did not invite Cheshire Police to investigate until May 2017. Letby remained on site until her arrest more than a year later. Cheshire Police said it would "carefully review" the contents of the report and "fully consider" relevant recommendations. Thirlwall said the hospital's former chief executive Tony Chambers behaved in a "dictatorial manner" and had "intended" to obstruct a police investigation into deaths on the ward. Chambers, along with director of nursing and head of safeguarding Alison Kelly and medical director Ian Harvey, "dismissed the idea that Letby was deliberately harming babies", Thirlwall added. But whether these managers believed Letby was harming babies or not was "irrelevant", Thirlwall said, adding that action should have been taken as soon as concerns were raised. In a joint statement, Chambers, Kelly and Harvey along with the hospital's former HR director Sue Hodkinson said: "We are carefully reviewing the Thirlwall report and its recommendations. "Given that there are a number of investigations under way, and that the work of the Criminal Cases Review Commission has not yet completed, it would be inappropriate for us to offer any further comment at this time. "Our thoughts remain with the families affected by the tragic events that took place at the Countess of Chester Hospital." This video can not be played Letby "should have been removed from the ward," Thirlwall says The inquiry also condemned wider NHS culture, finding evidence of "toxic negativity" that discouraged whistleblowers. The chair of the British Medical Association said on Tuesday that whistleblowers in the NHS "deserve strong protections, and the inquiry makes it clear that these doctors did not get them". Regulator the Care Quality Commission (CQC) was also criticised, with the report saying it did not show enough curiosity to look beyond what it was being told by the Countess of Chester Hospital. Responding to the report, the CQC's chief inspector of hospitals said "crucial information" was not shared by the Countess of Chester, but that the commission as a regulator did not take a "sufficiently investigative and inquiring" approach. Dr Tony Onon said the regulator had since changed its approach to assessments. Lucy Letby has twice been denied permission to appeal against her convictions Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said she was "profoundly sorry" on behalf of the government for the failures set out in the report. She said she had asked officials to "urgently develop plans" for cot-cams in neonatal units, and that the government would consider Thirlwall's other recommendations in full. Cooper also said she expected NHS leaders across the country to uphold their safeguarding responsibilities. She plans to meet Thirlwall, who made 17 recommendations including restricting access to insulin, later this week to discuss the inquiry in more detail. Thirlwall was clear that her inquiry was not an investigation into Letby's guilt, which some supporters of the jailed nurse still contest. A number of Letby supporters gathered outside Liverpool Town Hall to voice their concerns over her conviction, calling for her release, before Thirlwall delivered her inquiry findings. Now 36, Letby is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more. She was convicted in 2023 and has been denied permission to appeal against her convictions twice. title: Villagers voting on independence over asylum plans
description: One voter in the symbolic referendum in Piddington, Oxfordshire, calls it the "Battle of Britain".
body: Villagers in Piddington are voting over whether the village should leave the UK Voters in a small village are heading to the polls for an independence vote over government plans to house asylum seekers at a nearby former Ministry of Defence (MoD) site. The residents of Piddington, in Oxfordshire, are voting over Home Office proposals to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at MoD Bicester. The symbolic referendum on whether to leave the UK has been organised by the local parish council, with polling taking place between 07:00 and 19:00 BST. Ahead of the vote, council chair Tim McNally said the government "does not want to engage with villagers concerns". "They actually have played every possible trick in the book to avoid engagement," he said. "If we've got to do something, it has to be proportionate, and that is not proportionate - that is us having to assimilate into them, not them assimilating into us." Tim McNally is chair of Piddington Parish Council A spokesperson for the prime minister told the BBC that the government was "working to fairly house asylum seekers across the country". They said the government was "engaging with local authorities to reduce the impact on communities and we've saved taxpayers more than £1bn on asylum support costs since the election". "The Home Office has submitted an application to obtain planning permission to use the Bicester site for asylum accommodation, but it remains the case that no final decision has been taken on the site's future use," the spokesperson added. But speaking outside Piddington village hall on Tuesday, one villager said when it came to holding the vote: "We wouldn't do this lightly." "I think when you see a village like this feeling that they need to hold a referendum it sends a really powerful message to the government that we're being ignored and disenfranchised," he told the BBC. This video can not be played The BBC's Jamie Morris explained in July what the vote is and what it could mean Tuesday's ballot paper asked residents to respond either yes or no to the statement: "I support Piddington seeking to secede from the United Kingdom and pursuing self-determination." The outcome of the referendum, which holds no legal weight and bares a resemblance to the classic Ealing comedy Passport to Pimlico, is expected to be announced on Wednesday morning. Having just cast his vote, Herbert Owen said the referendum was not "just about Piddington". "It means everything our grandparents, our parents fought for – today is the Battle of Britain," he said. His wife, Jennifer Owen, said: "We can't actually leave the United Kingdom, but it just brings things out in the open more for the country as a whole." She added that the proposals would "change our lives forever" if it were to go ahead. The government plans to provide accommodation for up to 1,256 men at the site near Bicester The Home Office first announced its plans for MoD Bicester in June. "We are working to fairly house asylum seekers across the country, moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation," a spokesperson said. This, the spokesperson said, included former military sites that were "designed to be self-contained to reduce impact on the local community". But that is not how many people in Piddington see the proposals, with 96% of voters supporting a referendum on independence from the UK in a vote held on 4 July - a date synonymous with another declaration of independence from the British state. Last week, ahead of Tuesday's vote, 133 women from the village wrote to every female Member of Parliament saying "life as we know it will be destroyed" if the plans succeed. "We will not feel safe walking our streets. We are already living in fear," they wrote. An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence. The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026. About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) or former military sites. The government has pledged to stop the use of hotels by 2029. More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland. A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive Type in a postcode or the name of a local council below to see how many asylum seekers are housed in the area A total of 85,891 people applied for asylum in the UK from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 21% on the same period in the previous year. Most people who arrive in the UK by small boat claim asylum, but they were only 40% of all asylum seekers from July 2025 to June 2026. The rest include people who arrived by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and applied for asylum while holding, or just after holding, a valid visa. It can take years for the government to decide whether someone should be granted asylum. In June 2026, 40,168 people - across 32,401 asylum applications - were waiting for an initial decision. The number of people awaiting an initial decision was down by 56% on the previous year. As of June 2026, a further 90,341 refused asylum applications were part of a second backlog, waiting the outcome of an appeal in the courts. This was up by 51% on the previous year. Together, these initial decision and appeal cases form the government’s total asylum applications backlog, which it has pledged to clear. Refugee status was granted in about 38% of asylum decisions made by the Home Office from July 2025 to June 2026. title: Letby failings go beyond one hospital - the whole system has been found lacking
description: Inquiry chair Lady Justice Thirlwall set out how the culture of the health system created the conditions that enabled poor care and criminality.
body: The public inquiry into the Lucy Letby case may have reserved the strongest criticism for the Countess of Chester Hospital and its management, but there are big questions for the wider NHS to answer too. The Thirlwall inquiry's final report said there was a "complete failure" to protect babies on the neonatal unit where Letby murdered seven and attempted to murder seven more. But a third of the report was given over to the wider role played by the health system in England - and make no mistake, it was found lacking. Across more than 200 pages, inquiry chair Lady Justice Thirlwall set out how the culture of the health system created the conditions that enable poor care - or in this case criminality - to go unchecked for so long. The failures encompass everything from regulation and employment practices to the way the NHS and government struggle to learn the lessons of the past. They have prompted Health Secretary Yvette Cooper to say she "will not hesitate" to hold the system to account at every level. She has promised to set up a hub to track the progress on implementing the inquiry's recommendations and pointed to the creation of a new maternity and neonatal commissioner post as a sign of her commitment to improving standards. "This must be a turning point for the NHS," she told the House of Commons when responding to the publication of the report. So what needs to change? The inquiry said NHS managers have become pre-occupied with avoiding blame, leading to an "over-focus on process and reputation management". One witness described this as "blame engineering", with the inquiry concluding this was a key characteristic in the way Countess of Chester bosses approached the Letby case with the report describing it at one point as an "exercise in spin". Letby is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more. She was convicted in 2023 and has twice been denied permission to appeal against her convictions This approach to management means raising the alarm becomes difficult - a concern that has been repeated again and again in inquiries into other scandals. There have been plenty of initiatives to address this over the years. In the last decade, this has taken the form of the Freedom to Speak Up programme with each NHS organisation having a "guardian" whose job is it to support staff who want to issue a concern. But in a number of places the initiative has become a "box ticking" exercise The result? A "toxic negativity" persists around whistleblowing with staff discouraged from speaking out, the inquiry said. This view is supported by the NHS staff survey which showed a declining confidence in speaking out. There is, the Thirlwall inquiry said, a consistent inability within the NHS to deal with poor performance. Failing managers will be moved, often with the active assistance of NHS England, in a process referred to as rehabilitation, the inquiry heard. Countess of Chester chief executive Tony Chambers referred to it as "the donkey sanctuary". The report even noted how some failing managers receive pay offs and move on elsewhere "with few questions asked" as NHS trusts worry about the threat of employment tribunals. While there are many excellent managers in the NHS, profound change is needed in the way the NHS deals with those who fail, the inquiry added. The government wants to bring in a barring service, but the inquiry warned this will be undermined if the system continues to turn a blind eye like it does. In its closing submission to the inquiry, NHS England said it would never "knowingly" move "bad apples" into other jobs, but did believe moving capable senior managers could help improve services where improvement was needed as well as develop individuals. Key findings from Lucy Letby Thirlwall Inquiry Regulation has also been found lacking. The Care Quality Commission (CQC) inspected the Countess of Chester in February 2016 - Letby carried on attacking babies until June of that year. Key information was withheld from inspectors, but the regulator was criticised for not showing enough curiosity to look beyond what they were being told. Only a year before, the CQC had been warned by another inquiry into baby deaths at Morecambe Bay NHS Trust that it needed to take a tougher approach. Weaknesses have persisted since, the Thirwall inquiry said. An independent review in 2024 warned the ability of the CQC to spot poor performance was by that point deteriorating. The CQC has released a statement acknowledging it was not investigative or inquiring enough in 2016, but said it had since strengthened its approach. Meanwhile, the Nursing and Midwifey Council, which regulates nurses, was also told it should have been more curious - it renewed Letby's registration at a time when she was not permitted to work on a ward and a police investigation was taking place. It has offered an apology in response to the criticisms. As part of its work, the inquiry looked at why the lessons of previous inquiries have not been learned. There has been countless inquiries dating back 30 years, with thousands of recommendations made. But the Thirwall inquiry said most of these have not been implemented - and, when they have, it has taken too long or progress has not been tracked. It blamed, among other things, a lack of political will and disruption caused by repeated structural reorganisations. This had a potentially significant impact in the Letby case, the inquiry suggested. It cited the medical examiner system, whereby an independent doctor looks into deaths that are not reviewed by a coroner so that the cause of death is not down to the doctor involved in the patients care to sign off. The move was recommended in 2003 by the inquiry into the Harold Shipman murders and called for again a decade later as part of the inquiry into the failings at Mid Staffordshire NHS Trust. But it took until 2024 for it to be introduced. Former health secretary Sir Je

title: Dan Thomas resigns as Reform Wales leader after arrest on suspicion of assault
description: Thomas said he has done nothing wrong as Gwent Police confirms arrest on suspicion of assault.
body: Reform UK's Dan Thomas has quit as the party's Welsh leader Reform UK's Dan Thomas has quit as the party's Welsh leader, after he was arrested on Sunday of suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. Gwent Police confirmed that a 45-year-old man from Aberbargoed, in Caerphilly, was bailed pending further enquiries. In a statement issued by his party, the Member of the Senedd for Casnewydd Islwyn said he was "standing down" from his position due to personal reasons. He said he had been "released without charge" and had "done nothing wrong". Thomas was appointed Welsh party leader by Nigel Farage in February. Plaid Cymru, which runs the Welsh government, said: "Reform UK is descending into chaos." Thomas did not take part in First Minister's Questions earlier today. He was first elected to the Senedd in the elections in May, where his party went from having two politicians in Cardiff Bay to 34. Reform came second behind Plaid Cymru in the vote, with Thomas becoming leader of the opposition in the Senedd. Thomas said: "It has been the honour of my life to have been the leader of Reform Wales and see this party go from zero to 34 elected members and become the largest opposition group in Welsh history. "With deep regret, I am now standing down from this position due to personal reasons. "Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge." He added: "I will continue to serve my constituents in Casnewydd Islwyn and will fully back whoever the group selects as its next leader." The news came on the same day that Reform MS Sarah Cooper-Lesadd defected to Plaid Cymru. Who is Reform UK's Welsh leader Dan Thomas? Dan Thomas: The ex-London council leader in charge of big Senedd opposition group Gwent Police said: "On Sunday 13 September a 45-year-old man, from the Aberbargoed area, was arrested on suspicion of assault and engaging in controlling/coercive behaviour. "He has been bailed pending further enquiries." Plaid Cymru Senedd group chair, Marc Jones, said: "Reform UK is descending into chaos." He added: "Sarah Cooper-Lesadd's decision to leave and join Plaid Cymru says it all - Reform is interested in division and headlines, not governing Wales." Ken Skates, leader of Welsh Labour, told the Press Association: "This is quite incredible news and many questions will need to be answered. "Dan Thomas was a personal pick by Nigel Farage and this will surely demonstrate the appalling judgement of the Reform UK leader." Mims Davies, the Conservative Shadow Secretary of State for Wales said: "Reform are hitting the news for all the wrong reasons - massive crypto donations, on top of the jailing of Nathan Gill for pro-Russian bribery. "All this raises serious and deep questions about Reform's judgement and leadership at every level." Welsh Liberal Democrat Leader, Jane Dodds, said: "The wheels are rapidly coming off Reform in Wales and the entire country." Dan Thomas was appointed by Nigel Farage in February, and appeared with him during the Senedd election campaign Thomas grew up in Blackwood in the south Wales valleys. He said in February that both his grandfather and great-grandfather were miners, and he had "fond memories" of growing up in Wales - but left when he became an adult because "good opportunities" there were "few and far between". He worked in financial services in London and became a councillor, and later Conservative leader, at Barnet council in the north of the capital. During this time Thomas stood for the Conservatives in the Islwyn constituency at the 2010 and 2017 general elections, coming second to Labour's Chris Evans on both occasions. Thomas then led Barnet council from 2019 to 2022, eventually becoming opposition leader after Labour won the local election there until May 2024. In June 2025 Thomas defected from the Conservatives to Reform, and at the end of the year resigned from the council. Local media quoted him saying he moved away from Barnet so that he and his wife could raise their young sons in the countryside and live closer to their families in south Wales. title: GPS tracking of bailed suspects to start next year, says Swinney
description: A pilot scheme in Tayside, Central and Fife is expected to start in 2027, the first minister has announced.
body: John Swinney met domestic abuse survivors in Holyrood ahead of a debate on tackling violence against women GPS tracking of people on bail, including those suspected of domestic abuse, is to begin in parts of central Scotland next year, John Swinney has confirmed. The first minister updated parliament on his plans for a pilot scheme in Tayside, Fife and Central during a Scottish Parliament debate on tackling violence against women. It came after he spoke to domestic abuse survivors and relatives of victims at a Holyrood meeting hosted by Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay. The government has been criticised over the slow rollout of GPS equipment, which is used far less in Scotland than in some other countries. Swinney announced plans for the GPS tracking pilot in the annual programme for government, external earlier this month. He confirmed to parliament on Tuesday that regulations to launch the pilot scheme in the Tayside, Central and Fife sheriffdoms - to be led by Sheriff Principal Gillian Anne Wade KC - would be laid before the October recess, and that ministers were aiming to begin the rollout next year. He insisted the pilot would be "subject to robust local arrangements" to ensure public safety. Pilot tracking domestic abuse suspects to begin in 2027 - Swinney tells Holyrood Calls for GPS monitoring of domestic abuse suspects after murder We saw signs of domestic abuse, but we didn't know how to protect Stacy The programme for government also included plans to make permanent a £2m fund providing practical and financial support to women and children escaping abusive partners. The government has further vowed multi-year funding for charities that deliver crisis support to women and girls. And it announced plans to recognise misogyny as a "distinct form of prejudice and abuse", alongside a public health campaign to target toxic male behaviour. However, the brother of a woman murdered by her estranged husband in Renfrewshire this year said previously that the proposals were not "anywhere near good enough". Stacy Hunter, 35, was killed by Jim Mair, 43, at her home near Houston in July while he was on bail for attacking her. His body was found nearby. Sean Hunter - who attended the meeting at Holyrood before the debate - has called for immediate action to prevent further deaths. Sean Hunter has called for immediate action to protect victims following the murder of his sister Stacy Speaking to BBC Scotland News the day after his sister would have celebrated her 36th birthday, he said GPS monitoring would "absolutely make a difference". But he called for authorities to consider more specific offences when making decisions about bailing domestic abuse suspects. "There's so much - strangulation, attempted murder - that's going on that's being overlooked because it's coming under this umbrella of domestic violence," Sean said. "That shouldn't be the case. "When these people commit these crimes they need to be looked at for what they are and kept from harming more people." Liz Shanks, whose former partner Chris Forrest was jailed in 2022 for attacking her over a three-year period, also spoke to the first minister at Holyrood. The campaigner said survivors and victims had been let down by the justice system and that the meeting must not be a "media stunt". She called for reforms to tackle domestic abuse, and warned that victims may be reluctant to come forward if they do not feel the justice system is dealing with the issue robustly. Domestic abuse survivor Liz Shanks says the meeting with the first minister must not be a "media stunt" Opening the debate, Swinney said the so-called "manosphere" and extreme pornography had "warped views and attitudes in disturbing and profoundly harmful ways". He vowed the government would take a "public health preventative approach" to tackle violence against women and push for stronger regulations of social media sites. The first minister told MSPs: "We will work to build a Scotland where everyone is safe, accepted, and respected, where women and girls live free from all forms of violence, abuse and exploitation, and where all are free of the attitudes and stereotypes that perpetuate inequality." However, opposition MSPs noted a 14% annual increase in domestic abuse charges last year. Scottish Labour's Jackie Baillie agreed with Swinney's "sincere" willingness to tackle violence against women, but said a "multi-faceted" approach was required, including a misogyny reduction unit, extra work in schools and investment in police. Conservative MSP Stephen Kerr warned that GPS tracking was a "technology, not necessarily a solution", calling for more investment in community resources. Scottish Tory leader Russell Findlay praised the "extraordinary bravery" of survivors but urged ministers to strengthen bail laws and "robustly enforce breaches". He also called for ministers to scrap "ludicrous" sentencing guidelines that encourage rehabilitation rather than jail terms for under-25s. Scottish Green co-leader Ross Greer said extra measures were required to ensure that education in schools about harmful attitudes was being consistently delivered, and raised concerns about low reporting rates. He also called for men to "contest" harmful views expressed by their peers. Liberal Democrat MSP Yi-pei Chou Turvey called for the government to immediately launch its plans for special sexual offences court. Swinney told MSPs ministers planned to provide funding for the scheme in the next financial year. Reform UK Scotland's Amanda Lindsay questioned whether "some groups" committed more sexual crimes than others, calling for more data on offences against women and girls. In Scotland, electronic tagging has mainly relied on older radio frequency (RF) equipment which is focused on home curfews or detention. These devices are linked to a receiver in the offender's home and cannot track movements away from the property. In 201

title: Ed Sheeran says it was 'not my decision' to drop Macklemore from tour
description: The star says tour promoters took the decision, after Macklemore made pro-Palestinian statements on stage.
body: Ed Sheeran and Macklemore, pictured in 2014, have been friends for 13 years, the rapper said in his statement on Monday Ed Sheeran has posted a long statement on Instagram, saying it was not his decision to drop Macklemore from his current US tour. The US rapper - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - was ejected from the line-up after making pro-Palestinian statements at two dates in New Jersey. His comments drew criticism from Jewish groups, after which some venues put pressure on the tour promoters to have him removed from the line-up. In his statement, external, Sheeran said he had spoken with the venues "at length all week to try and build a bridge" - but the promoters, Messina Touring Group, had ultimately decided to remove Macklemore from the bill. "Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," he wrote. "Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me. "I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living." The star also attempted to explain his decision not to become embroiled in political issues. "I am not complicit," he wrote. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care. "Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own, personal way." He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds. "Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes. "However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: Peace. "I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change." The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine." He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which is dedicated to pro-Palestinian protestors at Columbia University and condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen. Some of the audience cheered - but there was almost immediate criticism online. The Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour; while the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda - a claim that was amplified by the pop star Pink, who reposted it on Instagram. The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience. "Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten. Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law. The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage. During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. After days of press coverage, Macklemore announced on Monday that he had been dropped from the line-up. In a statement on Instagram, he said the boycott had been organised by Robert Kraft - the billionaire owner of the Gilette Stadium in Massachusetts. Kraft - who once hired Ed Sheeran to play at his wedding - confirmed he'd made the decision to bar Macklemore, saying his venue would not "provide a platform for hate speech," accusing the rapper of "a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric". "I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said. However, he did not address the claim that he'd asked other venues to put pressure on the tour. Tour promoter, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone magazine that it had been told by venues that they would not allow Macklemore to perform, "which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans." In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran had been put in, but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance. "Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote. He also emphasised that, although he was only able to complete two shows on the tour, if his words succeeded in "turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I've ever been on." title: Repeatedly untruthful, callous and quiet: What we learned about Letby from inquiry report
description: The report has shed more details on Lucy Letby - the most prolific child killer in British legal history.
body: Letby was convicted of the murders of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others New details have emerged about Lucy Letby, the killer neonatal nurse whose name can evoke both staunch support and unequivocal disgust. Letby, now 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms after being convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, including one baby whom she tried to murder twice. In a lengthy report, published by Lady Justice Thirlwall earlier, she described how Letby was "repeatedly untruthful in her dealings with friends and colleagues" and "her inappropriate and callous nature was noted by patients and colleagues". The Thirlwall Inquiry was set up to look into what happened at the Countess of Chester Hospital between 2015 and 2016, while Letby was working as a nurse in the neonatal unit. The public inquiry was not tasked with examining Letby's guilt. Instead, it investigated how concerns about the neonatal nurse were handled by the hospital and whether action could have been taken sooner to stop her. Thirlwall found the deaths and near-deaths of some babies who were attacked by Letby could have been prevented if safeguarding practices had been followed. But the inquiry report has also shed more details on Letby herself - the most prolific child killer in British legal history, who has always maintained her innocence. The inquiry looked into the actions of managers at the hospital where Lucy Letby worked Following the death of Baby C, Letby was observed helping to make a memory box with another nurse on the neonatal unit for the infant's parents. However, Letby had not been asked to carry out this task and was "supposed to be somewhere else and was repeatedly told to be looking after a different child," Baby C's mother told the inquiry. Thirlwall noted how "nothing was done about Letby repeatedly ignoring directions from the shift leader and leaving the other child [who she was designated to care for] to intervene with Baby C". She found Letby ignored management instructions when she disliked them and had shouted at her manager. Baby 'cot cams' plan after inquiry finds Lucy Letby crimes could have been prevented Key findings from Lucy Letby Thirlwall Inquiry As it happened: Read the live coverage from the Thirlwall Inquiry Letby was also repeatedly untruthful in her dealing with friends and colleagues, the inquiry found. This included lying about the reaction of the father of Baby A and Baby B, following Baby A's death. In a message to a colleague, Letby said: "Dad was on the floor crying saying please don't take our baby away when I took [Baby A] to the mortuary, it's heart-breaking." Thirlwall said the mother of Baby A and Baby B, who Letby attempted to murder, was clear that this was not true and did not happen. "In her view, Letby's messages were 'attention seeking' and a 'red flag'. I agree," Thirlwall noted in the inquiry report. Throughout her training as a nurse, feedback of Letby's performance in the work place was mixed, the inquiry found. Early assessments pointed out areas for improvements, particularly in relation to enthusiasm, communication with families and drug calculations. But academically her personal tutor reported no concerns. While during her second and third years, she was described by a nurse as "one of the best students she had mentored", however, during her final placement "significant concerns were raised". The deputy ward manager described Letby as "quiet, withdrawn and struggled to build relationships with children, families and colleagues". Letby failed a mid-year assessment and observed structured clinical examination (OSCE). She later passed this examination and qualified as a registered children's nurse in 2011. But Thirlwall outlined how Letby's "inappropriate and callous behaviour" was noted by patients and colleagues. The mother, for example, of Baby E, who Letby murdered, and Baby F, who she attempted to kill, told the inquiry she had had "two thriving little boys" but that "in the space of a couple of hours it had all been taken". After Baby E's death, the mother told the inquiry she found her baby was still in his incubator, and she asked Letby why. "You haven't told us to take him," she says Letby told her. Thirlwall said Letby's remark to a "bereaved mother was shockingly cold and unfeeling." Lady Justice Thirlwall oversaw the inquiry into the Lucy Letby case The inquiry also found how Letby falsified Baby E's medical record. Thirlwall noted how Letby omitted Baby E's distress and the blood on the baby's mouth from her notes. She also failed to record the baby's mother's visit to the neonatal unit. While in Letby's care, Baby J was also found covered in their own faeces, leading to a complaint by the baby's parents. Letby, from Hereford, who maintains her innocence, has twice been denied permission in 2024 to appeal against her convictions. The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which investigates potential miscarriages of justice, is considering evidence presented on her behalf by an international panel of medics, who claim poor medical care and natural causes were the reasons for the babies collapsing. A number of Letby supporters gathered outside Liverpool Town Hall to voice their concerns over her conviction, calling for her release, before Thirlwall delivered her inquiry findings. title: Iran war has led to US munitions shortfalls, Pentagon inspector confirms
description: The inspector also found a bottleneck in resupply, despite President Donald Trump's claims that US supplies are "virtually limitless".
body: US Patriot air defence systems, seen here at Raytheon headquarters in Massachusetts, have been heavily used in the Iran war. The US defence department's inspector general says the war with Iran has led to "shortfalls" in munitions and a bottleneck in resupply, contradicting President Donald Trump who has repeatly denied the US is facing shortages. Trump has claimed US munitions supplies are "virtually unlimited" and said reporting otherwise is "fake news". But the independent watchdog said the US spent more than $22 billion on munitions from February through June, leading to "strategic inventory shortfalls". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment about the discrepancy. The new report provides a first-of-its-kind, independent glimpse into US weapons stockpiles, data that is typically classified. Previous estimates have painted a dire picture of the US shortages. Over the course of the war, US forces have expended vast quantities of both long-range ground attack systems and the air and missile defences used to intercept incoming Iranian attacks. A late July estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, or CSIS, found that stocks of some interceptors - such as the Patriot missile and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD - were significantly depleted, in some cases by more than half. The inspector general's report did not disclose exactly how many of the weapons remain. It did, however, note the inventory shortfalls and reveal "industrial base bottlenecks" for munitions resupply. The report added that the defence department is now working to "streamline procurement processes and production lead times" to address the shortages and "respond rapidly to a contingency". Trump and other administration officials have sought to cast reports of shortages as false and "treasonous". In a 4 August X post, for example, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth described news reporting on the shortages as "not true". And in a lengthy Truth Social post on 3 September, Trump claimed that the US had "virtually unlimited" amounts of ammunition and is "stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen". The watchdog's report also notes that equipment losses have totaled $3.7bn, with other $7.4bn in other expenditures. Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war from 28 Feb to 30 Jun. Among the losses have been four F-15e fighter jets, a highly advanced F-35 Joint Strike Fighter and 30 MQ-9 drones destroyed in "various circumstances". When US and Israeli strikes began, Trump repeatedly said that the conflict would be over within weeks. More recently, he said the conflict might not end until "right after" the November midterm elections in the US. Polls show that the war is unpopular among Americans. One Reuters/Ipsos poll released in early September found that only 23% of Americans - and only half of Republicans - believe the US to be in a stronger position with Iran compared with before hostilities broke out. As the US pauses the war with Iran, is Trump really running out of weapons? title: The key findings and recommendations from the Lucy Letby inquiry
description: Former nurse Lucy Letby is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more.
body: This video can not be played A report into how serial killer Lucy Letby was able to murder seven babies at the Countess of Chester Hospital has found that some deaths could have been prevented. Letby is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more. She was convicted in 2023 and has twice been denied permission to appeal against her convictions. Responding to the report, the hospital says it is "sorry for the events that occurred in 2015 and 2016", and it's a "different organisation today with new leadership, stronger governance and safety processes". Letby maintains her innocence. Protesters supporting Letby could be seen and heard near Liverpool Town Hall as the report was published. BBC correspondent Judy Moritz reports from Liverpool. title: British woman abducted in Malawi, police say
description: The mother of two young children was kidnapped in the middle of the day in the main city, Blantyre.
body: Police have offered a reward for details that could help find Nusrat Osman Police in Malawi are investigating the kidnapping of a British national who was abducted in the southern African nation's main city, Blantyre. Nusrat Osman, 47, was seized at around 12:30 local time on Friday by four men who had been travelling in a grey Nissan Dualis, according to a police statement. The authorities have offered a reward of more than $17,000 (£12,600) for "credible information" that could lead to the rescue of the mother of two young children and the prosecution of the perpetrators. Osman was reported to have been working for a local auditing firm. A Malawi news outlet reported that Osman's husband was in anguish about the disappearance. "I don't know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor and I have no issues with anyone," he was quoted by Nyasa Times as saying. Police said the motive behind the abduction was unknown and that so far the kidnappers have not contacted the victim's family or the authorities. BBC News has contacted the UK Foreign Office for comment. Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent. title: An inquest verdict at last - but many mysteries remain about Noah Donohoe's death
description: After years of delay, the jury has reached a verdict but some questions remain unanswered over what happened to the 14-year-old.
body: It's been more than six years since teenager Noah Donohoe was found dead 600m into a freezing underground water tunnel in Belfast. His death – and the speculation over what happened to him in the week between his daylight disappearance and the discovery of his body – became a huge news story that provoked countless unanswered questions. Now, after an inquest and months of exhaustive hearings and long deliberations by a jury, there is a verdict – but much is still unknown about what happened to Noah. Why, the night before he disappeared, did he leave his home in the middle of the rain-soaked night? Where did he go? Why did he come back 34 minutes later, as documented by CCTV, barefoot? LIVE: Noah Donohoe inquest jury finds failings by department officials possibly contributed to death Hours later, on Sunday 21 June 2020, he left the south Belfast home he shared with his mother for the final time. Why did he leave and go to an unfamiliar part of north Belfast? Why was the teenager naked when he was last seen in the area of the water tunnel entrance? And what might have been if he had seen the social media message sent him by one of two friends he planned to meet in north Belfast telling him their plans were cancelled? An autopsy found Noah had died from drowning, with the tunnel he was found in heading towards Belfast Lough and its tides. Now, after years of delays, a jury has found that it was possible, but not probable, that failings by the Department of Infrastructure over the tunnel in which he was found contribute to his death. They also found 13 failings by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) but that these did not in any way contribute to the 14-year-old's death. Having spent months in court following all the evidence, it was clearly not an easy process for the men and women of the jury. They heard from dozens of witnesses and received voluminous amounts of official and expert documentation. This week they deliberated on Monday and Tuesday. But it came more than two months after the inquest was dramatically adjourned in the early hours after three days of deliberations did not lead to a verdict. While these findings will help his family and the community to understand a little bit more about what happened after Noah went missing, there is no certainty about many of the mysteries surrounding some of the unusual and extraordinary events in the lead-up to his disappearance. It may be that there will never be definitive answers to many of those questions. But one thing was very clear at the inquest – there was no evidence of any physical interaction between Noah and anyone else during his final bicycle ride from his home to north Belfast. During his summing up, the coroner Mr Justice Rooney ruled out several possibilities, including drugs, foul play, suicide, or a psychotic experience. He told the jury before they began deliberations that there was no evidence to support such findings and their verdict had to be based "solely on the evidence you have heard and seen in this court". There was no evidence of drugs in Noah's body during the postmortem. Noah's journey from south to north Belfast was captured on a series of CCTV cameras But the inquest heard expert witness evidence that explained, in some cases, drugs can degrade in a body after a few days, so the possibility of drugs having been in his system "cannot be completely excluded". The inquest also heard no evidence of third-party involvement or any link to loyalist paramilitaries, at odds with years of endless social media speculation that sometimes leaned into conspiracies. Many phases of the inquest focused on next-of-kin concerns about the Police Service of Northern Ireland's (PSNI) investigation into Noah's disappearance, as well as public safety around the tunnel system where Noah's body was found. The tunnel is maintained by Stormont's Department for Infrastructure. The police accepted that they had missed some investigative opportunities and have since apologised to Noah's mum, Fiona Donohoe. And throughout it all, day after day, Fiona Donohoe was a constant, quietly dignified presence, often sitting alone in a corner at the back of the Coroner's Court. Noah's mother Fiona Donohoe attended every day of the inquest The road to the inquest was a long one for Fiona and her family. They mounted a high-profile public campaign around Noah's death, with dozens of supporters soon growing to hundreds and then thousands under the umbrella name of Noah's Army. They took their campaign to the streets in the form of cavalcades around Belfast, as well as protests at Stormont's parliament buildings and at PSNI headquarters. Frustration at the police came to a head in August 2022, when thousands of campaigners protested outside Belfast City Hall over the PSNI's decision to seek a Public Interest Immunity (PII) certificate in relation to the case. As the years went on, the pre-inquest process was plagued by delays. The original coroner in the case stepped aside and the Donohoe family made a request for the inquest to be heard in front of a jury. Finally, five-and-a-half years after he disappeared, the inquest into Noah's death began in January 2026. Questions about Noah's mindset and behavioural changes before he went missing featured prominently at the inquest. The inquest heard how the schoolboy went out onto streets beside his home in the Holylands area of Belfast in the early hours of the day of his disappearance. Shortly after 03:30 BST, Noah walked out of his home into the rain. He was alone and wearing light summer clothing, including shorts and flip flops. He also had a set of headphones. CCTV footage showed Noah leaving his home in the early hours of the day of his disappearance During the following 34 minutes, some of his movements were captured on CCTV as he walked along nearby streets barefoot. title: Former England footballer Raheem Sterling admits dangerous driving on motorway before crash
description: The former England winger crashed a Lamborghini into motorway barriers in May.
body: Sterling made eight appearances for Feyenoord earlier this year Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has admitted dangerous driving on a motorway after he crashed a Lamborghini into a metal gate in May. The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis. Sterling, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court, was arrested after crashing near the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of 28 May. Sterling has 82 England caps, the last of which was won at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. The former England winger pleaded guilty to driving a Lamborghini Urus dangerously on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road before he crashed. The court heard he strayed into the central reservation of the motorway and crashed into a metal gate in a layby on the A327. He was in possession of six canisters of nitrous oxide, a Class C drug. Sterling arrived at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Tuesday afternoon Witnesses described seeing a Lamborghini driver inhaling from a white balloon. Fiona Jennings, who saw the vehicle on the M3 at 8:45 BST, said she looked across and thought that an airbag had inflated, but then realised it was an inflated balloon. She told police she saw "absolutely horrendous driving" as the Lamborghini swerved in and out of lanes. Hampshire Police previously said the charges followed a single-vehicle collision near the M3 southbound, near the Minley interchange. The force said no other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported. Sterling most recently played for Feyenoord in the Dutch Eredivisie, having left Chelsea in January, but made just eight appearances in the Netherlands. In four years at Chelsea - including a season-long loan at Arsenal - he made 59 league appearances after signing from Manchester City in 2022. With City he won four Premier League titles, having started his senior career with Liverpool before moving to Manchester in 2015. He is currently without a club. In the 2021 Queen's Birthday Honours, Sterling was made an MBE for services to racial equality in sport. Sterling will appear in court on 25 November, and has been disqualified from driving in the interim. title: Ash from Mount Etna grounds flights at Sicily airport
description: All flights are suspended from one of Italy's busiest airports until Tuesday night.
body: All flights have been suspended from one of Italy's busiest airports because of volcanic ash released from nearby Mount Etna. It is the second time in recent months that Catania International Airport, on the island of Sicily, has stopped flights due to emissions from Etna, which is Europe's tallest active volcano and erupts frequently. Airport officials said arrivals and departures, which were first halted on Monday, would be suspended until 22:00 (20:00 GMT) on Tuesday. Ongoing activity at Etna prompted the INGV Etneo Observatory to issue a red aviation alert on Monday. In a statement on its website on Tuesday, Catania - Italy's fifth-busiest airport by passenger traffic - said further updates would follow. It also advised passengers due to fly from Catania to check with their airline for updates before travelling to the airport. Catania, which usually serves about 12 million passengers each year, was closed for almost a week during the peak summer season last month because of volcanic activity. There have been calls for the airport to shut and other facilities in Sicily to be expanded because of its proximity to Etna. The volcano, which stands at 3,324 metres (10,906ft), is about 40km (25 miles) away from the airport. Despite air traffic disruption, August's eruption drew large crowds of onlookers to Etna's lava flows. About 1.5 million people visit Etna every year. title: Draper decides not to play again this season
description: Former world number four Jack Draper will not play again this season, but says he is aiming to return to the tour at the start of next year.
body: Draper reached the US Open semi-finals in 2024 Former world number four Jack Draper will not play again this season, but says he is aiming to return to the tour at the start of next year. The 24-year-old has been suffering with bone bruising in his serving arm and has only played nine events since last year's Wimbledon. Draper missed the US Open, after losing in the first round in Montreal and Cincinnati last month - and was in tears during his defeat to France's Terence Atmane in Canada. "I am taking this time to reset and heal so when I return I am 100% ready to go," Draper posted on Instagram., external "Tennis is my purpose and passion and so when I step back on court I want to make sure that there's nothing holding me back from where I want to go." Why can't Draper play, and why won't surgery help? Tearful Draper struggles during comeback defeat Draper will not qualify for a protected ranking if he does return in January, as only those who are out for over six months are able to retain the ranking they had when they left the tour. He is currently ranked 155, which means he would require wildcards or have to come through qualifying to play in Grand Slams and ATP Tour events. But none of that will worry him if he is able to play freely and without so much pain. Draper peaked at four in the world last June after winning a first Masters 1000 title in Indian Wells and finishing runner-up at another in Madrid. "Last summer, all the dedication and work I had put into this sport was coming together," Draper added. "It was all going my way and the path seemed so clear. However a complicated injury made things incredibly challenging, and since that moment I've been desperately trying to get back and feel as I once did on the court. "Managing so much change, adversity and pain has helped me to grow massively in many areas of my life but has also made me feel a level of fatigue." Draper has taken a holiday with friends in recent weeks and has been trying to aid his recovery by taking a mental break from the sport. He is expected to make a gradual return to training over the next few weeks, as his team try to work out the principal causes of the injury. Draper used to play with polyester strings, but has been experimenting with natural gut - which is against his instincts, but should ease the burden on his arm. He has also started using a lighter racquet, and is making some changes to his serve. Diet is another area being examined to see if that, too, could be a contributing factor. Andy Murray remains part of his coaching team but will do a limited number of weeks on the road, and so further assistance will be required. Over the summer, Draper benefitted from the help of LTA coaches James Trotman (who was with him full-time as he rose into the world's top five) and Alex Lisiecki. A permanent coach to work alongside Murray will need to be found, however, once Draper returns to the tour. When he does, much thought will go into his schedule. Not just because the bone bruising is unlikely to have healed entirely by January, but also because of the concerns many top players have about the toll the modern game is putting on their bodies. title: Government to end ban on Catholic and Jewish PMs' involvement in Church appointments
description: Andy Burnham, himself a Catholic, says it is "unacceptable for there to be a legislative bar against people of any faith performing all the functions of my office".
body: The government has introduced a bill to end antiquated laws preventing Roman Catholic or Jewish prime ministers from being involved in the process of making Church of England appointments. It was among the first pieces of legislation to be introduced to Parliament under Prime Minister Andy Burnham, himself a Catholic, who has called the current laws "unacceptable". When appointing bishops and archbishops, the Church presents a candidate to the prime minister who then advises the monarch on who to install in the role. Although the involvement of the prime minister in this process has become more of a formality in recent years, legislation still exists that specifically bars Roman Catholics and Jews from exercising this responsibility. That is why earlier this month Burnham, the first Catholic prime minister, transferred the responsibility of advising the King on Church appointments to the Lord Chancellor. But the prime minster said it was "unacceptable for there to be a legislative bar against people of any faith performing all the functions of my office". The Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829 and the Jews Relief Act 1858 are the existing laws in question. When those laws were introduced, they actually eased some of the restrictions on Catholics' and Jews' participation in public life. This included what was, in effect, a prohibition on them becoming MPs. But the law still stipulated that prime ministers of those faiths could not be involved - "directly or indirectly" - in advising during the process of making Church appointments. The appointment of the Archbishop of Canterbury Dame Sarah Mullally was approved by then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, a self-proclaimed atheist The Roman Catholic Relief Act, for example, says that a Catholic advising a sovereign on a Church appointment would be "deemed guilty of a high misdemeanour, and disabled for ever from holding any office, civil or military, under the Crown". The law relating to Jews contains a similar threat. These laws and restrictions remain in effect. That is partly because, until now, they have had no practical effect - before Burnham, there has not been a Catholic or Jewish prime minister. Although Benjamin Disraeli - prime minister in the late-1800s - was born to a Jewish family, his father renounced Judaism and had his children baptised into the Church of England. Another former Prime Minister, Tony Blair, is a Roman Catholic, but his conversion formally took place six months after he stepped down. And because the existing laws only discriminate against Jews and Catholics, it meant that Rishi Sunak, a Hindu, and Sir Keir Starmer, an atheist, were not prevented from advising on Church of England appointments in the way that Andy Burnham has been. In practical terms, for nearly 20 years the prime minister has not had much of a role in the selection of Church of England bishops. In 2007, Gordon Brown decided the Church should only present a single candidate to the prime minister, who would then pass it on to the monarch to confirm. Some prime ministers have taken a more interventionist approach. Margaret Thatcher, for example, famously pushed back against candidates who did not align with her political or religious views. Although the archaic laws preventing Jews and Roman Catholics advising on Church appointments technically relates to the Church of Scotland too, in reality the appointment of elders and ministers within the Church of Scotland no longer has any outside involvement. But the bill introduced on Tuesday intends to remove discriminatory laws that mean one aspect of the role of prime minister can now be performed by people of any religious belief that hold the office. It must be approved by the House of Commons and House of Lords before any change would come into practice.
