title: What weapon could the US have put into space?
description: The announcement by the US points to a developing field of modern warfare in the Earth's orbit.
body: Some types of space weaponry could create a lot of debris and destruction The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena. Washington has given away little in its announcement. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit. So what could this weapon be, and what is wider picture like for military developments in space? Who else could have similar weaponry? Advanced militaries already deploy satellites in space for range of purposes, from supplying secure communications to reconnaissance, and providing precise location information for targeted strikes and detecting missile launches. As warfare become more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase. Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US. "I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said. "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless." Bowen also would not rule out some sort of more disruptive and riskier weaponry, which could create a lot of debris and destruction. "Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile of some sort that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said. "Possibly some sort of close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well." But while the weapon placed in orbit appears to be a first, the US - and indeed its Russian and Chinese rivals - have had weapons that can be pointed and shot into space for some time. In fact in the last 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites. "Theoretically, these RPO sats can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC. Bowen adds that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit." This, he says, can be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites. Thornton says that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability. "The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike sats in low Earth orbit. They also have ASAT missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he says. "From the Russian point of view they see Nato as having much better and more sats than the Russian military can call up, therefore they have invested heavily in ASATs in order to 'level the battlefield' somewhat." Thornton adds a sobering thought: "As a last resort, the Russians can also launch nuclear weapons into space and the EPM blast would 'fry' any unhardened sats over a wide expanse." He says that, having so few satellites, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, which would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring sats designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers". title: Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial oil pipeline
description: Experts tell BBC Verify the pipeline's closure could cut oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day.
body: Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher. The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war. The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen. New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week. The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis. While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks. It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping. The price of a barrel of oil has surged since Saudi Arabia said on Friday it was closing the pipeline as a precaution. Brent crude was trading as high as $108 (£80) a barrel on Tuesday, down slightly from $109.80 on Monday. Experts from trade intelligence firm Kpler said the pipeline's closure could reduce oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day - or about 3.6% of global demand. "Based on new information we've received, damage to the pipeline could take four to six weeks to resolve, given spare-parts availability and impaired supply chains," said Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler's head of crude oil analysis. Anne-Sophie Corbeau, from the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, said pipelines are "like sitting ducks" and recent strikes are a "very important signal" indicating workarounds being used to avoid the Strait of Hormuz "may not be super useful because they can be destroyed". The Houthis have targeted other Saudi oil infrastructure with drones and missiles which has led to some operations being suspended. There have also been attacks on military bases. New satellite images captured on Monday show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base near Khamis Mushait which the Houthis said they had targeted with ballistic missiles and drones last week after it was used to carry out air strikes on Yemen. At least three aircraft hangars or shelters appear to have been damaged at the Royal Saudi Air Force facility where US-made F-15 fighter jets are based. The Saudi-led anti-Houthi military coalition of Arab states said on Tuesday that a Houthi missile and drone attack had injured 13 people in attacks on what the coalition said were "civilian objects". The Houthis said Saudi Arabia had carried out with more than 50 strikes in western Yemen over the previous 24 hours. The UN Refugee Agency has said that more than 100,000 people have been internally displaced by the renewed conflict. title: How city's market became a CBeebies TV set
description: The show, filmed in Coventry, aims to help young children explore food through their senses
body: Aaron Roach Bridgeman and puppet co-host Zesty lead children through food-themed activities Coventry Market's fruit and vegetable stalls, fish counters and busy walkways have become an unlikely TV set. Cameras are rolling among shoppers and traders as local children explore unfamiliar foods for a new CBeebies series. I Can Taste It aims to help three to six-year-olds build confidence in trying different foods through sight, smell, touch, sound and taste. Presented by Aaron Roach Bridgeman and puppet co-host Zesty, the programme is being filmed at the market, which producers say offers children an authentic environment in which to learn about food. "It's important that children see themselves represented in real places with real people," said Dom Sant, founder of Common Story, the Leamington Spa-based company behind the series. He said the market's atmosphere, variety of stalls and sense of community made it the perfect location. Director Jess Matthews with Compost Monster, one of the programme's regular characters Among the young participants is six-year-old Oscar, from Bedworth. His mother, Hannah, said she applied after spotting an advert on social media. "Oscar loves his food and he's very chatty, so when they met him he made a good impression," she said. For Hannah, visiting the market has also brought back childhood memories. "My mum and dad used to bring me here every Saturday morning to do the shopping and I'd always beg to go on the roundabout," she said. "Every time I walk into the market it's nostalgic. I feel like I'm four years old again, holding my dad's hand." Betts and Sons traders are among those taking part in filming for the new CBeebies series Director Jess Matthews described filming as a "glorious chaos", with the production team often responding to children's reactions rather than following a strict script. Alongside Aaron and Zesty, youngsters are also joined by Compost Monster, a character designed to encourage sustainable food habits and reduce food waste. Market trader David Betts said the production had shone a light on one of Coventry's best-known landmarks. "It's one of the iconic places in Coventry and people take it for granted," he said. Fishmonger Clive Miller said the programme introduces children to foods they might not normally encounter Fishmonger Clive Miller, whose stall is due to feature in filming, said the programme would help children discover foods they might not normally encounter. "When children go to the supermarket, they don't get to see fish like this," he said. "It's a chance for them to learn about a wider variety of fish and where food comes from." The series is due to air in spring 2027. Common Story began in a garden shed six years ago with a £10,000 budget. It has since made more than 100 programmes for CBeebies, with a further 30 currently in production. title: More than 100,000 people in Japan are now aged 100 or older
description: Figures show 88% of the centenarians are women as the population continues to age and shrink.
body: When records began in 1963 there were only 153 centenarians in Japan - now there are 107,677 The number of people aged 100 or more in Japan has exceeded 100,000 for the first time, according to the health ministry. Figures show Japan is now home to 107,677 centenarians, the highest number in the world, of whom 88% are women. The oldest woman is Kishimoto Fuyo, a 114-year-old from Kyoto City and the oldest man is Kato Hikaru, a 112-year-old from Kumamoto. Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno said he was "delighted that so many people are living long, healthy and active lives", citing progress in medicine and technology. But Kenichiri also warned of the challenge the country faces in maintaining a sustainable social security system. Experts put the long lives of the Japanese down to several factors, including a healthy diet and an active lifestyle. The island nation's cuisine predominantly consists of fish, vegetables, and rice - and less saturated fat than many Western diets. Older people also regularly walk, use public transport, cycle and stretch. Japan has been aging for years and sales of adult nappies have been higher than those for babies for more than a decade. Companies have also developed new products for the older population, including a powered exoskeleton to support moving various parts of the body and eyewear that automatically adjusts its focus. Japanese people's diets - largely consisting of fish, vegetables and rice - are thought to contribute to living longer For a population to replace itself, each woman needs to give birth to 2.1 children on average. Last year Japan's total fertility rate dropped to a record low of 1.14. The total population is estimated to drop to 87 million by 2070, representing a 30% decline from its peak of 128 million in 2008, according to data from the National Institute of Population and Social Security research. Residents aged 65 and older currently make up around 30% of the population and are expected to make up nearly 40% by 2070. Japanese authorities have called the trend an "existential crisis" with Prime Minister Sanae Takichi describing the decline as a "quiet emergency". In 2025 Japan's total population decreased in all 47 prefectures but two, and the rate of decline is accelerating. The government's many programmes and subsidies to encourage young people to have more children do not appear to be boosting birth rates. Experts say the reasons are complex, ranging from lower marriage rates and more women joining the workforce to the increased costs of raising children. While immigration has risen in previous years, foreigners only make up around 3% of the population and opposition to accepting more has grown. Migration to Japan has increased in recent years but remains low compared to other major economies When Japan began its centenarian survey in 1963, there were 153 people aged 100 or over. That figure rose to 1,000 in 1981 and stood at 10,000 by 1998. The most recent figures were released ahead of Japan's annual "Respect for the Aged" public holiday, on which the government honours those turning 100 with a personal letter and traditional sake cup. Studies have previously cast doubt on the validity of global centenarian numbers, suggesting data errors, unreliable public records and missing birth certificates may account for elevated figures. A government audit of family registries in Japan in 2010 uncovered more than 230,000 people listed as being aged 100 or older who were unaccounted for, some having died decades previously. The miscounting was attributed to patchy record-keeping and suspicions that some families may have tried to hide the deaths of elderly relatives in order to claim their pensions. title: Canada is a 'safe harbour' for global finance, Carney says
description: The prime minister is hosting a major global investment summit, with the goal of attracting money into the country amid a trade war with the US.
body: This video can not be played Canada's Mark Carney tells a story about Trump gifting him a key to the White House. Prime Minister Mark Carney has pitched Canada as a "safe harbour" for some of the world's largest investors to spend their money in an era of geopolitical and economic uncertainty. The country is "perfectly situated to build in the new global economic order", he told more than 100 global investors and sovereign wealth fund representatives gathered in Toronto for a major investment summit. The group represent more than C$120tn ($86tn; £64tn) of assets. Carney's ambition is that they will invest in sectors like defence, energy, mining, AI and infrastructure. Ottawa hopes they can be sold on more than 160 projects, from data centres to pipelines, and help Canada weather its trade war with the US. Canada's dispute with its largest trade partner has prompted Carney to look to expand economic partnerships with Europe, Asia and the Middle East as he seeks to reduce his country's reliance on its neighbour to the south. "Our goal is simple: to make Canada the most attractive place in the G7 to invest," Carney said on Tuesday morning. As part of that move, Carney announced plans to privatise operations for four of the country's largest airports, saying it would raise billions of dollars that could be reinvested in transport infrastructure. Many of the business leaders attending the event in Toronto received a personal invitation from the prime minister, who worked in the top tiers of global finance and was a central banker before turning to politics. Much of the action will take place in private sessions and bilateral meetings over the course of the day. There will, however, be panels with speakers including Deutsche Bank AG CEO Christian Sewing, Bombardier executive Eric Martel, and BlackRock CEO Larry Fink and Blackstone president Jon Gray. Carney gambles on the world's biggest investors betting on Canada Carney eyes 'unique alliance' with EU as trade war with US intensifies The prime minister's office has played down the likelihood of any major announcements coming from the summit, with Carney saying over the weekend it was chance for deep-pocketed financiers to "come to 'peer into our shop window'". The event is also an opportunity for Canada to burnish its reputation as a good place to do business after years of lagging investment performance. Economic analysts say Canada needs to make significant policy changes to help attract investment, including more competitive tax and regulatory systems, and ensuring a supply of skilled labour. Protestors on Monday accused the Carney government of selling off the country For Carney, the event will be a test of whether he can deliver on his promise to strengthen the country's economic resilience. Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed last month and the two countries have since imposed tit-for-tat tariffs. On Tuesday, new US tariffs came into effect on a number of Canadian goods while some others were lifted, and bans on goods like alcohol and motorcycles are due to come into force next week. On Tuesday, Carney addressed the American executives in Toronto directly. "To our American friends, let me say this. We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US's most important partner in many key areas," he said. "After all, even at times of disagreement during our long history, we have always maintained deep ties." Meanwhile, protestors on Monday accused the Carney government of organising a "great Canadian sell-off" of public resources and infrastructure to corporate interests, and hundreds appeared outside the opening night gala at a downtown museum. "Half the buyers that he has invited here to Toronto are American," said Kai Nagata, with advocacy group Dogwood, on Monday. "Let's be clear, every piece of our country that we sell off to American billionaires brings us closer to becoming the 51st state." title: Number of people claiming key disability benefit hits record high
description: An ongoing review into Personal Independence Payments (Pip) has found the system is "not fit for purpose".
body: The number of people claiming Personal Independence Payments (Pip) in England and Wales has hit a record high, according to new government figures. As of July, just over four million people were entitled to claim the benefit, compared to 3.83 million the previous year, an increase of 7%, data from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) showed. Pip is designed to support people with the extra costs of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions, and eligibility is not affected by a person's income or savings. In July, Sir Stephen Timms, who is leading a review on Pip, said in his interim report that the system was "not fit for purpose". Of the 4.1 million claimants, those aged 50 and above accounted for more than half. Just under three in ten were aged 30 to 49, while 17% of claimants were aged 16 to 29. Pip seeks to offset the extra costs that can occur for those living with certain long-term health conditions. According to the charity Scope, the extra cost of being disabled – known as the disability price tag – has reached more than £1,100 a month. The DWP said the increase in the Pip caseload had actually "slowed", falling from a rise of 400,000 in the 12 months to July 2024, to 260,000 in the 12 months to July 2026. But they agreed the system was "no longer fit for purpose", adding that the Timms review's recommendations would "lay the foundation for sustainable reform". But Helen Whatly, shadow work and pensions secretary, said Labour was "too quick to write people off and too slow to help them into work" - adding that it was "costing us a fortune". Pip has been in the spotlight since the summer of 2025 when the government, led by former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer, proposed reforming and tightening eligibility criteria for the benefit as the cost of running the system increased. Spending on Pip stood at £16.3bn in 2019-20, when adjusted for inflation to today's prices, and had increased to £27.3bn by 2024-25, government figures showed. It is currently forecast to rise to £41.5bn by 2030-31. Reform proposes £50bn welfare bill cut with changes to disability payments for millions Disability benefit not fit for purpose, minister leading review says How a rise in ADHD benefits claims is adding to welfare spending challenge But dozens of Labour MPs expressed concerns about the plans and, fearing its own members would vote down the reforms, the government U-turned. Instead, it commissioned a review into Pip led by Sir Stephen, the minister for social security and disability, to make recommendations that would make it "fit and fair for the future". The interim report published in the summer said the system had become a barrier to work for many, and the process of applying for it was found to be "dehumanising". Under the current assessment system, a health professional scores claimants on everyday tasks such as washing, getting dressed and preparing food using a zero to 12 scale. Earlier this month, the review's "emerging recommendations" suggested more face-to-face assessments would take place, and while cash payments would remain the foundation, there would also be non-cash support available. The Timms review is expected to be published in full later this year. title: Youth star JJ Gabriel, 15, on brink of leaving Man Utd
description: Manchester United's highly-rated 15-year-old forward JJ Gabriel is on the verge of leaving the club.
body: JJ Gabriel scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut for Manchester United last week Highly-rated 15-year-old striker JJ Gabriel is on the verge of leaving Manchester United. Even though he was only 14 when the season began, he won the Premier League Under-18 player of the year award last term, in addition to being named United's Under-18 player of the year. He made his senior debut for United in their pre-season game against Atletico Madrid in Stockholm last month, scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut last week and had been expected to make his competitive bow in Wednesday night's Carabao Cup tie with Brighton. The precise issues have not been outlined but it is understood Gabriel did not train with Michael Carrick's squad at the end of last week amid issues in the relationship between the player's family and United. The club have not yet given up hope of resolving the situation given Gabriel has a contract that runs to the end of the season. Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are directly involved in discussions with the player's family, which underlines how seriously the club regard the situation. United sources say they are not sure what has led to the situation developing the way it has. Gabriel has sent a formal notice he wants to cancel his registration with immediate effect. United can challenge the request. Gabriel does not turn 16 until 6 October, when he would be able to sign a scholarship agreement. Born in London, Gabriel scored twice on his debut for United's Under-18 side when he was just 14. He was an integral part of the United side that reached both the FA Youth Cup and Premier League Under-18 finals last season. Gabriel moved into the club's Premier League 2 squad this season and scored sensational goals in his first two games. title: What in the World
description: We look at hacks to help you get around it
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·15 Sep 2026,·9 mins Available for over a year Ever wondered why you might feel a bit unwell after a flight? There are lots of reasons for that - from dehydration, jet lag, cabin pressure and altitude. Last month, a French court recognised that cosmic radiation was a factor in a flight attendant’s breast cancer diagnosis. Studies show that cabin crew and pilots have the highest level of radiation- related cancer deaths compared to more than 500 other jobs. We’re looking at what impacts flying regularly, and for long periods of time, can have on your body. We hear from Savannah, a pilot in the US, about what she does to keep herself healthy when sitting in a cockpit for hours. And Naomi, who is taking a break from being cabin crew, tells us how spending so much time in a plane has affected her. title: Woman jailed for claiming on Facebook her ex-husband was a 'rapist' and 'baby killer'
description: Jennifer Pritchard led a two-month smear campaign against her ex-husband, a South Wales Police officer.
body: Jennifer Pritchard was sentenced to 18 months at Cardiff Crown Court on Friday, 11 September A woman has been jailed for posting a string of lies on social media about her police officer ex-husband, claiming he was a "rapist" and a "baby killer". Jennifer Pritchard, 47, from Tredegar in Blaenau Gwent, created a Facebook page called "Jen's Justice" where she led a two-month smear campaign against Stephen Pritchard, a South Wales Police officer. Sgt Pritchard, who said he had been investigated by his force over the false allegations, said he wanted his "life back". Jennifer Pritchard, who had pleaded guilty on the day of her trial to a malicious communication offence, was sentenced on Friday at Cardiff Crown Court to 18 months in prison. Pamela Kaiga, prosecuting, said Pritchard had previously been prosecuted for perverting the course of justice with lies about her ex-husband. Pritchard had been "persecuting" him with repeated falsehoods about domestic violence, rape and being a baby killer. In a victim impact statement, Sgt Pritchard said: "I was the target of a false and malicious campaign on social media to ruin my career. "I've suffered anxiety, depression and other health issues. I just want my life back. "I don't think she will ever stop," he said. Sgt Pritchard said he had suffered financially because of the legal costs and had been investigated by his own force over the allegations. The judge told Jennifer Pritchard that she presented a "high risk of harm" to her ex-husband and police officers Pritchard has previous convictions for harassment against another ex-husband in January 2025, and later that year was convicted of making a public nuisance or causing annoyance via a telecommunications system to a different police officer. Tabitha Walker, defending, said Pritchard was "remorseful for the distress she has caused", and that there was a "realistic prospect of rehabilitation". But the judge, Recorder Andrew Hammond, said she appeared to "derive satisfaction from the harm you cause". "You say you're sorry for the harm you've caused, but I don't believe you," he said, adding that he had "not seen any evidence of substance to indicate any real remorse". "You have a background of inventing false accusations. You present a high risk of harm to your ex-husbands and police officers," Hammond added. Pritchard was also handed an indefinite restraining order, preventing her from contacting her ex-husband. title: Two sailors missing after tanker attacked in Strait of Hormuz, Oman says
description: Iran says El Gaia caught fire after hitting mines, but the US says the oil tanker was struck by a missile and then a drone.
body: Oman's Maritime Security Centre said a fire broke out in El Gaia's engine room following an attack Two sailors are missing and 23 others have been rescued following an attack on an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, Oman says. Oman's Maritime Security Centre said the Panama-flagged El Gaia was being towed to an Omani port on Tuesday after a fire broke out in its engine room, adding that the vessel was targeted 1.3 nautical miles (2.4km) north of the Musandam peninsula. On Monday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the tanker hit naval mines and caught fire while passing through what they described as a restricted and unsafe route. But the US military insisted the Iranian report was false. It said the tanker was struck by an Iranian missile last month and again by a drone over the weekend. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre, meanwhile, said it had received a report of a fire breaking out on board a vessel that was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz in the early hours of Sunday. Earlier this month, Iran made a similar claim about an incident that killed two Filipino sailors on a Saudi-owned oil supertanker in the crucial waterway. The Revolutionary Guards said the vessel, Sidr, caught fire after hitting a naval mine. But Saudi authorities said it was targeted by Iran and maritime security firms reported that it was hit by projectiles north of Musandam. The International Maritime Organization says at least 22 seafarers have been killed in 79 confirmed incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the Middle East since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran at the end of February. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports. The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. Iran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway and has targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters. title: Colombian ex-foreign minister charged over nanny's lie detector test
description: Laura Sarabia is accused of ordering police to interrogate her nanny after cash allegedly went missing from her flat.
body: Laura Sarabia was Colombia's foreign minister from January to July 2025 Prosecutors in Colombia have accused former foreign minister Laura Sarabia of abusing her power after she made her nanny take a lie detector test. The scandal erupted in 2023, when Colombian news weekly Semana reported that a woman Sarabia had employed to look after her son had been hooked up to a polygraph and questioned over the alleged disappearance of a case full of cash from Sarabia's flat. Sarabia, who was the chief of staff for President Gustavo Petro at the time, resigned in June 2023 but was later appointed as foreign minister and, following her resignation from that post, as Colombia's ambassador to the United Kingdom. She has denied any wrongdoing. The 32-year-old was one of the closest advisers of Gustavo Petro, Colombia's first left-wing president, who governed from 2022 to August this year. Prosecutors said Sarabia abused her position as his chief of staff by ordering police to question her nanny, Marelbys Meza, over the alleged disappearance of the cash, which was said to amount to several thousands of dollars. Meza told Semana that she was taken by Sarabia's driver to an official building opposite the presidential palace, saying it felt like "a kidnapping". Police officers then attached her to a polygraph machine and questioned her about the alleged disappearance of the money. Meza denied having stolen any money during the test, and has consistently denied any wrongdoing in media interviews since. Prosecutors allege that in ordering police to question Meza, Sarabia improperly used state resources to investigate a matter which was not related to her official post. Sarabia rejected the accusation during a hearing, without going into further details. She had earlier said in a social media post that her lawyers were dealing with the issue and that she respected the judicial authorities and trusted their decisions. title: Data centre could threaten rare species, says charity
description: Incredibly rare habitats would be destroyed, the Essex Wildlife Trust warns.
body: Emily Buttress said the Essex Wildlife Trust was not necessarily against development, but they wanted it to be sustainable Plans to build a new data centre could threaten the habitat of one of Britain's most endangered plants and a rare species of bumblebee, a wildlife trust said. A planning application has already been submitted for the Google data centre at Arena Essex Raceway in Thurrock, which is designated as a local wildlife site. It is home to the rare broad-leaved cudweed and shrill carder bumblebee and the Essex Wildlife Trust fears "incredibly rare" habitats would be "destroyed". A Google spokesperson said it took "our environmental responsibilities very seriously". Data centres are giant warehouses full of powerful computers used to run digital services, such as movie streaming, online banking and artificial intelligence. There are 568 data centres listed in the UK, according to the data centre map., external Emily Buttress, from the Essex Wildlife Trust, said her team was worried about the water and energy usage required, the warming effect on the surrounding land, and a lack of research about the long-term impacts of these buildings. "We are quite worried with the rapid development of data centres," she said. "What would it do for the local community in a water drought county? We are not against development, but it has to happen sustainably." There are hundreds of species that live on the site, the trust has said The Arena Essex Raceway announced in 2018 that it would stop hosting speedway fixtures for the Lakeside Hammers team. Meanwhile, the Essex Wildlife Trust says the surrounding grassland and woodland has become home to 687 invertebrate and 439 plant species. The trust said this included dingy skipper, which is a small moth-like butterfly, and the shrill carder bumblebee, which was only found in two areas in England. It was designated as a local wildlife site in 2006. This does not offer legal protection from development, but it means council planners expect developers to look after the ecology. Nightingale birds, the brown-banded carder bee and the five-banded weevil-wasp have also been recorded at the site. But Global Infrastructure UK Limited bought the 129-acre (52-hectare) site in July 2023 for £47m (exclusive of VAT). It submitted plans for the data centre on behalf of Google last year, and as part of the application, consultancy firm Mallory Land Ltd said the proposals took into account the ecology there. If plans are approved the data centre could bring scores of jobs to the area, Google has said In a statement submitted as part of the plans, Mallory Land Ltd said: "The demand for data centres has expanded significantly in recent years, driven by exponential growth in digital services, the emergence of artificial intelligence, cloud-based technologies, and the increasing adoption of smart infrastructure." Google said data centres were vital to the UK economy and for online services. "We share the Essex Wildlife Trust and Buglife's, external view that development at the former Arena Essex site must be sustainable," a spokesperson said. "Our goal is to regenerate the site, bringing long-term investment and jobs to Thurrock while taking our environmental responsibilities very seriously." The company had worked closely with Natural England and ecologists, they added, to "guarantee a 10% biodiversity net gain", "as well as ensuring a substantial part of the site is preserved for new public open space, green links, retained habitat, and the long-term enhancement of key woodland corridors". title: Unions warn against 'out of control' political spending
description: In a joint statement, unions say donations totalling £72m to Reform UK threaten the "integrity of democracy".
body: Head of the TUC, Paul Nowak, spoke about the recent donations to Reform UK at the TUC congress in Brighton Trade unions have called for "out of control" political spending to be reined in, suggesting that the "health and integrity of democracy" have been threatened by donations totalling £72m to Reform UK. In a joint statement, the TUC - the umbrella group for unions in the UK - called on the government to "protect our democracy from being captured by the super rich". There is no explicit call for a cap on domestic donations to match those the government plans to impose on foreign-based donations. But unions have signalled they are open to discussions with policymakers on any initiatives to "clean up" party funding. The statement, issued at the TUC's annual congress in Brighton, also makes the case that trade union donations should not be treated in the same way as big contributions to parties from rich individuals. The debate over donations to political parties has been reignited after Reform UK received two donations totalling £72m from two British crypto-billionaires who have both recently lived abroad. The government is planning to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British voters living overseas, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March. There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties. Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees. Political donors could face tougher residency rules Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules Many in the trade union movement - especially those with links to Labour - have been wary of a cap on domestic donations in case a future government used this to restrict their donations. But behind the scenes officials recognise the eye-watering donations from Reform UK have changed the game and some form of domestic cap may have to be considered. The leader of the Unite union Sharon Graham told the BBC she favoured a cap of £500,000 to £1m on individual donations from UK-based citizens. But she argued that as union donations are made of lots of individual members making a contribution through a political levy then this should be treated differently. She said: "There is a difference between a crypto-billionaire based in the UK or abroad giving millions and trade union members who are nurses, cleaners, bus drivers giving 10p a week which adds up cumulatively to what we give to Labour." The GMB union has been one of the most wary over the implications of a domestic donations cap. Its general secretary Gary Smith told the BBC: "Whether there will be a cap on political donations, we will wait and see. "We will talk to the government at the appropriate time but we can't have any confusion between the political voice working people have through their unions and crypto-billionaires." What is interesting about Tuesday's union statement is not just what it says but what it doesn't. There has been no consensus on calling for caps on the spending of political parties rather than donations - one option for dealing with the Reform war chest. Another option was to treat big unions donations as a series of donations from individual members. For example a million strong union that donates £1m to Labour would have been regarded as making donations of £1 a member - thus escaping a cap. Some believe this would be politically difficult to argue. Not all unions donate to Labour and those which do not are therefore very relaxed about a cap. One even said the events of the past few days have been helpful in arguing for more restrictions on political donations. But I understand discussions will continue amongst those unions with financial links to Labour - including the three biggest in the UK - to try to reach a common position on Wednesday behind closed doors in Brighton and possibly in days and weeks ahead. title: Pidcock and Backstedt lead GB at Road Worlds
description: Great Britain's best cycling talents including Tom Pidcock and Zoe Backstedt will lead the charge at the Road World Championships - live on the BBC.
body: Pidcock has won several of cycling's biggest races while Backstedt won last year's Under-23 world time trial title Tom Pidcock and Zoe Backstedt will lead Great Britain's challenge at the 2026 Road World Championships. The races for the coveted rainbow jerseys take place in Montreal, Canada, from 20-27 September, live across the BBC. The championships include both the road race and time trial disciplines, with Pinarello Q36.5's Pidcock leading the men's team in the road race, while Ethan Hayter races in the men's time trial. Lauren Dickson and Pfeiffer Georgi will likely lead the women's team in the road race and Zoe Backstedt will be expected to contend for the rainbow bands in the time trial. Not for a long time have GB men a better chance to win in the road race, with double world champion and record-equalling five-time Tour de France winner Tadej Pogacar forced to sit out the rest of the season after suffering multiple injuries in a crash at the Vuelta a Espana. Slovenian Pogacar has dominated the world road race for the past two years, winning in 2024 and 2025 to add to his numerous other honours. The time trials come first in Montreal, with riders setting off at one-minute intervals, racing against the clock. Backstedt steps up to the elite category after winning last year's Under-23 race and is joined by Anna Morris, 31, who has won a number of domestic races in 2026. In the men's time trial Hayter, who came second in the opening time trial of the recent Vuelta a Espana, losing out to Pogacar by just nine hundredths of a second, will be joined by Callum Thornley, while the favourite will be defending champion Remco Evenepoel of Belgium. Performance director for British Cycling Stephen Park said: "The Road World Championships are always one of the standout events in the cycling calendar, and we are excited to return with a highly competitive squad. "This squad showcases the very best of British road racing, at a time when more British riders are making their mark across Europe and on the wider international stage than ever before. "We're proud of the balance in this squad, from established world-class performers to riders taking the next step in their development." Backstedt is in her element on a sophisticated TT bike Hayter came agonisingly close to being one of the few people to beat Tadej Pogacar this year Pidcock won the Mountain Bike Worlds last month and has won Olympic gold in that discipline, but the Worlds Road race, which is not until the end of the event, still eludes him Elite Women: Zoe Backstedt, Lauren Dickson, Pfeiffer Georgi, Anna Henderson, Anna Morris, Flora Perkins, Alice Towers Elite men: Mark Donovan, Ethan Hayter, Oscar Onley, Finlay Pickering, Tom Pidcock, James Shaw, Callum Thornley, Fred Wright, Adam Yates U23 Men: Jacob Bush, Mattie Dodd, Elliot Rowe, Will Smith, Ben Wiggins U23 Women: Cat Ferguson, Abi Miller, Awen Roberts, Imogen Wolff, Morven Yeoman Junior Women: Aalia Clay, Peggy Knox, Gabriella McHugh, Zoe Roche, Melanie Rowe Junior Men: Leon Atkins, Gus Dutton, Finlay Storrie, Dexter Townsend, Evander Wishart Road World Championships streams on iPlayer and the BBC Sport website & app Women's Time Trial: 14:00-16:45 BST - iPlayer & BBC Sport website & app (14:45-16:45 BBC Two) Men's Time Trial: 17:30-21:00 BST - iPlayer & BBC Sport website & app (19:00-21:00 BBC Three) Women's Road Race: 14:00-19:30 BST - iPlayer & BBC Sport website & app Men's road race: 14:00-21:00 BST - iPlayer & BBC Sport website & app (19:00-21:00 BBC Three) Sterling admits dangerous driving on motorway before crash London misses out to Nairobi in World Athletics bid Sweeney ad a barrier for girls in sport - Hunt How did Jeffrey Epstein become so powerful? title: Building more data centres could push up electricity prices, expert warns
description: Scotland has been identified as a key location for building hyperscale AI data centres because of the high potential for renewable energy.
body: Scotland has been identified as a prime location for building hyperscale AI data centres due to the high potential for renewable energy Building more data centres could push up electricity prices for consumers and challenge climate change targets, MSPs have been told. Scotland has been identified as a key location for building hyperscale AI data centres because of the high potential for renewable energy, principally from wind. But academics have warned that could still result in more gas being used to create electricity at times of low wind and solar power, which has been driving up prices in the Republic of Ireland and the US. The National Energy System Operator (Neso) said plans were in place to decouple the high cost of gas from bills. But it added that building more data centres in Scotland would be an important way of keeping electricity prices lower. Will our peaceful rural life be destroyed by a huge AI data centre? Holyrood's Economy, Tourism and Energy Committee, external is investigating the energy use that will come from placing more data centres in Scotland. Dr Callum MacIver, research fellow at the University of Strathclyde, said data centres in Scotland would mop up excess renewable energy. This would cut the multi-million pound bill for constraint payments, which are made when there is too much wind power being generated. But he warned that the growth was still likely to increase the use of fossil fuels. MacIver said: "Adding demand in general is likely to put pressure on meeting decarbonisation goals. "It's not always windy or sunny so adding new demand to the system is likely to increase the amount of fossil fuel burn you have on it." The academic added that locating data centres in "the most sensible places" could mitigate how big those impacts are by using more wind energy. The inquiry also heard that it was unclear how the increased infrastructure costs, linked to a growth in AI data centres, would be shared between operators and wider consumers as additional costs on their bills. While the tech firms will pay their energy bills, connection costs and their network usage, Dr Wei Sun, from the University of Edinburgh, said it was unclear who would fund broader upgrades required on the transmission network. He added: "It's a concern of a lot of people worldwide. "It's a simple question of whether data centres are going to increase the bill or not. There's no simple answer. "Adding the data centre is probably going to trigger wider system upgrades. "Does the data centre also pay for that? I think that's really the question we need to answer." Scotcast: The Revolt Against Data Centres Matt Magill, from Neso, said modern data centres came with a degree of flexibility which allowed for supply and demand for electricity to be balanced on both sides. Bigger AI operators who use, for example, large language modelling are building in enough internet bandwidth to shift the data handling to different parts of the world when needed. Magill said: "Speaking to some of the large [companies] involved in this, they're looking at some of the [AI] training on a regional basis or even a worldwide basis and can actually move the load around the world depending on what's going on in those places." He said that offered flexibility to those that run the power service. The planned data centres would rely on renewable electricity, which is produced in abundance in Scotland by wind turbines. But turbines are often effectively "turned off" due to lack of capacity in the electricity grid - resulting in substantial "compensation" payments for the wind farm companies. ILI Group CEO Mark Wilson said they wanted to make better use of that surplus energy. He added: "Scotland is in a position not a lot of other countries are and we feel this is an opportunity we cannot afford to miss". Wilson also said the construction of hyperscale data centres across the country could create hundreds of new jobs. The issue was raised at Holyrood in June by the Scottish Greens at the final First Minister's Questions before the summer recess. The party called on First Minister John Swinney to back a moratorium on planning approvals. Swinney said he understood the environmental concerns over hyperscale data centres. He also pledged to give "active consideration" to whether local authorities should be given new national planning guidance. Swinney said such guidance might be a way of balancing the rapid expansion of such centres with national energy and climate goals. Could a huge data centre revitalise Ayrshire - or ruin it? title: Five things you may not know about Emmy record-breaker Matthew Rhys
description: The Welsh actor became the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night at the Emmy Awards.
body: Matthew Rhys, who grew up in Cardiff made history at the Emmy Awards, becoming the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night Hollywood actor Matthew Rhys has made history at the Emmys by becoming the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night. He was named best lead actor in a limited series for the psychological thriller The Beast In Me, and best lead actor in a comedy for his role in Widow's Bay. Here are five things you may not already know about the history-making 51-year-old. Turner and Rhys in the West End production of The Graduate in 2000 At the start of his career, Rhys was so desperate for work he considered joining the British Army. In 2000, he stared alongside American actress Kathleen Turner in the West End production of The Graduate. But for nearly two years afterwards he couldn't find work. So he met with an army officer who he said was "incredibly suspicious" of him because he was an actor, and told him "we'll be in touch". Rhys said: "Then about a week later, I got a rejection letter from the British Army saying, 'thank you for your interest, good luck in your career'. "And I went, 'oh my God, I can't even join the army'." Ioan Gruffudd, left, and Matthew Rhys have been friends since school In 2006, Rhys moved to Hollywood and surrounded himself with fellow Welsh actors - including Michael Sheen and Ioan Gruffudd. He lived with Newport-born Sheen and schoolfriend Gruffudd. He and Gruffudd both attended Welsh medium school Ysgol Glantaf in Cardiff. In an interview in The Big Issue Cymru in 2003, Rhys said the pair did not see each other often, despite living under the same roof, as they were both busy working. He affectionately called their group the 'LA Tafia'. In 2012, Rhys told The Independent newspaper how the trio would speak Welsh to one another, dream of good fish and chips and watch rugby together in a British pub. Rhys and Russell have a son, Sam A decade after first meeting actor Keri Russell, the pair finally became an item when they starred together in the TV series The Americans in 2013. They played a married couple who were Russian spies from 2013-2018. Rhys and Russell were a couple from 2014 and had their son, Sam, in 2016. Rhys has previously told the BBC he speaks Welsh to Sam in the hope he will understand the language for life. He joked he planned to "force" Sam to embrace Welsh culture. Rhys is also stepdad to Russell's children River and Willa. Welsh rarebit - the dish, not the boat Rhys owns a 1939 wooden cruiser boat, which shares its name with a famous Welsh dish. The boat is named Rarebit, which is also the name of a traditional Welsh meal consisting of seasoned melted cheese sauce served over hot toast. He told the US TV show Today he didn't realise "the disaster of buying an old wooden boat" before making the purchase. Rhys said the boat is "part of Brooklyn history" and is the same class of boat that acclaimed author Ernest Hemingway previously owned. Rhys admitted he has tried to sell Rarebit but now hopes to work with naval architecture at Brooklyn Boatworks to turn her into something "for Brooklyn and New York" in the future. Rhys attended Welsh language medium school Glantaf in Cardiff Rhys' first language is Welsh and regularly speaks it at home in New York. The passionate Welshman dedicated his second award "to the great and good people of Wales, who were as much a nurture as anyone else". "We are a small but mighty nation. This is incredible," he said, adding, "diolch yn fawr iawn" which means "thank you very much" in Welsh. Rhys has also been revealed as the voice of Han Solo in a new Welsh language adaptation of Star Wars. Star Wars will be dubbed in Welsh for the first time ahead of the sci-fi classic's 50th anniversary next year. Rhys told New York Times podcast The Interview that the Welsh language project brought up some unexpected feelings. "What was weird is obviously, they'd had to translate all these things that we'd grown up with, knowing Star Wars," Rhys said. "I was saying in Welsh things like, 'pelydr cyrchu' - it's kind of like, 'tractor beam'." He's keen to remain connected to all things Welsh, and in 2025, Rhys took on the role of Welsh icon Richard Burton in the one-man show, Playing Burton, raising funds for the Welsh National Theatre. Rhys said he first saw the play as a student in London more than 30 years ago and dreamed of portraying Burton ever since. title: Key findings from Lucy Letby Thirlwall Inquiry
description: The inquiry found a "complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit" where the nurse worked.
body: Lucy Letby was convicted of the murders of seven babies, and the attempted murder of seven others - one of whom she attempted to kill twice The deaths and near-deaths of some babies who were attacked by nurse Lucy Letby could have been prevented if safeguarding practices had been followed, the public inquiry into her crimes has found. Delivering the conclusion of her inquiry, chairwoman Lady Justice Thirlwall said it would never be possible to know for sure how many lives could have been saved. But she found there was a "complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit" at the Countess of Chester Hospital, where Letby, now 36, murdered seven babies and attempted to murder seven others - one of them twice. Thirlwall described a system of "dysfunctional management and governance". Letby was sentenced to 14 whole life terms in 2023 and received another in 2024 after a retrial found her guilty of one of the attempted murder counts the original jury had been unable to reach a verdict on. Thirlwall said: "If all the babies whom [Letby] was convicted of murdering were removed from the annual number of deaths in the neonatal unit, the mortality figures would have been three in 2015 and three in 2016 - broadly consistent with previous years," she wrote. "Since July 2016 there has been one death on the unit, in Sept 2019." Below are the key findings from the report. The first three deaths in June 2015 (babies A, C and D) were not viewed as a cluster of deaths, even though this was the annual number of deaths, concentrated into two weeks. The fourth death, (baby E) in August 2015, was unexpected and therefore reviewed at a serious incident panel meeting attended by the medical director and director of nursing - but it was treated as a formality. "What is surprising is that no connection was made by any of the people involved to the earlier deaths," Thirlwall noted. By August of that year, the total of four deaths was the highest since 2008, and was to double by the end of the year. Thirlwall found that if a doctor – named in the report as Dr ZA - had not disregarded the insulin test result for baby F in August 2015 then there should have been safeguarding action. The safeguarding action would have prevented the attacks on babies G and H, J, K, L, M and N and the deaths of baby I, O and P If safeguarding action had been taken by October 2015 - after the death of baby I - by moving Letby off the ward, the deaths of babies O and P would have been prevented, as would the attacks on babies J, K, L, M and N In, February 2016 Dr Ravi Jayaram should have reported what he had seen with regard to baby K In May 2016, no-one raised safeguarding at meeting with execs - if they had done it would have prevented the deaths of babies O and P Lady Justice Thirlwall oversaw the inquiry into the Lucy Letby case Thirlwall found hospital bosses "repeatedly failed in the duty of candour with parents, investigators and regulators". She added their behaviour was 'high-handed, against all safeguarding principles, and foolhardy." Medical director Ian Harvey "sought to control the narrative", and presented the case as he saw it. He made sure that only documents that supported his case were seen, if necessary writing them himself. Director of nursing Alison Kelly, the head of safeguarding, knew she had to act when there was a suspicion that a baby had been harmed, and others might be at risk – but did not Chief executive Tony Chambers was dictatorial in his approach to consultants, and executive presentations to the hospital's board were an "exercise in spin" He added to the unnecessary delay in contacting police His intention throughout was to stall or obstruct the police investigation, which he succeeded in doing for almost a year The report was critical of a raft of internal and external reviews commissioned by hospital leadership after concerns were raised about Letby Director of nursing for urgent care Karen Rees had "lost all judgement" and had a "hostile approach", Thirlwall found. She also found that unit manager Eirian Powell's judgement "was affected by the view that Letby was a very good nurse". The parents of babies were "kept in the dark for years" over concerns that their children may have been deliberately harmed. Thirlwall found their treatment to be "reprehensible", and said hospital executives used the risk of upsetting the parents as a convenient argument to justify not calling the police. In relation to the treatment of doctors, she said it should "never have been about nurses against doctors … it was about keeping babies safe". Doctors were found not to have been given the protection of the Speak Out Safely whistleblowing policy, and senior managers tried to "manage out" consultants, and suggested they might be referred to the General Medical Council watchdog. Letby was found to have falsified records Letby took out a grievance against the hospital in 2017, after being moved off her normal duties amid allegations about her. The report found that "the way Letby's grievance and its consequences were handled was deplorable", adding that the investigating officer in charge "could bring neither independence nor objectivity to it". The evidence of Alison Kelly and Ian Harvey was found to be "factually inaccurate and misleading", and the chair of the governance panel, Annette Weatherly, was "unfair in her approach", having initially described the allegations against Letby as a "witch hunt". Police were called into the hospital in 2017. Thirlwall added that "no-one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm - and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt". "All the safeguarding guidance in the world makes no difference to the safety of babies if those to whom concerns are expressed do nothing." title: Home Alone and Schitt's Creek stars pay tribute to late Catherine O'Hara
description: Tributes were also paid to Dolly Parton, James Van Der Beek and Tim Curry.
body: Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy delivered a poignant tribute to their late Home Alone and Schitt's Creek co-star Catherine O'Hara. Culkin remembered her as "our mom", and "like a good mom, she always showed up when I asked her to". Referring to the plot of the Home Alone films, he joked: "She may have forgotten me... twice! But we will always remember her." Noah Kahan then performed Bridge Over Troubled Water during the in memoriam segment, before Jamie Lee Curtis paid an emotional tribute to actor and director Rob Reiner. Heroes and Nashville star Hayden Panettiere, who died last month, was also remembered alongside other stars including Rocky Horror Show's Tim Curry and Dawson's Creek actor James Van Der Beek. Emmy winner O'Hara, who died in January this year aged 71, was known for playing Culkin's frantic mother in the 1990s film franchise, as well as the eccentric Moira Rose - mum to Murphy and Levy's Alexis and Dan - in Schitt's Creek. "You remember her as the forgetful mother, right?" said Culkin. "There are all kinds of words I could use to describe Catherine. She was encouraging. She was warm. She was funny, but the word that I think of is mom... She was, she was my mom. She was our mom. "So she may have forgotten me twice. But we will always remember her." Murphy noted how, since her death, many people had quoted O'Hara's most memorable lines from her show back at her. "These are only very few of the interactions I've been lucky enough to have that remind me how profoundly Catherine has impacted the world, and it's because she brought us joy," Murphy said. Levy added: "Always say yes to any opportunity to revel in the presence of greatness." The emotional moment, which featured a big image of a smiling O'Hara as the backdrop, appeared to bring actors Martin Short and Steve Martin, sitting in the audience, to tears. Reiner, who died last December, received a posthumous Emmy last week for his guest appearance in The Bear. Reiner was killed along with his wife last year. A tearful Jamie Lee Curtis paid tribute to the director, writer and performer, who made films such as When Harry Met Sally, This is Spinal Tap, Stand By Me, Misery and A Few Good Men, calling him a "cherished legend" and "our beloved meathead". The 48-year gap between Reiner's two most recent Emmy wins set a new record, beating his Dad, Carl Reiner. Curtis began her speech by first acknowledging the passing of Cheers co-creator James Burrows, who was also a good friend of Reiner's. There were also warm words for Farrah Fawcett, who died in 2009. Celebrating 50 years, Charlie's Angels stars Kate Jackson, Cheryl Ladd and Jaclyn Smith, handed out the Emmy for best drama and paid tribute to their fellow Angel. Jackson said Fawcett "was the shiniest angel of all, and she was loved by millions of people all over the world. And she still is today. And they'll never forget her and neither will we. And I'm sure you won't either." Buffy the Vampire Slayer stars Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreana paid tribute to the co-stars they have lost recently, including Nicholas Brendon, Anthony Head and Michelle Trachtenberg. Geller said: "David and I would like to acknowledge that it has been a tough two years for our beloved cast and crew, and we feel very lucky to have known and worked with such amazing people." Elsewhere on the night, Remarkably Smart Creatures actress Sally Field, who starred in Steel Magnolias opposite Dolly Parton, led a tribute to the country music star, who died last month. Field described Parton as "genuine, humble, supportive and blisteringly funny" as she introduced a special performance by country singer Reba McEntire. "She was a humanitarian whose contribution has made a profound difference across our country," Field said of Parton, who won an Emmy herself in 2021. "God bless you Dolly Parton my friend, I am not the only one on earth who will love you for ever and ever." title: Denmark says Russian warship fired flares at military helicopter
description: The Danish prime minister has accused Russia of "reckless" behaviour, while the Kremlin is yet to comment.
body: Denmark has accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea. The Danish government has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident, which it said happened during a "routine" monitoring operation on Monday. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen branded the Russian action "reckless" and said it was designed to "intimidate and divide". Russia said it would "thoroughly investigate" the incident but accused Danish helicopters of making "dangerous manoeuvres" near Russian warships. It came on the same day Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high during Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In a statement detailing the incident in the Baltic Sea, the Danish armed forces said: "One of the air force's Fennec helicopters was today fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser." Of the two flares fired at the helicopter, one passed close to it, the statement added. The Danish foreign ministry described the incident as "completely unacceptable". Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen accused Russia of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour", adding: "That is something we cannot accept." In a statement following the incident, Russian ambassador Vladimir Barbin accused Denmark of "recklessness" and "provocative actions". Barbin said this was "not the first time that Danish Air Force helicopters have carried out dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships". He said he had complained about a similar incident last year, adding that the latest event showed that "communication problems lie not with the Russian Navy's vessels, but with the Danish side". Danish Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters no attempt to make contact with helicopters had been made by the frigate's crew. Overnight, Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace. Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday. The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said, but the country's president pointed to increased Russian aggression in recent months. President Gitanas Nausėda wrote on X: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our Nato Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace." Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally. Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory". It said the overnight operations were of a "preventive nature" and aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions". Nato jets have been scrambled several times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year. Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones. title: Two dead after car hits group of pedestrians
description: A vehicle hit four people before colliding with two cars on White Rose Way in Doncaster, police say.
body: Police say they have arrested a 30-year-old man in connection with the incident Two people have died and four have been seriously injured after a car crashed into a group of people in Doncaster. South Yorkshire Police said officers were called to White Rose Way when a black Mitsubishi L200 hit a group of pedestrians at 11:00 BST on Sunday, before hitting a black Audi and silver BMW on the opposite carriageway. The force said two of the pedestrians had died at the scene while four other people were taken to hospital with serious injuries. The driver of the Mitsubishi, a 30-year-old man, was arrested on suspicion of two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, two counts of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and driving while unfit and later released on bail. The crash happened in White Rose Way, between Carriage Drive and Middle Bank Roundabout A police spokesperson said they were still "working to identify and inform" the families of those killed in the collision. Anyone who witnessed the crash, which took place between Carriage Drive and Middle Bank Roundabout, or who has dashcam footage is asked to contact South Yorkshire Police. title: Mother sentenced for killing son and attempting to murder daughter
description: The woman was convicted and jailed in 2023 but in 2025 senior judges ruled those convictions were unsafe.
body: Tributes were left outside the property in 2021 A woman, whose convictions for the murder of her baby son and attempted murder of his toddler sister were quashed, has been sentenced to 10 years for infanticide and attempted murder. The woman stabbed both children in July 2021 and they were taken to the Royal Belfast Hospital for Sick Children. The girl was successfully treated but the baby boy was pronounced dead. The woman was convicted and jailed in 2023 for murdering her eight-week-old son and attempting to murder his toddler sister. In December 2025, senior judges in the Court of Appeal ruled those convictions were unsafe. In March of this year, the court ordered a retrial. In August, the woman, whose identity is protected by an anonymity order, pleaded guilty to infanticide and attempted murder. Infanticide is legally defined as the unlawful killing of a child aged under 12 months, by its biological mother, when at the time the "balance of the mother's mind was disturbed". On Tuesday, Mr Justice Fowler referred to expert medical reports detailing that at the time of the stabbings the woman was experiencing postnatal depression. The court also heard that her relationship with the father of her children was "characterised by domestic abuse, sexual abuse and coercive control". She feared that her partner or people associated with him might kill her. The judge said diary entries by her suggest she was "overwhelmed by feelings of rejection, abandonment and emotional despair". Several medical reports said she felt in her circumstances that she had no alternative but to end her life and that of her children. A statement relating to the woman's surviving daughter detailed the "catastrophic impact" on her explaining that it would be lifelong. The court heard the incident happened at a crucial time in the child's development and she experienced "abandonment, rejection and loss". The young girl is now in foster care and was described as happy and settled but it was reported that she remains hyper vigilant and sensitive to changes in her environment. The woman was sentenced at Laganside Court in Belfast on Tuesday Following indirect contact with her mother the court heard that the child experiences "significant difficulties" and can wake at night and say "she is scared of the dark and mummy". The judge referenced the woman's admissions to police in the immediate aftermath of the incident. She indicated to them that she was suffering from depression, when asked if she had mental health issues she told police: "Considering what I have done, I probably do". When asked if she was depressed, she responded: "Depression? 100% I cry too much." The judge said he was "satisfied that she was suffering from mild to moderate depression. Probably more to the moderate range". He agreed that her judgement was impacted. He noted she had expressed remorse, was a victim of modern-day slavery, and said the offending was an isolated incident but also said it represented a serious breach of trust and that the level of harm done was high. She was sentenced to 10 years, half on licence. Due to time served she is set to be released to start her five-year-period on licence. Conditions imposed include that she is not to have any contact with anyone under 18 years of age and must attend any necessary medical appointments. title: London misses out to Nairobi in World Athletics bid
description: London has lost to Nairobi in its bid to host the World Athletics Championships in 2029, while the 2031 event will be held in Munich.
body: The London Stadium hosted the World Athletics Championships in 2017 London has missed out to Nairobi in the bid to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships. The decision, which means an African city will host the event for the first time, was confirmed at a World Athletics council meeting in Budapest. World Athletics president Sebastian Coe said Nairobi had presented "a compelling and emotional bid". "We were fortunate to have four outstanding bids for 2029 and 2031, and this was not an easy decision for the council," said Coe. "With this decision today, we continue to fulfil our mission of growing athletics worldwide with the hosting of our World Athletics Championships in Asia, Africa and Europe over its next three editions. "Nairobi presented a compelling and emotional bid, and taking the World Athletics Championships to Africa for the first time will be historic. "It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances. Nairobi has demonstrated emphatically that this is their moment." The London Stadium, home of Championship club West Ham United, was the proposed host venue for the UK bid. The stadium was also used for the 2012 Olympic Games and the yearly London Diamond League, and also when the city last hosted the Worlds in 2017. The UK's bid was led by Athletic Ventures, which consisted of UK Athletics, London Marathon Events and the Great Run Company. Jack Buckner, CEO of UK Athletics and co-founder of Athletic Ventures, said: "We are deeply disappointed that the 2029 World Athletics Championships will not be held in London. We believed we had an outstanding bid which would genuinely take the sport to new levels. "We would like to thank the Government, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, the Mayor of London and UK Sport for their fantastic support for our bid. Our thanks also to the London Stadium, West Ham United and our many stakeholders for their commitment and hard work to put the bid together. "Our congratulations go to Nairobi and we wish the organising committee all the best for a great event in 2029." Rome was the other city to miss out, as World Athletics also confirmed that Munich would host the 2031 event for the first time. Nairobi, the capital city of Kenya, submitted a bid for the 2025 championships but missed out to Tokyo. The city's Kasarani Stadium is being renovated before the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) in 2027, which strengthened its case as a host venue. Kenya finished second in the medal table at the 2025 edition, winning seven gold medals and 11 in total. This is a painful snub for London, so why did it fail? Those behind the bid had secured £45m in public money, and were confident of replicating the commercial success of the 2017 event. However, there had been uncertainty over whether West Ham would grant permission for the London Stadium to be used. That was finally confirmed last month, but only shortly before the bid had to be formally submitted. Another issue may have been the fact that nearly 10,000 seats were empty at Birmingham's 23,000-seater Alexander Stadium for the European Athletics Championships last month, with some fans blaming the cost of tickets. Lord Coe has refused to be drawn on whether either were factors in the decision, preferring instead to focus on Kenya's rich tradition in distance running, and the fact Nairobi will make history by hosting Africa's first world championships. However, the spate of doping scandals in Kenyan athletics in recent years will also lead to some scrutiny over whether it is an appropriate host. Britain is still hosting the Grand Depart of the men's and women's Tour de France cycling races in 2027, and then the men's Euros in 2028, and is bidding for the 2035 Women's World Cup. But at a time when government is also interested in a possible Olympic bid for 2040, today's decision is undoubtedly a blow. World indoor 400m champion and British record holder Amber Anning was in the stands as a fan for the 2017 championships, and although she expressed her disappointment to miss out on the experience of a home event as an athlete, added that Nairobi was a chance for something "really special". "There was a lot of disappointment, honestly," Anning told BBC Sport. "That was our dream. In 2017, I saw that we have the best crowds, the best atmosphere. So I would say it is a bit unfortunate that we weren't able to get the bid. "But seeing how Botswana was for the World Relays this year, I think it will be really special to have it in Africa for the first time. It's going to leave a legacy, so while it was not the result we wanted, it's still a chance for another country and another generation to inspire. It's an honour." Greg Rutherford, who memorably won Olympic gold in the long jump as part of Super Saturday at the London 2012 Games, echoed Anning's sentiments. Rutherford said it was a "bitter pill to swallow" for London to miss out but praised the strength of Nairobi's bid and highlighted the need for change. "We've seen over the years how well we can put on these incredible championships - 2017 was massive, record amounts of people through the doors, bums on seats watching some amazing performances," Rutherford told BBC Sport. "We also saw that in 2012 but at the same time, we are seeing something that is going to change the lay of the land. "Of course there is real disappointment but equally, it's going to be incredible to finally see this event in Africa. "I think what may have harmed it [London's bid] is that we had hosted one so recently, and Nairobi's bid was a very strong one. They are looking to invest into Africa so there is more chance for their nations to have the opportunity like this going forward and I do think we need to see change at times."
