title: My son was jailed indefinitely for stealing a mobile - we've waited 21 years to see him released
description: Leroy Douglas has spent almost as long in prison as one of Wales' most notorious murderers.
body: Leroy Douglas was given an indeterminate sentence in 2005 and has been in prison ever since "It's like your son being killed - he's here but he's not." Leroy Douglas was just 24 when he was jailed in 2005 for stealing a mobile phone and handed a minimum prison term of two-and-a-half years. More than 20 years later, he is still locked up. Leroy, who had a drug addiction, had a string of convictions for offences including petty crimes and shoplifting, before being sentenced for robbery and being given an indeterminate sentence of Imprisonment for Public Protection, external (IPP). His family said this came as a "huge shock" as it meant indefinite detention. Now 45, he is set to be released in October - a decision that came weeks before Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced he would end IPPs before the end of this parliament. Anthony Douglas said years of waiting had been "torture" for his son and his family as they remained in "limbo" over his future. He added: "In that time he's lost his daughter, lost his cousin, lost my parents." Leroy's sister, Natalie Douglas [left] and his father Anthony [right] have started a petition to bring Leroy closer to Cardiff when he is released Introduced in 2005, IPPs were established to keep serious offenders, who were perceived to be a risk to the public, in prison. They imposed a minimum sentence for offenders, but no maximum or end date, with criminals having to serve the minimum term before being considered for release by the parole board. But this is not automatic. They are also subject to licence conditions which they must follow or risk being recalled to prison once they are released. IPPs were scrapped in 2012 due to criticism for being handed out for less serious crimes but it was not retrospective, meaning - as of July - there were about 2,400 people still in prison on IPP sentences, according to the United Nations, external. However, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said there were 2,271 IPP prisoners in custody, as of 30 June. The organisation, which wants an end to IPPs, said the sentence "violates serious human rights". Anthony drew parallels between Leroy's sentence and offenders such as Jeffrey Gafoor, who murdered Lynette White in one of Wales' most notorious crimes. Gafoor was was released from prison in 2025 after serving 21 years for stabbing the 20-year-old to death in 1992. "Leroy stole a phone, how is it right?" Natalie says it's been incredibly sad for her family and she cannot wait for Leroy to come home Human rights lawyer Karen Todner was instrumental in securing Leroy's release as he was one of four prisoners she submitted an application for the writ of Habeas Corpus for. The writ, which requires a person detained by authorities be brought before a court so the legality of the detention may be examined, resulted in it being agreed their detention was unlawful. Despite this, Todner, said Leroy's release conditions were "so stringent, his liberty is restricted". His relatives are also unhappy as he will have to spend six months with an electronic tag, housed three hours away from them in Cardiff. Anthony believes his son is being "set up to fail" as he feels Leroy needs to be around his family for his well being. "It's like he's being taken out of the frying pan and into the fryer," he said. Leory's sister Natalie Douglas has launched a petition for to him be housed closer to home, calling on the justice system to correct "part of the years' worth of oversight". She said his family wanted to welcome him back with open arms and provide "the support system he never had while being lost in this unforgiving system". Natalie is campaigning to bring Leroy closer to home in Cardiff "I have a lump in the back of my throat just speaking about it," Anthony said. "I'm just astounded, 20 years they wouldn't let him out, but they still put conditions on it." Leroy applied for parole five times while in prison, but was rejected each time due to what his family said was incomplete courses. While going through addiction in the past, his family said he tested negative for drugs while in prison and did not have a history of violence. Anthony added: "I want to know why is he being released so far from home, and can't come home to family. "They're putting him with people from the same environment he's trying to leave behind." Natalie [left] says she and her mother visit Leroy every month and speak to him on the phone every day Anthony said he asked the prison for answers about the conditions of his release, but got no response and feels Leroy has been "tortured" for something. He added: "He went in as a kid and will come out as a man. "He's going to need counselling, he's suffering from mental pain and been sent away from family." The MoJ said: "It is right that IPP sentences were abolished and, as the prime minister and lord chancellor announced, we will set out plans to end the historic injustice of these sentences. "This will take a cross-party approach to propose a way forward with public protection and victims at the heart of these reforms. "As the IPP annual report shows, support has significantly improved for these offenders, with greater access to rehabilitation and mental health support." The MoJ said the number of people serving IPP sentences in the community had been cut from 3,018 in December 2023 to 891 in December 2025. title: Joint-worst start since 1992 and fan protests - Man Utd's day to forget
description: Manchester United fans protested inside and outside Old Trafford before Sunday's derby, then saw their team lose to 10-man Manchester City
body: Manchester United minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and co-chair Avram Glazer were at Old Trafford for the 1-0 defeat by Manchester City Sir Jim Ratcliffe cannot have imagined it would be like this. When Ratcliffe agreed on Christmas Eve 2023 to spend £1.25bn to buy a minority stake in Manchester United, his intention was to restore the ailing club to its past glories. Sitting in the directors' box at Old Trafford watching United lose 1-0 to a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men midway through the first half was definitely not part of the plan. Ratcliffe knew major decisions needed to be made in order to slash the club's losses. And he knew they were bound to be unpopular. But nearly three years on, he presumably felt the green shoots of recovery would be starting to grow by now. After all, the project chief executive Omar Berrada spoke to staff about in September 2024 was an aspiration to win the Premier League title in 2028. In other words, next season. On the evidence of this 199th Manchester derby, United are a very long shot to achieve Berrada's target. At this point, even pacifying the thousands of fans who protested against the club's ownership before the Old Trafford defeat by 10-man City looks beyond them. United now have four points from their opening four games. It equals their worst start to a Premier League season since 1992-93. Last season under Ruben Amorim, they also had four points from four matches. Manchester United fans unfurled a banner inside Old Trafford criticising the club's owners To be clear, United's fans have - to a greater or lesser degree - protested against the owners since the Glazer family landed £600m-worth of debt on to a previously debt-free club with their leveraged buy-out in 2005. In their most recent accounts to 31 March, United had an overall debt of £1.3bn, including outstanding transfer fees. Since then they have refinanced $425m (£314m) worth of bonds at a higher interest rate than they had been previously. They also took an additional $125m (£92.4m) but are yet to explain what the additional funds will be used for. The club's current financial position will be revealed on 23 September when it publishes its full year accounts to 30 June 2026. Ratcliffe's involvement promised to change the situation. Yet many fans argue that, if anything, things have got worse. Ill feeling has spilled over since United launched a ticket-touting investigation in the summer. Although they have admitted to underestimating the number of fans who shared their account details and toned down some of the threats around season ticket confiscation if supporters failed to respond as requested, United officials defended the investigation. Last week, they revealed 685 fan accounts had been banned, with a further 464 either sanctioned or warned. However, United added that "468 cases were resolved after supporters responded with the relevant information. No further action was taken, as the information provided satisfactorily explained the activity identified". Many match-going fans felt the investigation was an attack on them and decided to use the City game to protest - inside and outside Old Trafford. Huge numbers with flares gathered outside the ground, heeding a call from the 1958 Group, before making their way through the Munich tunnel under the stadium. Inside, The Red Army group of fans opted not to bring in their usual banners - instead display a single banner above the players' tunnel stating: "The way you treat us is a disgrace." It meant the only banners in the stadium were the ones the club had themselves put up. "Unless our generational match-going support is given a real voice that is actually listened to, the little that remains of our fan culture will soon be gone forever," said The Red Army group in a statement. "TRA aren't a protest group, we're an 'atmosphere' group but we've never shied away from making our position clear when we believe not doing so would be to the detriment of the interests of match-going supporters." It was noticeable many songs were sung in direct protest against Ratcliffe, as well as the Glazers. "We wanted the Glazers out and that will never change," said Steve Compton of the the 1958 Group. "Ratcliffe came in and gave us a glimmer, but his idea of putting Manchester back in Man Utd couldn't be any further from the truth. "The club have made many statements, but one thing they haven't done is actually apologise to anyone. We've had hundreds of messages directly - this has affected people's health. "These are regular Joes, working-class people who are sent an email telling them their ticket's been suspended with no actual evidence. How do you defend something you don't know what you're defending against?" The 1958 Group's allegation, which has been voiced by other fan groups, contradicts United's own comments on Friday that state they did advise fans what they were being accused of. The club declined to comment on the protests. Foden sees red as Mainoo impresses - Manchester derby ratings The 1958 Group of Manchester United fans display a banner in their protest outside Old Trafford There were boos from the home fans at the final whistle, although it was not entirely clear whether the reaction was triggered by their team's performance or the officials over the controversial offside call that confirmed Erling Haaland's second-half winner should stand. Since Berrada spoke to staff, United have delivered their worst starts in three decades. Many United supporters feel an overall transfer spend of £148m this summer was not enough after Carrick's mid-season arrival led to an improvement that secured a third-place finish. title: Will record donations to Reform go down as a moment of political change?
description: Andy Burnham is likely to face fresh pressure to further change the rules on party donations, writes Jack Fenwick.
body: When news of Reform UK's two record-breaking £36m donations emerged this weekend, it felt as if Nigel Farage's inner circle was attempting a fightback. The last few months have proved difficult for the party, with a dip in the polls, a spike in infighting and a series of questions about money that simply won't go away. In contrast, the mood within the ranks of Labour and the Conservatives has been fairly chipper. Most Labour MPs feel Andy Burnham has got off to an impressive start as prime minister, while many Conservatives are feeling confident about Kemi Badenoch's recent reshuffle of her top team. But Reform has been quietly - and as of this weekend rather loudly - building a formidable war chest. Even before these two mega donations, Reform had raised £30.5m since the start of the year, more than double their nearest rivals. This extra £72m takes them into uncharted financial territory, which the party says will be used to hire the brightest policy minds, as well as up to 400 campaign managers in every target seat around the country. In a world of fractured politics, when seats can be won on increasingly smaller percentages of the vote, having a ground campaign that is effective at getting out the core voter base could become increasingly important. Some in Westminster have been less than convinced by Burnham's insistence that he won't call an early general election. It might be tempting for the prime minister to go to the polls before Farage has had time to splash the cash on a shiny new party machine. Some Labour MPs think that could factor into his thinking, but one Number 10 source insisted Reform's extra cash does not make an early election any more likely. Burnham is now likely to come under increasing pressure to further change the rules on party donations. Labour is already planning to introduce a cap on the amount of money a British citizen living overseas can donate. There has been much talk about whether that could impact the donations to Reform by cryptocurrency billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, but when interviewed by the BBC, Angela Rayner refused to say whether the two would be caught up in the rule changes. The Liberal Democrats and Greens have also called for a cap for people based in Britain too, to prevent future mega donations. Burnham has indicated that he's open to having that conversation, but chose not to support an effort by some Labour MPs earlier this month to tighten the rules. Rayner confirmed this morning that it was still something being considered by ministers. The Electoral Commission is looking at what more should be done in this area and the calls from within Labour for further change will now grow stronger. Government sources insist this weekend's donations are not being viewed inside Downing Street as a game-changing moment in this debate. But people across the political spectrum are now asking whether this massive injection of money will be remembered as a key moment when politics in this country changed. title: Nepo baby is a horrific term, says Zeta-Jones
description: The Chicago star's children Dylan and Carys have both gone into showbiz, following in her footsteps.
body: Hollywood star Catherine Zeta-Jones has declared the phrase "nepo baby" is "horrific". The Mumbles-born actor told The Sunday Times: "These kids didn't ask to be born into this." The term nepo baby refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs. The 56-year-old is married to Kirk Douglas' son, Michael Douglas, and they have two children - Dylan and Carys - who have both followed their parents into showbiz. Dylan, she said, was pursuing acting while Carys was interested in directing. She insisted her children were "plugging away". Catherine Zeta-Jones describes herself as "a bit of an eclectic collector" "You have to go with your dreams, your passion," Zeta-Jones said. "It's hard for them to forge a way forward on their own. "This horrific phrase 'nepo baby' is horrible because these kids didn't ask to be born into this, they're finding their own way in life. "But they love it, and they're good. "Otherwise, Michael and I would be the first to go, 'you know what? Maybe law school looks really good'." Zeta-Jones' big break came when she landed a West End role in 42nd Street in 1987, becoming a household name in the UK in 1991 when she starred in ITV hit The Darling Buds Of May with Only Fools and Horses legend David Jason. She has since become a global superstar, with roles in The Mask Of Zorro, Entrapment, Traffic and 2002's adaptation of Chicago. "I had a sniff of the joy of being in the theatre so young," she said. "I went, 'I want to do this. I can't imagine going through school and A-Levels in Swansea.'" Zeta-Jones met Romancing The Stone star Douglas, 81, at France's Deauville Film Festival, in August 1998. With a 25-year age gap between them, they were engaged a year later, marrying at The Plaza hotel in New York in 2000. Dylan was born in 2000 and Carys in 2003. title: Reform confident it won't need to repay any of £72m under proposed new donor rules
description: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner says rule changes on donations from UK expats would apply retrospectively and anyone not complying with them would have "to return that money".
body: This video can not be played Watch: Donations 'entirely in line with the law', says Jenrick Reform UK believes the £72m in donations it has received from two cryptocurrency billionaires were "entirely in line with the law", the party's economic spokesman has said. Robert Jenrick told the BBC he did not expect that the party will have to return any of the money from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas. The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March. "These two donations are entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it's going to be in the future," Jenrick said. As well as limiting how much British citizens can donate to political parties from overseas, the government has proposed a minimum residency period in which the £100,000 cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK. This would be in place for the remainder of the calendar year and the following calendar year after the person returns. Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the rule changes would apply retrospectively and anyone not complying with them would have "to return that money". Rayner added she was not commenting specifically on Delo and Harborne as she does not "understand" their "circumstances". Answering questions about the donations following Rayner's remarks, Jenrick said: "It might be that Angela Rayner or the government keep trying to change the law to make it even harder for people to donate to Reform, nothing would surprise me. "But, as it stands, we believe these are entirely in line with the law." BBC News has been told that both Delo and Harborne have returned to the UK. Delo is understood to have been back in the country since last year. Jenrick said Delo had returned to the UK "in part so that he can comply with the changes to the law". In a statement after the programme, a Reform UK spokesman said: "We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won't ever have to be handed back." One person familiar with the government's proposed changes said the issue of whether Delo and Harborne are affected would likely come down to how ministers choose to define UK residency. They said one way would be to adopt the same definition used in tax laws, but stressed how complex the rules around residency are. Who is Reform donor and crypto billionaire Ben Delo? Reform receives second £36m donation in two days as crypto investor matches record The government's proposed changes were added to the Representation of the People Bill after they were approved by MPs this month. The bill still needs to be scrutinised in the House of Lords. Rayner said the proposals were "directly as a result" of a review by former top civil servant Philip Rycroft, external, published on 25 March. Rayner said: "We said that because of the intention of the legislation and the recommendations, which we accepted, was known in the public domain that it would be retrospective to that date. "That legislation is going through Parliament at the moment and we've also written to the Electoral Commission, which is an independent body, to see what further measures we need to take to protect our democracy." There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties. The government has previously said it was "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors", and has established a new taskforce to do this. It did not support calls from some MPs for a cap but Rayner left the door open to the possibility of further restrictions. "It's not as simple as we're saying we won't put a cap [on donations], it's a question of making sure that the task and finish group look at how we implement this." Since the 2024 election, the Conservative Party has raised £37m, Reform has raised £35m before Delo and Harborne's large donations, Labour had raised £21m, the Liberal Democrats £17m and the Green Party £1.9m Rayner said the aim would be to "protect our democracy in the spirit of individuals not being able to overpower and buy their way into democracy at the expense of those people that are at the ballot box". Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free". He said people should be able to support the democratic movements they wished but added that "what we've got to be careful about is where different industries, where different financial sources raise questions". Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart said there should be emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending. She said: "No politician should be able to buy the keys to Number 10." A Green Party spokesperson said there needed to be "more robust laws" around political donations, adding: "The Labour Party urgently needs to find its spine and support a tight cap on donations from individuals." Jenrick said Delo and Harborne - who each gave £36m to the party in two days and now share the record for the largest ever donation given to a UK political party - were "not buying anything, they simply support our agenda". Both men had already donated millions of pounds to Reform ahead of the announcement of their latest contributions. The Times reported in June that Harborne, who has been based in Thailand, had registered to vote in the UK, while Delo had told the Telegraph in April that he was moving back from Hong Kong. Harborne wrote in the Telegraph on Saturday that Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage". title: 'Slim chance' government will hit 1.5m new homes target, Rayner tells BBC
description: High construction costs and the Iran war are threatening the key manifesto pledge, the housing secretary says.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Angela Rayner says target will be difficult to meet but government "taking action" on social housing There is only a "slim chance" the government will meet its target of building 1.5 million homes in England by the next election, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has told the BBC. "Headwinds" including the Iran war and rising construction costs are making it harder to meet the key Labour manifesto pledge, Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. "But I'm definitely not giving it up," she said, and stressed that the government was "making a difference" through investing billions in social and affordable homes. Data up to June this year suggested the government was behind on the rate of construction needed to meet the goal, which housebuilders have previously warned was too optimistic. Labour promised to hit the target through building both private and social housing by the end of the current parliament, meaning summer 2029 at the latest. This implied an average of 300,000 new properties would be needed each year - a rate of construction not seen in decades. Rayner told the BBC on Sunday: "It's a slim chance, but I'm definitely not giving it up." She said it was important to keep the goal - which she said had always been a "stretch target" - in place, but that she was "being honest with the public" that it would be difficult to achieve. "The prime minister wants us to make sure we're building council houses. He's made that absolutely, fundamentally clear," she said. "We're seeing home starts up by 15% last year, so we are making a difference." Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period" - although he has not provided details on exactly what this will entail. BBC Verify analysis showed a decline in the number of new houses being built during Labour's first year in power - continuing a fall that began under the Conservatives. Rayner's predecessor in the role, Steve Reed, last year admitted a sharp surge in construction would be needed to reach the goal - but said he expected it would just about be met once the impact of planning reforms took hold. Analysts have said reforms introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government should help increase construction in the long term, including changing the rules on green belt development to increase the area in which homes can be built. But some argue that construction is being held back by factors including high house prices relative to average incomes, higher costs due to global conflict and labour shortages since Brexit. BBC Verify has been tracking performance against the target using government data on Energy Performance Certificates (EPC). Each newly created dwelling must have an EPC by law, making it the most timely indicator of new homes being built. Data for the 12 months to June 2026 suggested about 203,000 new homes were delivered in England that year, far short of the 300,000 needed to meet the target. title: 'Forget Notting Hill - we set our new romcom in the east end of Glasgow'
description: Romantic comedy Premature is out in cinemas next Friday, despite a microscopic budget.
body: Elle Watson and James Rottger star as mismatched flatmates in Premature Film fans have had plenty of chances to spot Glasgow on the big screen in recent years, from superhero blockbusters to futuristic sci-fi thrillers. Now the city is to star in cinemas once again - but the difference is that it won't be doubling for another location. It is actually set in the city. Romantic comedy Premature is out in cinemas next Friday, despite a microscopic budget that is the fraction of Hollywood productions like Spider-Man: Brand New Day. The indie film - by writer and director Kevin Walls - was shot across the city, meaning landmarks such as Kelvingrove Art Gallery pop up - a well as the less obvious location of an east end flat. This video can not be played Rom-com stars fall in love with filming in Glasgow The film stars James Rottger and Elle Watson as Cameron and Eilidh - mismatched flatmates who face the prospect of parenthood after a one-night stand. "We shot quite a bit in a flat in the east end, maybe about nine days there," Walls said. "There is a key scene we did in a close there. It is not necessarily the most romantic location you would think of for a romcom, but in real life that's exactly where these things happen. "Why can't we set a romcom in a flat in the east end? It looks really beautiful on the big screen." The production was shot throughout Glasgow, including in an east end flat That vibe is something the film's leading lady agrees with, despite Glasgow's film appearances often being due to it looking Gothic. "We are so used to Glasgow being this dark and gritty place, but that's not reflective of the city overall", Watson said. "It's great having it on screen as a bright and funny place, with people falling in love there. Shooting in locations I've grown up around was great too, as I've been going to Kelvingrove since I was a little kid. "Part of me wanted to run around the building when it was all quiet. But when you see it on the screen it looks beautiful. Being from Glasgow you are so used to it that you almost become immune to the spectacle of the building, and how grand it is." Director Kevin Walls and stars James Rottger and Elle Watson are delighted to see Premature getting a cinema release Walls admitted to BBC Scotland News that some of the choices were made through necessity. "The locations were tricky because we didn't have any money," she said. "So we were begging – I'd usually go down and speak to people about what I was trying to do. I explained I wasn't going to tear up their space or anything like that." Premature is the first feature film Kevin has directed, having worked on short films and adverts in the past. He has also juggled other jobs, including lecturing and editing highlights of football matches for YouTube channels, with money raised going back into Premature. A Kickstarter campaign helped secure funding needed for a cinema release. "Cinema-going is really important to me, and through sheer determination I was going to get this on a cinema screen too, as it deserves to be seen there", Walls said. City centre pubs were used by the crew as locations Watson's character Eilidh harbours dreams of being an artist, but is frustrated that life is not going to plan. Her flatmate Cameron is meticulous and career driven, but everything changes for both of them when they drunkenly sleep together. "This whole film is about two people being chucked out of any sense of control they thought they had," said James Rottger, who plays the leading man. "Particularly for Cameron, that's the point of the film – I leaned into the bit of me that's a control freak and likes to do things a certain way, and then brought that out in the character." Like his co-star, he was delighted to see so much of Glasgow on screen, and being presented in a bright light. "It's brilliant big productions are coming here and using Glasgow as a double, but it's important we see Scotland on the big screen as itself," he said. "The film Kevin has written shows Glasgow in a warm light, literally and figuratively. The red sandstone flats, Kelvingrove, the pubs – it's all there." Kelvingrove Art Gallery is a location for some of the film's key scenes Premature marks Scotstoun native Watson's big screen debut, after mostly working in theatre and short films or adverts. Unlike his co-star, Rottger has a fair number of screen credits, including roles in Gary: Tank Commander and a couple of rom-coms regarded as a bit cheesy - Irish Wish with Lindsay Lohan and festive TV film A Hot Cocoa Christmas. However, for this film both stars say they could relate to their characters. "I'm probably closer to where Cameron ends up than where he starts off," said Rottger, who has two young daughters. "As a dad waiting for a baby to be born, you are out of having any control. The nerves you feel knowing you will be a parent is terrifying for the first time." More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland For Watson, the relatability came in a different way. "Any woman in her late 20s or 30s will have thought about children, it's omnipresent," she said. "You feel you need to be confident about your choice as it will soon be taken away from you as you get older. "But it was important the film is not just about Eilidh being pregnant – it's using that for her to discover who she is and what she wants from life." Elle Watson's character Eilidh is stunned to become pregnant in Premature Walls admits he had to overcome his own doubts during the creative process, having put so much effort in. "There were so many times you'd think 'what am I doing here, this is a terrible idea and won't work' – I had to push past that and be confident," he said. Seeing the finished product in cinemas will make it all worth it though, as Watson sums up. "It feels like a miracle for this film with a tiny budget an

title: Some dentists say more young people are grinding their teeth - are you one of them?
description: Millions of us do it, though few of us realise we do - but getting the right treatment can be life-changing.
body: Nearly one in four people are thought to have bruxism, although most are unaware they grind their teeth Ella can't remember when she first started grinding her teeth at night, but she can vividly recall the excruciating jaw ache, the headaches, and being told her molars were disappearing. "I was in so much pain," Ella says. "My face was changing shape and my teeth were at risk of breaking - I knew I had to do something about it." The 31-year-old has bruxism, a condition which can cause regular and often intense teeth grinding, but says the treatment she's recently had has "without a doubt" changed her life. Bruxism affects millions like Ella across the UK, external. Some studies suggest nearly one in four people experience the condition, although many may be unaware until symptoms appear. According to the British Dental Association there is some anecdotal evidence that bruxism is becoming more common, but no specific figures. However, some dentists have told the BBC they are worried about the increasing number of young people they're seeing with dental problems caused by incessant gnashing. "It is definitely on the rise," Dr Aditi Desai, president of the British Society of Dental Sleep Medicine (BSDSM), says. "And it's no surprise given that life itself nowadays can be so stressful." Ella says constant teeth grinding enlarged her masseter muscles and widened her jaw (pictured, left, before treatment and, right, afterwards) Studies, external suggest many of us Bruxers do it because of stress - but why do our jaws carry the burden of our everyday lives? What can we do about it? And can it actually be a good thing in some cases? Bruxism is an umbrella term which groups together four different jaw movements - clenching, grinding, bracing and thrusting. Some people grind at night, others through the day. Some barely notice they're doing it, while others can gnash through mouthguards and wake even the deepest sleeping bed partners. So how can you tell if you do it? Here are the signs to look out for: Worn, chipped or flattened teeth Headaches or facial pain in the morning Disrupted sleep and daytime tiredness Earache or pain near the temples without infection Teeth grinding is also mentioned more frequently in therapy according to the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy, which says people nowadays are more aware of how their mental health impacts their body. Psychotherapist Rahi Popat says more of his clients - particularly younger ones - say they or someone else have noticed they've been grinding their teeth, "and they can often link that to a really stressful time in their lives and realise that's when their teeth grinding either increased or even started". Trauma and stress can put you in "fight or flight" mode, where your heart rate increases, you release adrenaline, and your muscles tense, preparing the body for an external threat, he says. And because the jaw and the nervous system are so closely linked through the major cranial nerves, our muscles are triggered and we clench and grind our teeth. "If we do it overnight, it's a way of our bodies releasing some of the stress and tension we might have felt through the day," Popat explains. For Ella, nocturnal teeth grinding in her sleep became a way to release tension that had built up while she was awake. "I know it's to do with my stress levels," Ella says. "I have high functioning anxiety - you wouldn't think it if you met me. "I'm busy, and I go out a lot to mask it." In her 20s, she says she just "put up" with the pain. But a few years later, when her dentist told her that her teeth were at risk, Ella decided to get treatment. After her dentist injected her jaw muscles with Botox, Ella says her sleep and mental health improved Even though it's not routinely offered on the NHS, Ella decided to pay her dentist to inject Botox into her masseter muscles - the ones that control her jaw. The procedure relaxed them and reduced the tension in her face, and should last 3 to 4 months. "Over the past few months I've been able to sleep properly," she says. "I've got so much more energy in the mornings, the pain has reduced and my face is not as square." Dr Simon Cove, a dentist who treats both private and NHS patients, says the physical impact of grinding on our teeth can be huge. He uses a 3D scanner to assess his patients' teeth, and can see the wear over time. "Often people are not even aware they are doing it, but then we get to see the damage," he says. "If the teeth have been worn down to such an extent, treatment can be extremely complex and can cost thousands of pounds." But he says such cases are relatively uncommon and can take years to develop. A 3D scan can reveal the damage that teeth grinders are doing to their teeth While you can treat the symptoms - by wearing a mouthguard, for example - getting to the source of what's causing your teeth grinding is just as important, says dental sleep specialist, Dr Aditi Desai. "Too often," she says, "dentists give out mouthguards without checking why it is happening." It's vital that serious, underlying conditions like obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) are considered, she says. OSA is caused by a blocked airway, so a patient may grind their teeth to move the blockage in order to be able to breathe again. "That's a very good example of why bruxism can keep you alive," says Prof Frank Lobbezoo, a leading researcher on the condition. And even though bruxism has its negatives (tooth damage, sleep disruption, jaw ache, to name but a few), it's not always the "bad guy", he explains. "Bruxism is also important for the production of saliva," Lobbezoo says. "Moving the jaw muscles activates the big salivary glands. It cleans the mouth, it protects the teeth and it's vital for digestion." Some studies also suggest that chewing can help with cognition. "We know this in animals, and our prelimi

title: Drag Race co-creator warns of TV representation 'crisis' after BBC drops show
description: The BBC is cutting the show because of financial pressures, sparking discussion about LGBTQ+ representation on TV.
body: Drag Race UK judges Michelle Visage, RuPaul Charles, Graham Norton and Alan Carr The executive producer of Drag Race has said there is a "crisis of representation" on TV, following the BBC's decision to axe the UK edition of the show. Speaking exclusively to BBC News, Fenton Bailey said he did not believe there was a "hidden agenda" behind the decision, but feared "vulnerable communities are going to be even more vulnerable". The move led viewers to raise concerns about the corporation's on-screen representation, after it also cancelled two LGBTQ+ dating shows. A spokesperson for the BBC said the decision was down to "significant financial pressures", as it attempts to make £500m of savings. Other shows being cancelled include Celebrity Mastermind, Blankety Blank and Live at the Apollo, and more than 500 job losses have also been announced. World of Wonder (WOW) announced future series of Drag Race UK, including a new All Stars version, will be broadcast exclusively on the company's own streamer, WOW Presents Plus. BBC News spoke to Bailey, screenwriters, TV critics and former Drag Race contestants about the move and what it means for on-screen representation. When Drag Race UK launched in 2019, co-creator Fenton Bailey, who was born in Portsmouth but now lives in Los Angeles, said working with the national broadcaster felt like a "very special homecoming" for his production company, WOW. The US version of the show, created by RuPaul Charles and produced by WOW, had been on air for more than 10 years and was a runaway success, with dozens of Emmy awards and an international following. Fans were eagerly awaiting a UK series to showcase the unique British style of drag. Now, eight series and three spin-offs later, the programme will stop broadcasting on the BBC after the current series ends. "Even at the best of times, queer culture is vulnerable and you can't take anything for granted," Bailey told BBC News. "Just because a door opened yesterday doesn't mean it won't be slammed shut the next." BBC News understands discussions to renew the BBC's deal with the show lasted months, with producers hopeful an agreement could be reached, but talks ultimately failed due to the scale of the savings the corporation is trying to make. Randy Barbato (left), and Fenton Bailey (right) with Drag Race judge Ross Mathews Bailey said it was a sign of the "horrible financial situations" broadcasters are currently facing. "The team at the BBC are amazing and so passionate about the show, this is not an easy thing for any of the people I interacted with, or something they wanted to do," he added. Drag Race UK was consistently one of BBC Three's most popular offerings, but according to Barb Audiences data, while average viewing figures for the series rose between 2022 and 2024, overall they've fallen around 15% over the past four years, against a backdrop of declining TV viewing figures across the board. Bailey said the figures "haven't plummeted," but had instead fallen in line with other terrestrial TV shows, and said the number of viewers watching on social media had risen "because that's where the audience has gone." Following the announcement, some viewers speculated the show could be acquired by another UK broadcaster, but Bailey suggested the show's creators may prefer to go it alone. "We love partnerships, but in this particular moment, having the freedom to make the show the way we want may be preferable to getting into bed with another broadcaster and potentially be in the same situation a few more seasons down the road." A BBC spokesperson said: "As the BBC continues to navigate significant financial pressures and deliver the savings required of us, we have had to make some very difficult choices, none of which have been taken lightly." The Vivienne rose to fame after becoming the first winner of RuPaul's Drag Race UK in 2019 Scott Bryan, TV critic and author of Out Now: A Queer Journey Through Modern Television, says the move is indicative of just how severe the financial pressures facing broadcasters have become. "I can imagine Drag Race is an expensive show to make," Bryan told the BBC, "I can see the pressures the BBC are under, but it's rather concerning in regards to queer storytelling. "You see LGBTQ+ lives reflected on soaps and primetime dramas much more casually, but there still needs to be shows specifically catering to a queer audience, and it feels like very quickly the drawbridge is pulling up." Earlier this year the BBC announced LGBTQ+ dating shows I Kissed a Boy and I Kissed a Girl were also being cancelled. The corporation said at the time that it was "exceptionally proud" of the shows, but they had to make "difficult choices in light of our funding challenges". Author and screenwriter Juno Dawson says viewers have begun to notice a "pattern". She said: "I think that's why perhaps eyebrows have been raised, because Drag Race hasn't been cancelled in isolation. A couple of other LGBTQ+ shows have gone as well. "It's a shame this is happening at the BBC, because commercial channels don't necessarily have an obligation to represent all the communities in the UK, but the BBC does and it's supposed to represent all of us, including LGBTQ+ people." The BBC recently announced Smoggie Queens would return for a third series The BBC recently announced Smoggie Queens, which features predominantly LGBTQ+ characters, would be renewed for a third series, and it represents the community elsewhere through storylines in shows including Mr Loverman, Amandaland, Vigil and EastEnders. A recent report from GLAAD, an American advocacy organisation, found film representation had fallen for a third consecutive year, external and more than 200 LGBTQ+ TV characters would disappear from screens in 2026 because of cancellations, endings or limited-run series. title: Tom Felton: I'm so excited to see Rupert Grint play Ron Weasley again
description: The Harry Potter actor talks about taking on Broadway and his friendship with former co-stars
body: Every night on Broadway, Tom Felton walks on stage to a roar from the audience. He had expected the reaction to die down after the first week, but it never did. Almost 15 years after his final appearance as Draco Malfoy on screen, Felton has spent the past 10 months playing the character again in the Broadway production of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. I meet the actor in a dressing room at NBC Studios, just off Times Square in New York. He's just finished a live television appearance and in a few hours will be back on stage for his next performance. He greets me with a hug and says he is excited to speak to BBC News because his mum and 100-year-old grandfather will see it. His family are some of his biggest supporters - his mum has seen the show five times already, while his dad is due to visit next month. That support mirrors the enthusiasm Felton has encountered from Harry Potter fans, which he says still surprises him more than two decades after he first played Draco. "I thought the applause would stop in the first week and it has not. "It's very humbling and lovely to know how much the characters still mean to people now and if it brings them to the theatre, that's the best." He is also struck by how many of the fans now approaching him were not alive when the first Harry Potter film was released. "There are fans that approach me shouting 'Draco' who weren't even born when I was in the first film," he says. Felton was the first of the original Harry Potter cast to reprise his role in the theatre show, but he will not be the only one for much longer, as Rupert Grint is set to return as Ron Weasley on Broadway in February. The 38-year-old actor says he called his former co-star as soon as he heard the news. "We are typically - and he will agree with me - pretty bad at our phone game, but when I heard the news I called him immediately and I'm so excited for him," Felton says. "Who doesn't want to see Rupert Grint play Ron Weasley again? Come on!" I ask whether Felton offered any advice to his co-star but he laughs and says absolutely not, pointing out that Grint has already appeared on Broadway. "I don't think he needs any advice from me. If anything, I would be taking it from him." He adds that Grint has a "Ron Weasley laissez-faire approach to these things". More than two decades after they first met on the Harry Potter set, Felton says the friendships between the young cast have endured. He describes Grint, Daniel Radcliffe and Emma Watson as "best mates" and "family", even if getting them all in the same place is now difficult. "We are usually in four different corners of the Earth, so it's hard to get together," he says, adding that their support since his return to Draco has been "fantastic". Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson, Rupert Grint and Tom Felton are pictured in 2010 at the premiere of Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows - Part 1 As Felton and Grint return to familiar roles on stage, a new generation is preparing to take over the characters in HBO's television adaptation of the books set to air later this year. Felton recently met his successor, Lox Pratt, and "saw a lot of myself in him". Felton says he was struck by Pratt's confidence and describes him as a "charming young man and fabulous actor". Their families have even been in touch. "My mum is in contact with his mum and I'm encouraging him to be as cheeky as possible - but professional first." Felton says he is not worried about the level of scrutiny Pratt and the other young actors may face as they take on some of the best-known characters in popular culture. "You just enjoy it for what it is. "I'm not worried about that at all for him. He's got a very good head on his shoulders and what you don't know doesn't hurt you. I'm sure he's not one to scroll through negative comments." This video can not be played Tom Felton on Harry Potter remake Nor does Felton appear concerned that Harry Potter is being adapted again relatively soon after the films. Instead, he says the longer television format offers the chance to explore parts of the books that the films did not have time for. "We had two hours to fit in a lot of content and the wizarding world is vast, so it's exciting to know they can dive in deeper." "I hope the fans of the books and films explore more about Draco," he says. While some actors might want to distance themselves from the role that made them famous, Felton has embraced his connection to Harry Potter. He says the franchise has given him "a life I could never have imagined" and that, even today, it is "bringing people together from every corner of the earth". Asked whether this really is the last time he will play Draco, Felton is reluctant to rule anything out. "I suppose I said 15 years ago that was the end of Draco and I was leaving him forever, but here I am. "It's hard to say with any certainty what's to come." title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England
description: Changes will spell out that governments can change rules and that career choices affect repayments.
body: University applicants in England will be given clearer information about student loans before they take them out, the government has said. Ministers said they would spell out that governments can change repayment rules and that different career choices can affect how much borrowers repay. They agreed to some but not all of the recommendations made by MPs after an inquiry into student loans, and did not say whether they would reverse a freeze to the repayment threshold for some graduates. The inquiry found the way loans had been presented to teenagers amounted to mis-selling, after the BBC revealed the Department for Education (DfE) had compared repayments to £30-a-month phone contracts. The recent debate has centred around Plan 2 loans, which were issued in England between September 2012 and July 2023, and are still issued in Wales. The interest rate on those loans is the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation plus up to 3% depending on earnings, and borrowers repay at a rate of 9% of everything they earn over a repayment threshold, which is meant to rise with inflation every year. The loans are written off after 30 years. Campaigners want a lower interest rate, a lower repayment rate and for the government to reverse a decision last year to freeze the threshold at £29,385 for three years in England. Freezing that threshold means graduates start repaying their loans sooner and, once they do, they pay more than they would have done if it had risen with inflation. MPs on the Treasury Committee called for a U-turn on that decision as part of a series of recommendations after an inquiry this summer. The Treasury and the DfE did not say whether ministers would unfreeze the threshold in their response, but said: "We keep all aspects of the student finance system under review." The government rejected recommendations to: Split the cost of university evenly between the student and the government Stop using RPI to calculate interest rates Ensure promotional materials comply with Financial Conduct Authority's Consumer Duty, saying student loans were "very different to commercial loans" However, it agreed to "making it more prominent that... regulations may be amended by government and Parliament". It also said "more can be done to help student loan borrowers understand how their loan balance may change over the long term". The government also said giving students long-term predictions of how much they might ultimately repay risked being "misleading" because of "limited" accuracy. It proposed instead to "demonstrate how different life and career choices may affect repayment trajectories", including salary progression, retraining, part-time work, and career breaks. How student loans work for tuition fees and living costs 'Deeply misleading' school talks compared student loans to £30 phone contracts Phone contract comparisons 'amounted to mis-selling' student loans, MPs say Students starting university in England now have Plan 5 loans, which have a lower interest rate but also a lower threshold and longer repayment term. Nick Hillman, director of the Higher Education Policy Institute, who helped design the Plan 2 system, said the government had "absolutely rejected" most of what the Treasury Committee had recommended and its response would not meet the concerns of Plan 2 graduates. Oliver Gardner, founder of the Rethink Repayment campaign, said the government's response "does not go far enough" and he wanted to see "concrete action" in the autumn Budget. While Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury Committee, said making information clearer was "an important step" but "doesn't help graduates who are angry that they didn't receive the same service and are now facing punitive repayment terms on a loan which keeps growing". She urged the chancellor to reverse the threshold freeze in this autumn's Budget. In March, a BBC investigation found that as well as comparing monthly student loan repayments to phone contracts, the government told presenters to "avoid words [or] phrases like debt" during presentations in schools across England a decade ago. More than 120 MPs and peers recently signed a letter coordinated by the campaign group Rethink Repayment calling for an "urgent review" of the system. One of the signatories, Liberal Democrat MP Tom Gordon, who is a Plan 2 borrower, is set to introduce a bill calling for a review in Parliament next week. Education Secretary Lucy Powell has previously said the interest rate on Plan 2 loans was "egregious" and the issue was at the top of her in-tray. The Student Loans Company said it was working with the government to "provide clear, relatable and trusted guidance". Have you been affected by the issues discussed in this story? title: Diljit Dosanjh makes history under the famous Wembley arch
description: Wembley Stadium billed Diljit Dosanjh as the first Punjabi singer to headline the iconic music venue.
body: On Saturday night, under the world-famous Wembley arch, five words rang out: "Punjabi Aa Gaye Wembley Oye!" Indian megastar Diljit Dosanjh famously starts all his concerts by announcing that "the Punjabis have arrived". But this time, it was a play on the usual catchphrase. Dosanjh is the first ever Punjabi singer to headline Wembley Stadium, the music venue has said. Addressing his fans, he reflected on the significance of the occasion. "This moment will go down in the history books," he said. And as Bhangra beats blared out, fans erupted with cheers while Dosanjh launched into his biggest hits, from Born to Shine to Lover. Over two decades, Dosanjh has built a huge global fanbase, topping charts and singing with the likes of Ed Sheeran. He has even busted Bhangra moves with Jimmy Fallon, external, with the US talk show host labelling him "the biggest Punjabi artist on the planet". His landmark concert at Wembley further cements his status as a global star. Ahead of the show, the singer spoke exclusively to the BBC backstage, describing the moment as "a dream" for him. This video can not be played The first Punjabi artist ever to headline Wembley Stadium In London, Dosanjh's crowd was largely - but not entirely - South Asian. The hype for his appearance was building all afternoon, with fans arriving early to get in place. "MJ [Michael Jackson] and Madonna, he's that level for us," said one fan. "He's so good looking, and so down to earth," said another. "Diljit. I love you more than my husband," declared a third. When he came on the stage shortly after 8pm, dressed in traditional attire, the stadium erupted and the screams barely stopped for the next two-and-a-bit hours. His soulful voice echoed around the stadium, demonstrating his range, as he blended homegrown Punjabi music with rap and hip-hop. Throughout the show, the audience waved lights, sang along and - of course - danced. At times, the standing area closest to the stage resembled an Indian wedding, with fans copying Dosanjh's energetic moves. But despite performing in such a vast venue, Dosanjh proved again his ability to connect on a personal level with fans. He brought fans on stage, giving them gifts and taking selfies, and also shouted out those in the back rows of the 90,000-seater stadium, saying they were "full of heart". There was also exciting news for fans in India, as he announced he would be performing in November at the Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad. The concert was capped off with the emotion of the night - his track Main Hoon Punjab, which means "I am Punjab" - set to a spectacular firework display. "What an incredible show, the energy and vibe was unparalleled!" concert goers Amit and Rani told the BBC. They added that it was not only a privilege "but a moment to celebrate for Punjabi culture". Diljit Dosanjh performed under the famous Wembley arch From humble beginnings as a small village boy from Punjab, he made history in 2023 by becoming the first Punjabi-language singer to perform at the US music festival Coachella. He also famously made his Met Gala debut decked in majestic Punjabi attire. His meteoric rise has seen him perform across America and Europe, and collaborate with pop stars from Sia to Sheeran. His authenticity is a big part of his appeal. He remains true to his Punjabi roots, wears his turban as a sign of pride, and sings in his mother tongue. Away from music, Dosanjh is also a popular Bollywood actor - and a social media sensation. Even those who haven't heard his music have probably viewed his funny Instagram videos - such as him arguing with an Amazon Alexa device, external that couldn't understand his accent. From Coachella to Fallon: Decoding Diljit Dosanjh's stardom Now, he's performed on a stage that's previously been home to titans of music from Taylor Swift to Coldplay. For Dosanjh and his millions of global fans, it means Punjabi music, Punjabi culture and Punjabi vibrancy has reached an historic moment. Speaking to the BBC before his gig, he said he felt "thankful" to be here. "When we were going to book this venue, everyone said, 'Think again before you book, it's a big stadium'," he said. "I said: 'We'll see whatever comes. I want that our people are happy and can say yes, we can do this too!'" He reflected on the many artists who had performed there before him, adding that to follow their footsteps "means a lot, a lot". "It may not mean as much for someone like Harry Styles, as much as it means for us. He has performed on such stages, but for us, it's very special. Coming from a village to here - it's very special." "I feel good. I feel happy. And I feel good for my people. I feel good for the next generation," he said. And of course, there was only one way he could end. "We are here. Punjabi Aa Gaye Oye!" title: Fire at nursing home in Chile kills 16 residents
description: Ten people were evacuated from the home in Araucanía region in central Chile.
body: At least 16 elderly residents have died in a fire at a nursing home in Chile, according to authorities. Ten others were evacuated after a blaze broke out at El Edén home in Pitrufquén, around 640km (400 miles) south of the capital Santiago, on Friday evening. Jorge Granada, a prosecutor leading the case, said it was not clear at this stage what caused the incident. Chile's President José Antonio Kast said he had ordered a review into the condition of nursing homes across the country. "We will fully collaborate with the justice system to clarify what happened, determine where failures may have existed in oversight or prevention, identify what alerts were raised and what actions were taken in response to them," Kast said. "We need to know the truth and, based on that, correct whatever is necessary to do everything possible to prevent a tragedy like this from happening again," thre president added. The fire, which began at around 22:30 (01:30 GMT) was finally put out on Saturday morning. On Saturday, firefighters were still clearing debris and removing collapsed corrugated metal roofing. Police cordoned off the area for safety. "It is a situation that fills our souls with great sorrow and pain. We have been... providing support to the families," said local mayor Jacqueline Romero. title: Burnham and Badenoch revive red versus blue politics as Reform land 'gobsmacking' donations
description: As Reform slip back in the polls, Labour and the Conservatives rediscover a familiar political divide, writes Laura Kuenssberg.
body: Burnham and Badenoch revive red versus blue politics as Reform land 'gobsmacking' donations Look closely at the posters, placards and online posts. Your eyes aren't deceiving you if Labour's red seems a little deeper and the Conservatives' blue a little truer. Politics seems to have found a new rhythm, one that feels a little familiar, despite Reform's jaw-dropping new donations putting it back in the headlines today. For the avoidance of doubt, the scale of that initial £36m gift to Nigel Farage's party alone is like something from a different political universe. "It's a gobsmacking sum," a senior figure involved in running successive election campaigns for one of the big parties tells me. That was even before another Reform donor pledged to match that astonishing sum with another £36m, saying the first donation had provoked his "competitive spirit". But one cabinet minister is enjoying what they see as a newly obvious difference between Labour and the Tories. "It's clarifying," they say, a clear gap between Labour and the Tories' "sense of purpose and values". A member of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's top team tells me, "normal jogging is reasserting itself", hopeful they're at the start of a more straightforward, routine moment in politics after years of craziness, with smaller parties vying to shove the traditional tribes out of the way. The standout moment was at the despatch box this week when Prime Minister Andy Burnham declared that national security couldn't come at the expense of social security - a phrase immediately seized on by the Tories, interpreting it as the PM saying he'd never cut welfare spending to pay for defence. One senior conservative said: "It was a real line in the sand, we could never have imagined Sir Keir Starmer saying that." The party seems cock-a-hoop at a line they can use again and again, asserting the prime minister cares more about welfare than guarding against war. But there is a positive atmosphere in No 10 too, one source telling me that the face-offs between Badenoch and Burnham have "breathed new life into the Labour versus Tory dynamic". How can they both be happy, when ultimately politics is a contest and there can only be one winner in the end? Well, on the security spat, Burnham's backers are adamant he does want to cut welfare spending, and find more money for defence. How does that stack up with his words this week? I'm told No 10 will explain in more detail his belief that security also means secure communities, which aren't created by slashing benefits. Crucially, they reckon while cutting welfare might appeal to some voters, "once you dig into the 'who' and the 'how' of doing that, public support wavers, and when Kemi talks about housing benefit cuts, public opinion goes all over the shop". They even cite that moment as evidence that the prime minister is "happy to grab thorny issues and put himself at the centre of them", as he did with the early release of prisoners. He'll give a grabby-sounding view before the government has found a solution to a problem, stake part of his reputation on it, and make the case, hoping it will work out. The choices are only going to get harder and harder though. "Hope" as a slogan and a strategy could never be enough. But when politics is fundamentally a contest, how can both the traditional political tribes be buoyant? For Labour, it's not just the obvious change of leader to a more effective politician who is much more at ease talking to the public, whether that's an eight-second TikTok or his long explanations of his positions expressed in a newspaper opinion piece and posted on Facebook. It's that Burnham is making arguments that are more appealing to Labour's psychology – build council houses, take stronger action against the worst excesses of the Israeli government, stand up for those who need to rely on benefits from the state. Labour believes, for now, they have a leader who is simply a better politician, who is making arguments many of them find instinctively more appealing. The party knows what its leader believes, broadly at least. As one senior figure said: "He has a worldview which the last one didn't - he's clear what he wants and he's grabbed the reins of power." Another who has worked under Starmer and now Burnham said: "It's just chalk and cheese." And don't underestimate the importance of keeping backbenchers content, feeling understood. A government source joked the whips, the party managers, are becoming a bit "like an HR department" listening to concerns rather than driving the troops forward. But as Starmer found to his cost, backbenchers weren't prepared to be loyal to him when many felt he hadn't shown much care or loyalty to them. But Badenoch's tribe also seems more chipper because, as she has told friends, there is now a sharper ideological divide between the two parties saying, "it's much clearer to have those arguments rather than a process discussion with Starmer". Shadow ministers reckon it's easier to make classic Conservative arguments because in the words of one, "Andy Burnham is a classic old leftie and we're the obvious answer to that". Shock, horror, Labour sources I put that to dispute that is the case, one close ally calling him "a pragmatist", another denying he's further to the left than Starmer, because, "Keir was so hard to place". But one conservative source also pointedly wonders how long Labour's happiness with their new leader will last, given Burnham's rapid return to Parliament saying, "looking at the benches opposite there is a vision of somebody who has turned up to a Tinder date and doesn't quite look like his profile pic". title: MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying
description: The proposed law sought to introduce one of the biggest societal changes in recent years.
body: This video can not be played Watch: MPs share personal stories in assisted dying debate MPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end. Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270 - a majority of 16 - against the proposed legislation. The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards. A similar bill in the last parliamentary session was supported by MPs before stalling in the House of Lords. The decision from MPs on Friday rules out the prospect of changes to the law on assisted dying in the short term. The bill tabled by Labour MP Lauren Edwards will make no further progress, although MPs and peers could make another attempt in the next parliamentary session. Assisted dying is an issue that has been debated for hundreds of hours in Parliament over the last two years and would have represented one of the biggest societal changes in recent years had it been approved. MPs were given a free vote, meaning they were not required to vote along party lines. Safeguards within the bill included a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death had the approval of two doctors and an expert panel. But critics said it included too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority. Please upgrade your browser to view this interactive Enter your full postcode or the name or constituency of your MP Note: a small number of postcodes do not give an accurate constituency for all properties. There were emotional scenes outside Parliament from both sides after MPs voted against giving the bill a second reading. Dame Esther Rantzen, who was unable to join supporters in Parliament Square, told the BBC that it was "so sad that people in this country won't have the choice" that terminally ill adults in other countries have. The Childline founder said: "I am sure a change in the law will come. I am deeply sad that it won't come soon enough for many of the people who need it, it's a tragic day." The broadcaster, 86, is terminally ill with cancer and has said she was now "too physically fragile" to travel to Switzerland to end her life at an assisted suicide clinic. Opponents of the assisted dying bill react after MPs voted against it Edwards, the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood, said: "Parliament has dropped the ball today. "It will be picked up again as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand." Labour peer and former Home Secretary Lord Blunkett told BBC Newsnight that it was a "bad day for democracy". The issue was "clearly not going away" and would re-emerge "in a year or two's time", he added. This video can not be played Watch: A 'bad day for democracy', says Labour peer Those in favour of a change in the law have said they will try to bring forward legislation again, with Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced the original bill, telling the BBC another attempt could come as soon as next year. Labour MPs Ashley Dalton, Dame Meg Hillier and Jess Asato, who all opposed the "unsafe and unworkable" bill, welcomed the MPs' decision. They said in a joint statement: "This is not a moment for celebration, we understand the deep concerns of so many people across the country who have campaigned hard for a change in the law. "But the truth is none of the relevant royal medical colleges, professional groups or experts will attest to the safety or workability of this bill." They said there was a need to "fix our NHS and sort out social and palliative care before we even consider introducing assisted dying". Sarah Wootton, chief executive of Dignity in Dying, said "thousands of terminally ill people will continue to suffer against their wishes in their last days and weeks". She added that she still believed law change was "inevitable". Care Not Killing chief executive Gordon Macdonald described the vote as "decisive". He said: "Our hope is that MPs now focus on repairing palliative care in the UK and securing the necessary funding to make sure that no matter what part of the country you live in, you can access the best possible care available and are treated with dignity and respect." Supporters of assisted dying react in Parliament Square following the vote in the Commons The bill in the last parliamentary session brought by Leadbeater cleared Commons with a majority of 23. But it ran out of time to progress through all the necessary stages in Parliament after some peers in the House of Lords tabled more than 1,200 amendments. During the debate, Labour MP Janet Daby was among those to confirm she would vote against the bill despite previously supporting it. She told the Commons she had "nightmares about dying and death" after voting in favour of the last bill, adding: "I had to wrestle with myself, knowing that I was not entirely comfortable with the decision I had made and my conscience was not at peace, and I cannot again, in good conscience, vote for the bill." In another of the personal testimonies during the debate, Labour MP Claire Hazelgrove spoke about her mother's decision to bring her late-stage terminal illness to an end "on her terms". The MP for Filton and Bradley Stoke said the "harmful status quo" meant her mother had died alone in October of last year, after living with a rare blood cancer for half her life. Hazelgrove argued that "not all pain can be palliated". Conservative MP Martin Vickers said his "firm" view was that "if assisted dying is legalised we will be poorer as a society, we will have a crossed a line", adding it would also change the "relationship between doctor and patient". title: I never got to experience my baby's scan, but blind parents like me can now feel them
description: Tactile 3D models created from pregnancy scans are just one innovation to support blind parents-to-be.
body: When I attended pregnancy scans a decade ago, the best the sonographer could do to involve this blind expectant mum was to turn up the volume on the heartbeat. But now, parents like me can receive tactile 3D models created from their scans, allowing them to have a special moment with their unborn baby. Reece Finnegan-Knight, who has been blind since his teens, is one of the first people to experience a 3D-printed model of his baby's scan with his wife, Sophy, as part of a new pilot scheme. At their routine 12-week scan, Sophy had attempted to describe what she was seeing for Reece, but he struggled to feel involved in the moment. Afterwards, when the couple showed the sonogram to their loved ones, Reece said it felt like "friends and family knew more about my baby than I did". But he said the 20-week scan was more positive. "The sonographer described everything to me, and explained why what she was seeing meant that everything looked good," he says. Reece says he wants to be able to fully support his wife Sophy as her due date approaches They also now have the model of their 20-week scan picture, through the scheme by the charity Guide Dogs. "I can't stop feeling it to be honest," Reece says. "It's so nice to be able to fully access something without the need for other people's descriptions or interpretations. It has enough detail that I know what things are and it just makes everything feel more real." It's an innovation which has made me reflect on my own experiences of pregnancy and parenting. Before my partially sighted husband and I started trying for kids, I researched absolutely everything it would entail, from how to use specialist apps to read pregnancy test results, to the bells and squeaky shoes I could use to keep tabs on a fast-moving toddler. I immediately discovered a community of people in my position ready to share their wisdom, and a host of tried and tested workarounds for almost every scenario. But a decade on, there are even more advances, and I've spoken to other blind parents to find out the best ways they tackle the challenges they face. This video can not be played The 3D scans giving blind parents-to-be a new way to meet their baby For Kim and Sean Randall, who have a teenager and an 11-month-old, the progress of technology is one of the biggest changes they have noticed in the 15 years between the births of their children. For their youngest child, maternity notes came in an app which could be accessed with a screen reader on their phone, rather than being handwritten in the traditional NHS blue book. Kim says it put her on more of an equal footing with other expectant parents, and helped her feel more in control. "I could check the notes, and any test results, when I wanted rather than waiting to have them read to me," she says. For the 20-week scan, she says Sean had researched the meaning of the different numbers on an ultrasound - like the baby's thigh length or head circumference - and used a specialist AI screen-reading app to have the text read out and the images described. Some parents say they prefer this method to a 3D model, because they can get more detail from audio description of the image than from physical touch. Parents Kim and Sean Randall found that much had changed in the 15 years between the births of their two children But it's not just scans where visually impaired parents can struggle. Reece, like many blind parents, says he wants to be extra prepared for when the baby comes, "so I don't get in the way or feel like a liability". "We've been labelling clothes, putting Braille in baby books and organising the baby bag so that I know where everything is," he says. Kim, meanwhile, runs Facebook and WhatsApp groups for blind mums. Together, we have collated a host of tips and tricks from blind parents over the years for what to do when the baby arrives. Carry your own folding mat for nappy changes and always have everything you need close at hand When changing a nappy, if you think you can stop, "keep wiping" - and use barrier cream, because the start of a nappy rash can be hard to feel Score a raised mark on any syringes or scoops you might use for making up feeds so you know where to fill them to Use a baby carrier or pram which can be pulled as well as pushed, in case you walk with a guide dog or cane in front of you to get around Once they start toddling, bells clipped to clothing are a handy way of knowing where they are at home When weaning, use a wipeable high chair with a waterproof mat underneath, to keep mess contained and know what they've eaten and what's gone on the floor The Royal National Institute of Blind People , external(RNIB) has also produced guides for expectant parents and those with young children. They suggest ideas like using baby gates to block off the kitchen when you are removing something from the oven, or the hall when you are answering the door. For parents who have some but not total visual impairment, Kim says children can be dressed in brightly coloured clothing while out and about so they are easier to spot. "I put them in feelable clothes so I don't grab the wrong child," says Kim, who has no vision. "One of my favourites is a shirt with a castle on it. You open the door and there's a dragon inside." When her eldest started walking, she says "we always held hands, but had a wrist strap connecting us in case she tried to run off". For me, clothes pegs were always useful for keeping outfits together wherever possible. Also consider buying socks the same style and colour - matching those is still a nightmare for me a decade later. If two items feel the same but are different colours, cut the label on one of them. Me with my youngest several years ago - I had researched everything that being a mum could entail Parents Reece and Sophy are just at the start of their journey, but are making sure they are fully prepared for what lies ahead.
