title: We've followed their lives for six decades - now the stars of 7 Up are bowing out
description: 70 Up is the final instalment in a series which began in 1964 and has followed the lives of 14 people.
body: 70 Up stars from left to right: Peter Davies, Symon Basterfield, Paul Kligerman, Tony Walker, Neil Hughes, John Brisby, Andrew Brackfield, Bruce Balden, Jackie Bassett, Suzy Lusk, Sue Davis Six decades have passed since Jackie Bassett first appeared on TV aged seven, skipping down the road with her little sister. It was 1964 and she had been selected by teachers at her east London primary school to appear in a documentary called 7 Up. The show interviewed 14 seven-year-olds from vastly different socioeconomic backgrounds. Inspired by the Jesuit saying: "Give me the child until he is seven and I will show you the man", it was intended as a one-off - a snapshot of Britain's class system and how it shapes us from a young age. "They only picked me because I never stopped talking," Jackie told the BBC, with an infectious giggle that hasn't changed since childhood. Little did she know then, but Jackie was being filmed for a show that would go on to be the longest-running documentary series ever made. In 2024, it was voted the most influential TV show of the past 50 years. Now the curtain is falling, with the final instalment - 70 Up - airing on ITV this Tuesday. "We didn't really know what we were doing, we had no idea what was happening," Jackie said of the day the Granada TV crew turned up at her school. In the first episode, Jackie appeared alongside her friends, Lynn and Sue, as they were asked questions about boys at school and their hopes for the future. Jackie said she would like to marry a boy "that's not got a lot of money, but has got some money". The nation was also introduced to the likes of wide-eyed Neil, who explained his plans to become either an astronaut or a coach driver; anxious Paul, who ruminated on the idea of one day marrying a woman who made him eat his greens; and pensive Bruce, who said his "heart's desire is to see my daddy who is 6,000 miles away" in Rhodesia. In 7 Up, friends Jackie Bassett, Lynn Johnson and Sue Davis were asked questions about boys and their hopes for the future 7 Up was intended to be a one-off snapshot of the class system in Britain The first episode was directed by Canadian Paul Almond, with the help of a young researcher named Michael Apted, who was involved in selecting the children. Apted then decided to follow up on the children seven years later. "The material was dreadful – as teenagers, they wouldn't say anything," he later said of the second episode, 7 Plus Seven. "Yet we started to realise the power of the idea; despite the film not being very good, everyone was interested in it." Apted went on to become a big name in Hollywood, directing blockbusters including James Bond's The World Is Not Enough, but he always returned to the show and said it was his most significant achievement. Every seven years, millions would tune in for updates on the cast's lives. Neil's dreamy outlook on the world as a child descended into battles with depression, isolation and homelessness, only to turn up as a Liberal Democrat councillor at 42 and then a lay preacher seven years later. Jackie initially said she did not want children, but by 42 Up was an adoring mother to three boys. Neil Hughes had battles with depression and homelessness but went on to be a Liberal Democrat councillor and a lay preacher As the series grew in popularity, Apted started receiving push-back from some of the participants, who felt they had been typecast based on their backgrounds. At 21, Apted asked Jackie - who had recently got married - whether she had met "enough men" before she decided to marry. For the rest of the interview, she mostly looked to the floor while Sue and Lynn answered questions. It took her 28 years to fully confront Apted over his questioning. In 49 Up, she told him: "I was really angry… you wouldn't have asked some of the other people in this programme that question. You will edit this programme as you see fit, I've got no control over that." Recalling the tense exchange, Jackie said she felt Apted could be out of touch, particularly over the changing roles of women in society. "I think he still thought we were all in the kitchen, as I mentioned to him at 21. I just thought, 'No, come on, it's about time one of us called you out on it, because he never never asked us questions about politics. It was nearly always domestic," she said. Jackie, Lynn and Sue filming 28 Up... ... and filming 35 Up with director Michael Apted on the left Jackie was not the only cast member to clash with Apted. John Brisby, who became a leading barrister, declared in 35 Up that the show felt like a "little pill of poison" injected into his veins every seven years and he wished his headmaster had never put him up for the show. He appeared in later series but refused to be interviewed by Apted. And Charles Furneaux, who later worked at the BBC before becoming commissioning editor at Channel 4, refused to appear after 21 Up following an off-camera argument in which Apted later admitted he went "berserk". Apted acknowledged flaws with the show, saying it was a "horrible error" to have only four women in a cast of 14 when making the original selection. Michael Apted became a Hollywood director, but always returned to the show Five years ago, Apted passed away, aged 79. The effect he had on the cast is clear in the final episode. Despite their differences, Jackie maintains deep affection and respect for the man she said "opened up a world to me that I would never have known". "I've always said it's a bit like having an uncle in the family. Sometimes you love him and cuddle him to death, and other times you think: I wish he'd just go away. "He would always, always help anybody and anything." Nick Hitchon died from cancer in 2023, becoming the second member of the cast to pass away after Lynn Johnson 10 years earlier. title: Running costs of vaccine damage scheme more than double amount paid to victims
description: The cost of administration and medical checks has now topped £83m, according to new figures.
body: More than 24,000 Covid vaccine-harm claims have been made - most relating to the AstraZeneca jab The government scheme to support people injured by Covid vaccines and other jabs has cost £83m to run since April 2022, new figures have revealed. The amount spent on administration costs and medical assessments is more than double the £32m paid out in financial support to victims so far. The Taxpayers' Alliance think tank said the public would be "stunned" at the cost and called for the government to urgently review the scheme. NHSBSA which runs the scheme for the government says rising numbers of claims are behind the increasing administrative and medical assessor supplier costs. Firm assessing Covid vaccine harm replaced after costs spiral to £48m Families failed by Covid jabs tell inquiry of pain The latest data, external shows there have been 24,260 claims since November 2021, although just 264 have been successful. The Vaccine Damage Payment Scheme (VDPS) was set up in 1979 to provide financial support to people who, in rare cases, had been harmed by vaccines of any type. Since the pandemic the number applying for damage payments has increased sharply. The vast majority of applications are now linked to the AstraZeneca vaccine and other Covid jabs. The benefits of vaccination are well documented. The AstraZeneca Covid jab is credited with saving millions of lives worldwide. But for those who were harmed, the resulting injuries are devastating. The full costs of the VDPS have now been revealed, external for the first time in the answer to a parliamentary question from the backbench Conservative MP Sir Christopher Chope. In response, health minister Dame Diana Johnson said a total of £83m had been spent on staffing costs, administration and medical reviews between April 2022 and March 2026. Under the scheme, claimants must have their application reviewed by an independent doctor, to check whether they have met the threshold of "severe disablement". If approved, they can then receive a one-off, tax-free payment of £120,000. The process can take months or even years. The costs of those medical assessments have increased from £4.3m in 2022/23 to £19.3m in 2025/26, according to new data published by the government. Based on the latest available data up to June 2026, the total amount paid out in damages to those who died or were injured after being given a Covid vaccine has risen to £31.6m. "The administrative costs and medical assessor supplier costs of the VDPS are driven by the number of claims received," said the NHSBSA, which runs the scheme on behalf of the government. "We have seen a significant increase in the number of claims received since taking over administration of the VDPS in November 2021." The campaign group Vaccine Injured and Bereaved UK (VIBUK), which was set up to support families affected, said the scheme was not fit for purpose. "It offers too little, too late, to too few and the cost of running it shows how inefficient it is," said the group's representative Kate Scott, whose husband Jamie was left severely disabled by the AstraZeneca Covid vaccine. Scott called on the government to act on the recommendations from module four of the Covid public inquiry and reform the scheme. Earlier this year, the Covid inquiry's chair, Baroness Heather Hallett, recommended increasing the payout and basing it on the degree of injury suffered. The government is due to respond to her recommendations. The BBC has previously reported on the large sums paid to an external medical provider which has been carrying out medical assessments. The Taxpayers' Alliance, a right-leaning think tank which campaigns for lower taxes and spending, said that the public would be "stunned" that the running costs of the scheme appeared to be "far more than has actually been paid out to those harmed". "When administrative costs are running into tens of millions, ministers need to explain why the system is so expensive and whether victims are getting value from it," said the organisation's chief executive John O'Connell. He called for the government to urgently review the scheme, cut "unnecessary bureaucracy" and make sure "more of the money goes to those it was created to help." The Department for Health and Social Care said it is "carefully considering" the COVID-19 Inquiry's recommendations on reforming the scheme and "will respond shortly". "In the meantime, we are working to speed up claims and improve the experience for applicants," the government said. NHSBSA said it continued to work "closely" with the government on "managing the costs of the VDPS". title: An extraordinary result - why did MPs reject assisted dying bill this time?
description: Although supporters say they will try again, for now the momentum has fallen away from a change in the law.
body: There were gasps and – to the intense irritation of supporters – cheers from opponents of assisted dying when the vote was read out in the Commons. This was an extraordinary result. After twice voting in favour of the bill, MPs have rejected proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing to an end the latest effort to change the law. The debate itself was tetchier, more irritable than when Kim Leadbeater introduced a similar bill in 2024. Then it was the first time MPs had voted on assisted dying in nine years. Since then the Commons has voted on this issue three times and had hours of debate. The sombre, respectful tone from 2024 has become more embittered. Given the strength of feeling on both sides over such an emotive issue, perhaps that is unsurprising. But on a deeply divided issue, both sides agree on why the result was different. "We always said it would come to turnout and it did," one supporter of the bill text me. An opponent messaged to say the same. The numbers tell a story. Last time MPs voted on assisted dying in June, 315 were in favour and 291 against. Today, the numbers opposed were similar: 286. But support for this bill has ebbed away. Just 270 voted for this bill, a fall of 45. So why have fewer MPs backed it, compared to a year ago? There are a number of reasons why support for assisted dying has dropped off. Some MPs have changed their mind. Janet Daby, the Labour MP for Lewisham East, for example told the Commons that after she previously backed the bill "my conscience was not at peace, and I cannot again, in good conscience, vote for the bill." But in reality those switching their position are a small minority. For others, the influence of Andy Burnham may have been a factor. When MPs last gave their collective view on assisted dying, Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister and supportive of this bill. Burnham, however, is not. For Labour MPs wanting to follow Downing Street's priorities, abstaining might have seemed a more appealing option. There will be other reasons why supportive MPs did not turn up today. A wedding, I'm told, took some away from Westminster. A trip to Ukraine meant others missed the vote. Already those in favour of a change in the law promise to try again. Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced the original legislation last year, has told the BBC another attempt could come as soon as next year. Supporters have told me they see this parliament, with such a large proportion of Labour MPs who tend to support assisted dying, as a "unique moment" to pass this change. "This result doesn't mean there isn't still a majority in parliament in favour of the principle of assisted dying," said one of those behind the bill. But for now the momentum has fallen away from a change in the law. That is a relief to those who worry such a change would risk harming vulnerable people. But it is a bitter disappointment to those who see it as a necessary and compassionate alternative to the status quo. That bitterness from supporters is aimed in part at the House of Lords. It was opponents' efforts there that ultimately led to this defeat. And it could hasten those calling for reform of Parliament's second chamber. title: Police boss criticised for 127-date theatre tour
description: Colin Sutton says it will not impinge on his police and crime commissioner work.
body: Colin Sutton was elected as Norfolk's Police and Crime Commissioner two months ago A newly elected £79,000-a-year police commissioner is facing criticism for announcing a 127-date national theatre tour. Opposition parties have questioned how Reform UK's Colin Sutton will be able to focus on his job overseeing Norfolk Police, which he was elected to in July. The former detective is due to present his true-crime show in theatres across the UK next year discussing police investigations, with tickets priced at around £40. Sutton insisted the tour "wouldn't impinge" on his day job, but Labour MP Ben Goldsborough warned "you can't police a county from the back of a tour bus". Labour MP Ben Goldsborough was surprised to learn of the commissioner's tour plan Sutton became one of the UK's most high-profile detectives in the 2000s, leading the investigation to catch serial killer Levi Bellfield, who murdered Milly Dowler, Marsha McDonnell and Amelie Delagrange. After retiring from the Metropolitan Police, Sutton wrote a book about the case, which was later turned into an ITV drama. He has also become a regular commentator in the media and last year was named as Reform's national policing and crime advisor. In July, after the former Norfolk Police and Crime Commissioner (PCC) Sarah Taylor resigned, Sutton comfortably won the election to replace her. PCCs are elected officials who set the priorities of a police force, appoint a chief constable and hold them to account. This week, promoters of Sutton's "Makings of a Murderer" show announced he was set to tour the country from January to November next year. One stretch will see him visit Consett in County Durham, Tamworth in Staffordshire, Hunstanton in Norfolk, Llandudno in north Wales and Leeds over five consecutive nights. A drive from venue to venue in that run would cover almost 700 miles (1,126km). Plan for drone-busting missile motor factory lodged New £38m jail wing adds 10 cells - not promised 170 Hosepipe ban could last until winter, firm says Promoters of Colin Sutton's show say it will offer "an unforgettable evening of real-life detective work" South Norfolk MP Goldsborough criticised Sutton's decision and said: "If Colin Sutton wants to be a celebrity that's his choice, but Norfolk deserves a police and crime commissioner whose first priority is Norfolk." Matthew Taylor, a Conservative county councillor who finished second in the PCC election, said he was "shocked" to learn of the former detective's plans for a long run in theatres. "If there is a major incident, you would expect the police and crime commissioner to be there, front and centre," he said. "Not operationally, that's down to the chief constable, but in terms of lending his support, communicating with the public, being active and visible." Defending his decision, Sutton said "I spoke to the people around me and we decided that it wouldn't impinge". He continued: "The logistics of each evening are that I turn up at about 7pm, I go on stage at 7.30pm and I'm clear by 10pm. "I don't do any rehearsal… I just literally turn up, talk and go away again. "The time I'm actually incommunicado is really reduced to the two-hour slots when I'm actually on stage talking. "I'm not a blue light service where I go round and turn up at things." Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? Contact us below. title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world
description: About 400 million people have access to some form of assisted dying - what are the policies of other countries?
body: Around 400 million people now live in countries which have legalised assisted dying. Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Spain and Austria have all introduced assisted dying laws since 2015 – when UK MPs last voted on the issue – some allowing assisted death for those who are not terminally ill. Just last month, France adopted an 'aid in dying' law for adults with incurable conditions causing them unbearable pain. While most jurisdictions forbid medical help to die, assisted dying laws around the world vary. Across the US, assisted dying - which some critics prefer to call assisted suicide - is legal in 30 out of 50 states, as well as in Washington DC. Oregon was one of the first places in the world to offer help to die for some patients, in 1997, and so has nearly 30 years' experience. It has become the model on which other US assisted dying laws have been framed. In Oregon, assisted dying is open to terminally ill, external, mentally competent adults expected to die within six months - and must be signed off by two doctors. Since 1997, external, 5,520 people have received a prescription for a lethal dose of medication - with 3,691 deaths. In a 2025 report, external, 61% of patients who ask for help to die had cancer, 14% had a neurological condition like motor neurone disease and 11% had heart disease. Of the 400 patients who took a lethal dose of medication last year, the vast majority (89%) said loss of autonomy was a key concern, while others cited: Losing control of bodily functions (47%) Concern about being a burden on family and friends (43%) Financial implications of treatment (4%) In Oregon, as in other US states that permit assisted dying, the lethal medication must be self-administered - the same is proposed in England and Wales. Around one in three of those prescribed a lethal dose don’t go ahead with it. Oregon is important for supporters of assisted dying in England and Wales as they point out it has remained restricted to terminally ill adults since its introduction. However, opponents say some of the rules have been relaxed. A residency requirement has been lifted, which means it is open to people from outside the state. The number of assisted deaths has also risen substantially over the years. Canada is the country often cited by opponents of assisted dying as an example of the so-called "slippery slope" - a place where assisted dying has been extended and made available to more people since it was first brought in. Medical assistance in dying (Maid), external was introduced in 2016, initially just for the terminally ill. This was amended in 2021 and extended to those experiencing "unbearable suffering" from an irreversible illness or disability. It had been due to be extended to people with a mental illness but that is now on hold. Critics say the more the law is widened, the more disabled and vulnerable people will be put at risk. There has also been a dramatic growth in the number of people using Maid. Roughly one in every 20 deaths in Canada are now medically assisted, external, compared to about one in 100 in Oregon. Across Europe, six countries have some form of legalised assisted dying: Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Spain, Austria and - most recently - France. In all of them - unlike the proposals in England and Wales - help to die is not restricted to the terminally ill. Switzerland was the first country in the world to create a “right to die” when it made assisted suicide legal in 1942. It is one of the few countries which allows foreigners access to help to die via organisations like Dignitas, in Zurich. More than 600 Britons have died at Dignitas, external in the past two decades, including 43 last year. The lethal medication must be self-administered. The Netherlands and Belgium both legalised assisted dying more than 20 years ago for patients experiencing unbearable suffering from an incurable illness, including mental health issues. It has since been extended to children - the only European countries to allow this. Both allow euthanasia - or physician-assisted dying. Most recently, Spain and Austria have legalised assisted dying for both terminal illness and intolerable suffering. In Austria, the drugs must be self-administered, whereas in Spain a medical professional can administer them. In England, Wales and Scotland, parliament has so far rejected assisted dying proposals. But assisted dying has already been legalised in one part of the British Isles. In July, Royal Assent was given to a bill in Jersey. Unlike at Westminster and Holyrood, the legislation was introduced by the Jersey government, which says it will take about 18 months to set up the service. The first assisted death could happen late next year. There will be a residency requirement of one year, in a bid to prevent so-called 'death tourism'. The measure, which most sets apart the Jersey legislation from the rest of the British Isles, concerns the manner in which those eligible for an assisted death can end their lives. Individuals will be able to choose to have a doctor administer a lethal dose intravenously, as happens in Spain, Canada, New Zealand and most of Australia. This is, in effect, voluntary euthanasia. It has become the preferred method of assisted dying in jurisdictions which allow this choice. The laws proposed at Westminster, Holyrood and Tynwald - Isle of Man - all state that death must be by self-administration, which usually means the individual swallowing a lethal dose. The Isle of Man assisted dying bill was passed by Tynwald (the Manx parliament) in March last year. As a UK Crown Dependency - like Jersey - it could not become law until granted Royal Assent. This was declined earlier this year by the UK Ministry of Justice, but Tynwald has since passed an updated bill which has been sent back to the UK government for a second time. title: 'Game-changing' suicide prevention charity expands
description: The charity provides safe spaces for men to talk about their emotions without being judged.
body: This video can not be played A national men's mental health and suicide prevention charity marking its 10-year anniversary is expanding further in Devon. Andy's Man Club, founded in 2016 in Halifax, West Yorkshire, was named after Andy Roberts, who took his own life at the age of 23, and describes itself as a safe space where men can talk about their emotions without being judged. After opening its first Devon club in Newton Abbot in 2018, there are now 14 clubs in the county. On Monday, the charity is launching a new club in Ivybridge. Roger Bond, from Plymouth, who went to his first session when he was "in a very dark place" about three years ago, said he had "never looked back". 'Game-changing' suicide prevention charity expands. title: Polanski selected as Green Party candidate for Starmer's former seat
description: The Green Party leader said the party is the "underdog" in Holborn and St Pancras but "can win".
body: Green Party leader Zack Polanski has been selected as the party's candidate in the by-election for Sir Keir Starmer's former seat in Parliament. Polanski, who is a London Assembly member, will stand in Holborn and St Pancras on 8 October as he seeks to become an MP. He was voted to be the party's candidate by members of the Camden Green Party ahead of local councillor Hamza Chowdhury. Polanski said the Greens "might be the underdog in this election but we have the momentum and we can win". He also spoke of how he made Camden "my home" when he first moved to London 20 years ago, adding he has "lived and worked across Holborn and St Pancras for many of the years since". Polanski said: "I love this place but I also know times are tough here in Holborn and St Pancras. My story of constantly moving around flats is such a common story for Londoners and I know so many people are struggling right now." He argued that voting Green "sends a clear signal" to the council and government that "we demand better for our communities". Polanski added he is "confident but not complacent" about his chances. He also said the election is about "putting pressure" on Prime Minister Andy Burnham, noting a Green MP would "work with him constructively to challenge him on the gaps in his plans". Announcing the result, Green MP Hannah Spencer said members had "overwhelmingly" chosen Polanski. The Greens finished second to Labour at the elections for Camden Council earlier this year. The by-election is an early test of Burnham's popularity with the public and whether Labour under his leadership is able to fend off the challenge from the Greens in inner-city constituencies. For Polanski, it will be a test on whether he can provide evidence that he can deliver on his ambition for the Greens to "replace" Labour. Labour has held the inner London seat since it was created in 1983 and the party's candidate for the by-election is Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali. The seat became vacant after former Prime Minister Sir Keir announced he was standing down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs. Who are the candidates in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election? title: Henry Zeffman: How Burnham got ready to govern with four key moments mapped out
description: As the prime minister looks ahead to autumn, Labour figures are asking whether his government represents continuity or change.
body: At the start of summer, in the pillared room in 10 Downing Street, Andy Burnham looked out at his new special advisers, the few dozen political officials tasked with driving hundreds of thousands of civil servants to deliver his government's agenda. Some had been with him in Manchester or Makerfield. Others had spent the past few months trying everything to prevent his hostile takeover of Sir Keir Starmer's government - and the new prime minister showed he was aware of it, going out of his way to praise those who had stayed on, for their efforts in the preceding years. At that meeting, Burnham's team mapped out four key moments in the coming months. First, the return to Parliament in September, when Burnham and other leading ministers would make their first statements to MPs. Second, Labour's annual conference at the end of September - Burnham's first as leader. Third, the Budget, taking place on 28 October. And fourth, the 10-year plan for Britain which Burnham intends to unveil in November. As MPs prepare to leave Parliament on Tuesday for almost a month and party conference season gets underway, the first phase of that route map is almost complete - enough for figures at all levels of the Labour Party to begin answering some questions about the shape of this new government. Most importantly, perhaps, how new actually is it? Does Burnham represent continuity or change? That question is especially relevant because those Labour MPs who pushed for Sir Keir to be replaced always fell into two broad camps: those who wanted a change of style and emphasis but continuity in policy, and those who wanted a major shift in policy. Both groups saw what they wanted in Burnham. Andy Burnham speaks during his first Cabinet meeting since becoming prime minister Going by the words of the new prime minister himself, he represents a profound break with the past, and not only the immediate past. In his first speech as Labour leader in July, Burnham described his ascendancy as "the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years". That is the timeframe he has returned to again and again, signalling not just a desire to reverse issues he believes stem from the Thatcher era but also to break with aspects of the Labour governments since then, including his immediate predecessor's. Some in government are already quietly questioning, though, whether the ambition of that rhetoric can be squared with the early signals emerging from the Treasury under the new Chancellor John Healey. Who's in Andy Burnham's cabinet? In interviews over recent weeks, and especially in his first major speech on Monday, Healey has said he will stick to Rachel Reeves's commitments not to increase the main rates of income tax, national insurance and VAT, as well as her rules on government borrowing. In the speech, he promised to "control public spending", and hailed Reeves for beginning to "recover Britain's fiscal discipline". It led to opposition parties labelling Healey a continuity chancellor. A similar critique is being voiced among some of his government colleagues. Most are more generous for now, arguing that Healey's first imperative - especially at a time of turmoil in the global bond markets - is reassurance, and that the Budget is the moment for him to show how he plans to substantiate Burnham's rhetoric. Even one official sympathetic on that point, though, asks: "Why did he do a big speech before he has something to say?" Those close to Healey argue that his emphasis this week on securing the economic growth which has eluded successive governments by spreading wealth around the country is a clear difference from Reeves. And finding ways to boost regional growth has been one of Healey's major causes since he was a junior minister at the Treasury more than 20 years ago - long before it was at the heart of Burnham's political personality. There is no question, though, that this week the minister who most starkly signalled change from the previous government was a man who coveted Healey's job - Ed Miliband, who was instead appointed foreign secretary. In announcing new sanctions on Israel over illegal settlements in the West Bank, Miliband explicitly cast the policy as a break from Sir Keir's approach, telling MPs: "We should have acted earlier, and it has taken the new prime minister to come in and recognise the gravity of the situation." On the other hand, acting alongside Canada and France in announcing the sanctions represented - in form if not substance - continuity with the previous government, the three countries having moved together to recognise the state of Palestine a year ago. The sanctions announcement was received with near-universal warmth from Labour MPs, itself a marker of change from the Starmer government. It was also seen as a sign of the ability of Miliband in particular, but this government in general, to drive its agenda through the civil service machine. "There is a much clearer sense now from No 10 of what they want," one official who worked under Sir Keir as well as Burnham says. "Before there was a bit too much of 'let us know your ideas for what we should do', now it's 'this is what the PM wants, give us options to deliver it'." That is a culture shift which Burnham sought to drill into his cabinet at their weekly meeting on Tuesday, still only their third such meeting. According to one present, the prime minister said: "We need to be on the front foot. We need to be bolder. Let's get on and do things. It's about deeds not words." Burnham has called for "growth in every postcode", and the establishment of No 10 North is a key part of that agenda Perhaps the most significant way in which Burnham is trying to make boldness easier for his ministers is by encouraging them to press ahead with policies when there is a risk they will face a serious legal challenge. title: Rayner defends pause to local council overhaul
description: The cabinet minister tells the BBC she wanted to ensure the plans could survive potential legal actions.
body: Angela Rayner has defended her decision to pause plans to redraw local council boundaries, saying she wanted to ensure they would survive legal challenge. The local government secretary also told the BBC she wanted to be "clear-eyed" about what the planned shake-up in 16 areas of England was likely to achieve. It comes after earlier this week she abandoned proposals in four other areas, in the face of legal threats from Reform and Conservative-led authorities. The surprise announcement on Monday has thrown the reorganisation plans into doubt, and drawn criticism from local leaders preparing for the changes. Councils in affected areas have been drawing up proposals and consulting with residents since the reorganisation was announced in late 2024, in a process that is already thought to have cost millions of pounds. Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Rayner conceded the decision to press pause had been "difficult" and she understood local authorities had put a "lot of time and effort" into their plans. But she added she wanted to have "all the information" about the proposals before going ahead with them, after her reappointment to her cabinet role under Andy Burnham, ten months after her resignation last year. "I got the legal advice and I hadn't had the time to review and to go through all of that, and court cases were looming," she told the podcast. "If I'm making a decision that is highly likely to be in legal challenge, I want to make sure I've dotted my i's and crossed my t's," she added. Rayner also said she wanted was "really clear-eyed on where we were going" with the plans, after Burnham had asked her to look again at the blueprints, which were announced by her predecessor Steve Reed. Political Thinking with Nick Robinson Plans for major overhaul of councils halted Council to take government to court over reforms In her announcement on Monday, Rayner said she was withdrawing plans to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk. Those proposals, announced in March, were already subject to legal challenges from Reform-led councils in Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk, and the Conservative-led administration in Hampshire, which were lodged over the summer. She also said she wanted to review plans for 16 other areas, including 14 announced by Reed days before Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister and reappointed her to her old role. Some councils affected by those plans, including Kent and Leicestershire, had threatened similar bids to challenge the lawfulness of the decision-making process. The government has argued that the plans, which will abolish remaining two-tier areas in England where county and district councils share responsibility for services, would make local government more effective and cost efficient. However, critics said the plans would not save money, while diverting resources from front-line services and leaving councils more remote from their communities. Others have also complained that the reorganisation could stymie or delay parallel efforts to merge councils into regional authorities led by mayors, which Burnham has cited as a key part of his economic plans. Elsewhere in her interview, Rayner said Labour under Sir Keir should have been quicker to recognise a Palestinian state, having promised to do so as a "contribution to a renewed peace process" at the last election. Starmer took the move in September last year, having spent much of the prior year resisting pressure to do so from Labour MPs. "It's always been Labour policy to recognise a Palestinian state, and it felt like we got there too late. It was something that should have been really clear," she said. She also denied that UK sanctions against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, announced on Tuesday, had been made to help Labour ahead of the forthcoming by-election in Holborn and St Pancras in central London. Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months. Pointing to the fact that Western allies had also announced sanctions, she said: "The French and the Canadians are not going to be like 'oh well, we'll just signal something to help you with a local by-election in London'". Reflecting on her return to government, she said a "big difference" between Burnham and his predecessor in Downing Street was his inclination to tell "the story of why we're doing something" in government. She said both men shared "passion and the commitment" to deliver for Labour in office, but added: "Andy is probably more like me, in terms of [he] wears his heart on his sleeve". The interview with Angela Rayner will be broadcast on BBC2 at 12:30 BST on Friday 11 September, and 17:30 BST on Saturday 12 September. Do you have any comments or questions about this story? title: People long for simpler times, say Practical Magic reboot stars
description: Actresses Maisie Williams and Joey King feature in the upcoming sequel of the 1998 fantasy romcom.
body: Actresses Joey King and Maisie Williams are joining the cast of the sequel to portray the daughters of Sandra Bullock's character Mix together a beloved film simmering for decades, a sprinkling of social media hype and a generous glug of star power and you just might conjure up the long-awaited sequel to Practical Magic. The 1998 fantasy romcom, starring Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman as witchy sisters Sally and Gillian Owens, received mixed reviews from critics when it was first released. But it's put a spell on a new generation discovering it online, with some now regarding the film as a cult classic and autumn staple. The demand for a follow-up by this new wave of fans helped convince Bullock and Kidman to reprise their roles nearly 30 years on, they say. "You never get the opportunity to do something where people really are asking you, 'please do it'," says Bullock. "It's usually us going to them." Actresses Joey King and Maisie Williams are joining the cast this time round to play Sally's daughters, Kylie and Antonia. Kissing Booth star King tells BBC Newsbeat she feels this desire for nostalgic content, which has become one of the defining forces within entertainment in recent years, has been influenced by "the world moving so fast". Practical Magic 2 sees the cast return to a world which is steeped in powerful ancestral magic "I think with technology moving at the speed that it is, we're really missing the times when we were less reachable," she says. "If we couldn't figure out something, we'd stare out the window until it came to us, and I think we're nostalgic for a time like that." She feels this can also be a strength of cinema as it can help "make memories" and "feelings" for people that they can revisit by rewatching. The upcoming release comes at a time when reboots, reunions and remakes are dominating film and TV lists. Game of Thrones star Williams agrees the drive for nostalgic content feels like a "symptom of people longing for simpler times", but says she is "very grateful" that they have made a sequel and not a remake. "I do believe in pushing the story forwards and I do believe in telling new stories," she says. "And I do believe stories can come back around and they can still be meaningful. "But I am not the biggest fan of the remake because I think it's a shame to withhold ourselves from telling a new story." The bond of sisterhood is at the heart of the 1998 film and continues into the sequel Practical Magic 2 sees the cast return to a world which is steeped in powerful ancestral magic with the characters once again confronting a family curse which condemns anyone who loves and is loved by an Owens woman to death. There are also nods to the original throughout, with bubbling family tension, dark romantic "witchcore" fashion and the iconic midnight margaritas. US acting stalwarts Dianne Wiest and Stockard Channing return to their roles for the follow-up, while Guardians of the Galaxy actor Lee Pace, Cobra Kai's Xolo Maridueña and House of the Dragon's Solly McLeod are new additions. Reviews so far have been mixed, with the Guardian describing it as a "nostalgia-bait return", external which is as "strange and messy as the first" but with "warm seasonal pleasures to be had". Meanwhile The Hollywood Reporter, external says the "slapdash" sequel "works better the less you look for any sense of logic, and the more you just lean into the transient joys of watching these actresses bounce off each other". Joey King says the idea of "being witchy" can be "empowering right now" Amid the scrutiny around the film, Williams admits joining the Practical Magic world was "a little bit overwhelming", but says the cast were "so supportive the whole time" and "welcomed us into the sisterhood". The bond of sisterhood is at the heart of the first film and continues in the sequel, but Bullock has recalled this was initially one of the criticisms of the original, external, with some branding it as "too witchy" with "too many women". With women's rights under pressure in some countries, Williams says it is a "challenging time" and she feels it's "so important in a time like this for women to be supporting one another". "We are in a time when young women are staying in education longer and women, before having children, are sometimes being paid more than their male counterparts, which I do find to be really exciting," she adds. "But there's a lot of work to do. "And this feeling of witches, symbiosis and power - I feel like there's something in that which can just push us forwards." title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health
description: Sleeping next to a snorer could be having a negative effect on your health, experts tell the BBC.
body: Have you ever slept next to a snoring partner and woken up feeling stressed, unfocused or forgetful the next day? As snoring is relatively common, it is often left untreated and dismissed as a harmless irritation. But according to experts, sleeping next to a snorer could be impacting your health. Snoring is caused by the vibration of the soft tissues in our upper airways during sleep, explains Dr Clare Simon, a dentist with a special interest in dental sleep medicine. About 40% of the UK adult population snores, with the issue affecting more men than women, says the British Snoring and Sleep Apnoea Association (BSSAA). And 75% of people with a snoring partner say they have had their sleep impacted, according to a US survey by the Sleep Foundation. Here's what you need to know about the impact on partners - and what you can do about it. Prof Ama Johal, a consultant orthodontist and sleep expert at Aerox Health, explains that the partner of a snorer can become "so impacted upon that it's almost a last-ditch effort on their part to get up and go sleep in a separate room because they have to sleep". He adds: "As humans we physically can't function without that necessity." Prof Ama Johal says many couples put up with the negative effects snoring for too long During the night, we cycle through different stages of sleep in repeating patterns, usually every 90 minutes. The deeper stages of this cycle are important for physical restoration. If sleep is frequently disrupted, you may spend less time in the restorative stages, meaning you can wake up feeling tired, even if you've spent a lot of time in bed, the BSSAA explains. Your brain processes and stores information from the day during sleep. Fragmented sleep - which can happen if you're waking up due to a snoring partner - can interrupt this process, impacting your focus and memory. Disrupted sleep can also impact hormone regulation, which affects your energy levels and motivation. Sleep also plays a role in regulating the brain systems involved in stress and emotional response. When it is disrupted, these systems can become less balanced, which may make you feel more irritable and less able to cope with stress. This is something Meg Warren, 29, experienced when her former partner's snoring would keep her up. She says: "Without fail, after a snoring-induced wake up I would feel on incredibly high alert." Meg, a charity media officer, would prod him throughout the night and try to coax him from his back to his side. She says she would wake up "feeling groggy and dazed, sometimes so much so that it would feel like a hangover". The snoring tested the relationship, with Meg explaining: "I always said if we lived together we'd have to have a spare bedroom for the nights of truly unbearable snoring." Simon says that broken sleep, caused by a partner's snoring, can lead to irritability, arguments, and - if it is decided that sleeping in separate rooms is needed - reduced intimacy. Meg Warren felt 'groggy and dazed' after a night of little sleep due to her former partner's snoring Anna-Louise Dearden, a 52-year-old journalist, says she sometimes sleeps in a separate room from her partner due to his snoring. Having this option allows her to prioritise getting enough rest when the snoring is particularly bad. Anna-Louise Dearden says her partner's snoring has led to her sleeping in another room at times Anna-Louise said: "If you wake up and you've had a bad night's sleep, you eat more, you feel more irritable." She used to wake up often in the night due to the snoring, but has found that wearing ear plugs is a "life saver" as they allow her to sleep through most of the noise when she shares a bed with her partner. There are things that can be done, say both Simon and Johal. But first, it is important to distinguish whether your partner is simply snoring, or whether they have sleep apnoea. "What you don't want to do is simply make someone quieter at night while potentially missing an underlying sleep-related breathing disorder," Simon says. Signs of sleep apnoea, a disorder that causes a person's breathing to repeatedly stop and start during sleep, include pauses in breathing, choking at night, waking frequently, and suffering from morning headaches. If this is what you are dealing with, you could be recommended a Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) machine, or even surgical treatment in some cases, Simon explains. For simple snoring, Simon said that lifestyle changes can make a difference, such as losing weight, stopping smoking, reducing alcohol intake before bed, or changing your sleeping position - such as laying on your side rather than your back. You can also suggest to your partner that they see a GP, who will be able to advise further or refer you to a specialist. An expert might suggest treating nasal obstruction or allergies, if this is what is causing snoring, or wearing a custom mouthguard to gently push the lower jaw forward and keep the airway open. Johal says too many couples put up with snoring "for too long", which impacts their relationships and wellbeing. "The key thing is that there is help out there, it's just tapping into it." title: Watch: Is the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition worth the hype?
description: Crowds have been flocking to the British Museum to see the Bayeux Tapestry as it's on public display in the UK for the first time since it was created nearly 1,000 years ago.
body: This video can not be played Visitors flocked to the British Museum in London on Thursday as the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition opened its doors to the general public. The Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidery almost 70m (230ft) in length and nearly 1,000 years old. It tells the story of the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066. Adult tickets to see the tapestry are priced at £33 during peak times and £27 at off-peak times, with an additional £3.50 donation. The BBC's Katie Razzall asked the first visitors if it was worth the price. Read more about the Bayeux Tapestry and why it's currently in the UK. title: What in the World
description: More people are doing it to feel confident socialising - but what are the risks?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·10 Sep 2026,·11 mins Available for over a year A series of recent studies suggests that drug use is increasing among Gen Z. Some young people are taking prescription anti-anxiety medications — such as propranolol and pregabalin — without a prescription. They’re buying them online or on the black market, exposing themselves to additional risks. Jacqui Wakefield, our Global Health Reporter, explains why some young people see these drugs as an alternative to alcohol. They want to reduce social anxiety on a night out and experience a feeling of euphoria, but without the calories and hangover that can come with heavy drinking. We discuss the risks associated with using these drugs without medical supervision, and the potential consequences for young people’s health. Warning: This episode includes references to suicidal thoughts. If you are affected by any of the issues discussed in this episode, or are experiencing distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. title: E-bike crime crackdown leads to 187 arrests
description: Footage released by the Met shows officers using high-powered Sur-Ron bikes to pursue suspects.
body: This video can not be played Watch: More than 185 arrested in Met crackdown on robbery and theft in central London The Metropolitan Police has arrested 187 people and seized 157 vehicles as part of a crackdown on prolific thieves using e-bikes and mopeds in Westminster. The arrests were for a variety of offences including possession of dangerous weapons, drug-related crimes, robbery and theft. The force said plain-clothed and uniformed officers carried out patrols in hotspot areas and stopped offenders known to police. The operations ran from February to July. Det Supt Gareth Gilbert, who led the operation, said officers were "staying one step ahead of the criminals who use high-powered bikes or mopeds to steal from Londoners". The Met said e-bike-related crime fell by 22% during the operation in key transport and tourist hubs in Southwark and Lambeth, including Waterloo and London Bridge. The Sur-Ron electric motorbikes are being used in several inner London boroughs Footage released by the Met shows officers using high-powered Sur-Ron electric motorbikes to pursue suspects who were trying to evade police. The force has recently expended its fleet of these bikes from five to 25. Gilbert added: "By disrupting this criminality and making hundreds of arrests, we're making London a safer place to live, work and visit. "Our approach is working, with neighbourhood crime down 14% over the past year and 13,000 fewer phone thefts." title: 'My cancer spread while I waited months for surgery': The cost of England's cancer wait times
description: Cancer care has got worse since the government announced plans to speed up waiting times and save more lives, BBC analysis shows.
body: Alan is one of thousands each month who are not being treated within the cancer target timeframe Alan was diagnosed with lung cancer after a nodule was found in June last year. The 70-year-old was meant to be operated on within weeks but ended up waiting nearly five months, by which time the cancer had spread, making his surgery more complex. "I was so frustrated and angry and couldn't understand why they would leave me like that," says Alan. On two occasions, scans were cancelled because machines had broken and for weeks he heard little or nothing from the hospital about when he would eventually have the urgent surgery. Alan is one of thousands each month in England who are not being treated within the target timeframe. Earlier this year, the government's National Cancer Plan, along with the NHS Planning Guidance, set out that 80% of patients in England would start treatment within 62 days from urgent GP referral by March 2027. This was to reach 85% by March 2029. But in the months since the government announced this ambition, performance has got worse, according to NHS England data, not better. Now, 71.2% of patients start cancer treatment within the 62 day timeframe. Previously it was 71.9%. Prof Pat Price, a leading UK clinical academic oncologist, says the government targets "are now simply impossible to hit", after what she describes as a "complete loss of momentum". Price attributes the current failures to a "complete lack of a plan or accountability". The plan stated that a new independent cancer board would be established, but it is still not known who will be leading this group. NHS data released on Thursday, for July, reveals 10 out of 120 hospital trusts in England managed to get 85% of patients to start treatment within 62 of their urgent referral by a GP. Radiotherapy UK analysis, shared exclusively with the BBC, suggests more than 2,800 extra patients would need to start treatment every month - a near 15% increase on current numbers - to achieve the March 2027 target. That is likely to grow as referrals keep rising across nearly every cancer type. Price says thousands of patients "are going to die unnecessarily, just because the government can't get their act together to treat people on time". For every month a cancer patient waits before starting treatment, their chance of survival falls by around 10%, on average. By the time Alan had his operation, the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes and the nodule "had grown at an alarming rate", according to the lung specialist. He has since been told the cancer has cleared awaiting his one-year review, but the operation has left him in debilitating pain. "I used to play golf and get out and about. Now I can't do any of the things I love," says Alan. Roughly 54,000 more patients will need to start treatment within 62 days before 2029 for the government to hit its goal. One NHS trust that is gaining traction on its waiting list numbers is Salisbury, but it is still not hitting targets. Staff say there is no single fix, just a relentless focus on getting the basics right; making sure patients know about their appointments and turn up, keeping IT systems working, recruiting the right people, making sure surgical lists are full and expanding capacity. Much of the visible progress has come through skin and prostate cancer, two of the most common cancers in the country. Diane had a cancerous lump removed from her face at Salisbury District Hospital a few weeks ago, using an innovative procedure, which checks tumour margins are clear while the patient is still in surgery. That means no follow-up operations, and it allows for complex reconstruction that leaves hardly a trace. "It's amazing, you literally can't see I had a large cancerous lesion removed from my cheek," she tells the BBC in the waiting room. Consultant plastic surgeon Neil Wickham checked her face, confirmed a biopsied lump on her arm was benign, and referred her to ENT for a separate lump in her neck. It is the kind of joined-up care the government's Cancer Plan was meant to trigger in cancer units across England. Diane benefited from an innovative procedure when she had a cancerous lump removed from her face But over in pathology at the Salisbury trust, head of department Lee Phillips is feeling the pressure. His histology lab receives cancer service biopsies from across the hospital for diagnosis. "The sheer volume of specimens we have coming in is our problem," he says. "We need more staff and more kit if we're going to keep up with demand," Phillips says. Radiotherapy is another bottleneck crying out for staff and kit. Like many trusts, Salisbury has no machine on site, so patients needing daily sessions over one to three weeks must travel up to an hour to Southampton, and sometimes Bath. But staff in Salisbury also say missed appointments, whether down to late letters, illness, transport problems or anxiety, are a constant drain on a system already stretched thin. Emilia Scutt, cancer manager in Salisbury, says that efforts to reduce missed appointments have really helped their numbers. "We know cancer can be terrifying so we are a bit like a dog with the bone, backing up patients and supporting them wherever we can." Trusts with the sharpest declines in performance - including Buckinghamshire Healthcare, Bolton NHS Foundation Trust, Royal Devon University Healthcare Trust, East Cheshire, and Torbay and South Devon - told the BBC they face pressures across the board. Rising demand, workforce shortages and diagnostic bottlenecks have all played a part. Some pointed to industrial action and staff sickness, others to reliance on outside diagnostic providers or major changes to how their systems work. All say they are investing in extra capacity, working through backlogs and redesigning pathways, and are already seeing early signs of improvement. "If government is serious about delivering on the ambitions of the National Cancer Plan

title: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog
description: The technology will soon be routinely used within the NHS, MHRA chief Lawrence Tallon tells the BBC.
body: The UK needs new regulations for AI products used in the NHS and other healthcare settings, says Britain's industry watchdog. The Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which regulates all medical devices and licenses treatment drugs in the UK, has published 44 recommendations to update its policies as the use of AI in the sector rises. The technology will soon be routinely used within the NHS, MHRA chief Lawrence Tallon told the BBC. "What I would expect is that patients will... increasingly see AI as part of the way that normal NHS healthcare is delivered," he said. "That should happen in a way that they can maintain their trust and their confidence in what's happening." The report was compiled by an independent commission and involved input from more than 12,000 people including patients and clinicians. Continuously monitoring AI products and removing them from regulatory approval if they malfunction or become less effective over time Giving patients the right to know whether AI is involved in their care, and easy access to information about the products involved The power to penalise the developers of an AI product if it fails to meet required standards An AI "L plate" system which would make it easier for new AI models to be trialled by healthcare professionals under close supervision "The medical devices regulatory framework predominantly dates from a period where we were thinking about things like hip replacements and knee replacements, or smaller things like stethoscopes and plasters," Tallon said. He added while current guidelines may work for simple AI products trained to spot known symptoms on scans, for example, the rules do not apply to more complex models. "Unlike most of the medical products we're used to regulating, these products continue to change after the point of authorization," he said. "As new data gets fed in, they learn, they adapt, they drift." And he acknowledged trying to regulate AI is a global challenge. "I don't think at this moment in time we can point to a single country, a single regulatory framework, and say that they have absolutely cracked it," he said. AI note-takers known as scribes, which are powered by LLMs, are reportedly used by 40% of UK-based GPs to record consultations and generate reports. But a recent study from the University of Edinburgh found patients could be less likely to share personal information such as substance abuse history if they knew the conversation was being processed by AI. Professor Henrietta Hughes, a GP who was part of the report commission, said that many of her patients were happy for AI being used during their consultations, but some chose to opt out. "Some say, 'I don't want to talk to a robot', and that is also fine," she said. Prof Hughes acknowledged that the scribes could make mistakes in their notes but said it was the responsibility of doctors to correct them. While currently AI is more likely to be used to assist with administrative tasks, or carry out symptom spotting overseen by a human expert, there is a lot of excitement about its potential in the health and medical research industries. Professor Alastair Denniston, an ophthalmologist who also worked on the report, described the technology as "an exceptional opportunity" for healthcare which was "likely to rank alongside step-changes such as antibiotics and MRI". In September Rene Haas, the boss of chip designer Arm, told the BBC he believed the tech would come up with a cure for cancer "within our lifetime". But there are also concerns about AI models making wrong decisions as a result of biases in the patient data used to train them, and incorrect medical advice being given by AI chatbots. title: Migraines and acne among five more conditions pharmacists can treat
description: Pharmacies in England will soon offer treatments for a total of 12 common conditions which save people going to their GP first.
body: People will be able to go to their local chemist in England this autumn and get on-the-spot treatment for 12 common conditions without going to their GP first. Pharmacists can already prescribe medication for seven conditions - sore throat, earache, sinusitis, shingles, impetigo, infected bites and urinary tract infections. Five more - migraines, acne, scabies, ear infections and badly blocked noses - are now also being added to that list. NHS England said the move was to ease pressure on busy GPs and A&E departments while making sure people could get treatment quickly and conveniently. After a very hot summer and three of the busiest months on record in A&Es in England, the NHS says it wants to make it as easy as possible for people to get help when they need it for everyday conditions. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said people were "fed up with the scramble for routine appointments" and wanted help close to home, with no more taking time off work or waiting to get seen. "For five more common conditions, you'll be able to walk into your local pharmacy and get treated on the spot," he said. Mr Burnham said families would feel the change, and the plan would give people back "precious time". The five conditions which can now also be treated via pharmacies are: low frequency migraines in adults hay fever or allergic rhinitis in children mild to moderate acne in young people and adults mild skin infections and scabies That's in addition to these seven: Initially, a few hundred chemists will offer treatments for the five new conditions, NHS England says. There will be a gradual rollout and the service will eventually be available at thousands of community NHS pharmacies across England. Community pharmacies also offer support with healthy eating, exercise, stopping smoking, monitoring your blood pressure, contraception, flu and Covid vaccinations. The charity the Migraine Trust said it was delighted by the news after calling for more help for migraine care in pharmacies. Chief executive Rob Music said having this support for people with migraine through their local pharmacy was "a wonderful opportunity for a faster and improved care pathway". Dr Amanda Doyle, director for primary care and community services at NHS England, said she wanted to make sure that patients can get as much support as possible in their communities, "so they do not have to be admitted to hospital unnecessarily". But bodies representing pharmacies across England have consistently said that the funding provided by the goverment does not cover the workload for the new plans. "Pharmacies are still under significant financial pressures," said Henry Gregg, chief executive of the National Pharmacy Association. "This shows why the government should go much further and invest in our pharmacy network that has the power to transform people's experience of everyday health issues." The Pharmacy First scheme started in England in 2024. NHS figures suggest it has delivered 14 million consultations since then, including two million appointments for sore throats and 1.7 million for urinary tract infections (UTIs). People can be referred to their local pharmacy via NHS111 or by their GP, or just go direct to their high street chemist. Scotland has a scheme which was seen as the model for England's Pharmacy First - Northern Ireland and Wales also have systems allowing pharmacies to treat patients with certain conditions. Patients can be treated for 27 different conditions at chemists in Scotland. Have you been treated in a pharmacy setting for one of these conditions? title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts
description: Menstrual cycles are highly individual, making blanket advice found on social media difficult to apply, researchers say.
body: Sarah Mackay, known as @fitwsarah online, says her energy levels change through her cycle A woman points to a colour-coded grid dividing the menstrual cycle into four phases, each paired with a different list of exercises. "When you're bleeding, you want to be doing steady-pace jogging, Pilates, barre, walking, resting," she tells viewers. This is one of thousands of videos on TikTok and Instagram suggesting that people change their workouts depending on where they are in their menstrual cycles - something known as 'cycle-syncing'. So-called cycle-syncing workout plans have surged in popularity online, with Google searches for the term rising 740% since 2022 and more than 55,000 TikTok videos now using the #cyclesyncing hashtag. Most of the advice is shared by fitness and wellness creators rather than medical or research experts. They divide the menstrual cycle into phases, recommending: gradually increasing intensity in the follicular phase leading up to ovulation harder strength or high-intensity training around ovulation easing off again during the luteal phase (between ovulation and the start of your period) So what does the science say? Kelly McNulty, a researcher at Leeds Beckett University specialising in menstrual cycles and exercise, says there is evidence that some women experience changes in symptoms, energy or perceived strength across their cycle. But that is different from evidence that all women should train in a particular way at a particular point, she tells the BBC, adding that these videos are "a trend based on marketing rather than any kind of research or evidence". "There isn't any research to support that kind of phase-based prescription," she says. This video can not be played Should you sync your exercise routine with your period? A key issue is that menstrual cycles are highly individual, McNulty adds - they can differ between women, and one woman's experience can also change from one cycle to the next. That makes the blanket advice often found on social media difficult to apply, she explains. Many cycle-tracking apps and programmes are also designed around relatively regular menstrual cycles that are 21 to 35 days, which can make their recommendations less applicable to people with irregular periods, or those using hormonal contraception. "It's not so much about doing certain exercises in certain phases, it's about working with your own individual body and what your needs might be." There are now thousands of videos on Instagram and TikTok recommending women sync their workouts to their menstrual cycles Cesci Burgoyne, a nurse based in Sydney, Australia who is also a qualified personal trainer and nutritionist, adjusts her training depending on how she feels in her cycle. She doesn't follow a prescriptive plan, she says, but instead makes changes intuitively. "In my luteal phase I'll try and ease off in the training," she tells the BBC. "In my follicular phase, I'm so energised, I feel like I can lift so much heavier. I like to try and get my long runs in." Burgoyne also welcomes the growing attention on women's health, and says that exercise and nutrition research has historically focused heavily on male bodies, with findings then often applied to women. Sarah says she has sometimes hit personal records while on her period Fitness creator Sarah Mackay, known as @liftwsarah on Instagram and TikTok, has also noticed her energy, motivation, cramps and mood change through the month. But she deliberately avoids strict plans because, she says, "there are too many variables at play". Some online plans advise women to avoid intense training during their period, she says, yet she has sometimes hit personal records while menstruating. "The problem is not that the menstrual cycle is irrelevant," she says, but that "not everything is predictable". Dr Faye Bate, a trained medical doctor and women's health expert, is also wary of advice suggesting all women should train differently according to their menstrual phase. "A one-size-fits-all model of 'you should be exercising this way in this phase and a different way in a different phase' shouldn't be advice that applies to all women," she says. She is concerned that repeatedly telling women they are likely to be weaker or less capable at particular points in their cycle could create a "nocebo" effect - where negative expectations themselves influence how someone feels or performs. McNulty tells the BBC that routinely easing off resistance training could also limit progress. Strength training is particularly important for women, who face a higher risk of osteoporosis later in life. Building strength requires consistent, progressively challenging training, she says, and "we don't want to create another barrier by suggesting women train less for almost half the month." Dr Bate also warns against normalising severe symptoms: if pain, fatigue or mood changes interfere with exercise or daily life, women should seek medical advice rather than assuming it is an inevitable part of their cycle, she says. While cycle-syncing itself may not be backed by strong evidence, the experts we spoke to did suggest being "cycle-aware". McNulty says tracking your cycle can be a useful way to understand your own patterns, while Dr Bate also encourages women to become more familiar with how they feel at different points in the month. Both welcome the fact that menstrual health is being discussed more openly, but say the focus should be on individual experience, rather than rigid, phase-based rules. In practice, that might mean having painkillers ready before your period, taking a rest day when symptoms are worse, or easing off a workout if you feel unusually fatigued. For Dr Bate, "the most important part is tuning in to how you feel". In other words, use your cycle as information rather than a set of rules. title: Wellbeing walks praised for keeping people active
description: The free walks range from 10 to 90 minutes and are aimed at all abilities.
body: The free walks are held in partnership with Ramblers UK and other local partners People say taking part in free wellbeing walks has changed their lives "dramatically". Active Cornwall coordinates the walks in partnership with Ramblers UK and other local partners across the county with the aim of helping people of all ages stay healthy and connected. Led by trained volunteers and held over coast paths and garden estates to town parks, the walks range from 10 to 90 minutes and are aimed at all abilities. Kathryn, who takes part in walks at Heligan Gardens near Mevagissey, noted the walks helped lift her spirits when she felt down. Kathryn said the walks have dramatically changed her life More news stories for Cornwall Listen to the latest news for Cornwall "It has changed my life dramatically, I've built up a really beautiful friendship group," she said. "We see the animals, we see the plants and every week there is something different going on. "The people I'm with, they ask how you are - it's just good to talk." Toni, who also takes part in the walks, said they provided a good opportunity to talk with others. Toni said the groups provide an opportunity to talk to others "I've also just had a knee replacement, so this is helping me along," Toni added. "I come out and walk, we have a chat and a cup of coffee, getting fresh air and being with human beings." Professor Chris Whitty, Chief Medical Officer for England, recently recommended adults aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week - and a brisk walk counts towards that amount. Active Cornwall's Rob Harrison said there were obviously physical benefits of getting out but stressed "the social element is massively important" too. "You could come to walk on your own, but you go away with friends and have that network and community," Harrison said. Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. title: Alan Carr holds back tears on special night at National Television Awards
description: The comedian and Celebrity Traitors win big - see a full list of winners and nominees from the 26th edition of the awards.
body: The comedian was surprised with a top NTA honour You can see a full list of winners at the bottom of this article Alan Carr had an emotional night at the 31st National Television Awards on Tuesday as he received the Special Recognition prize following a whirlwind year for the comedian. The London audience had just been treated to a Traitors-themed musical performance in his honour, which included fellow cast member Paloma Faith emerging from a coffin, when he was given the surprise award. Speaking to BBC News on the red carpet before the ceremony, Carr had played down his chances of winning for his semi-autobiographical comedy Changing Ends. He joked: "Comedy is so subjective... Mrs Brown's Boys wins every year, why am I even here?" This video can not be played Watch: 'I still felt bad about Paloma', says Alan Carr Carr was right - Mrs Brown's Boys went on to win the Comedy prize. But the night was just beginning. The Celebrity Traitors favourite had predicted there would be "ugly crying" if he did take home a prize - and he stayed true to his word as he accepted the Special Recognition award, the only category not voted for by the public. Carr told BBC News that being part of The Celebrity Traitors had brought him a level of attention he had never experienced before. "I've never had popularity like it," he said, describing the show as a "phenomenon". The Celebrity Traitors won an award after a critically-acclaimed series Carr had more reason to celebrate when The Celebrity Traitors beat the original version of the show to win the Reality Competition prize. His co-star, singer Charlotte Church, praised the show's final, which attracted 15 million viewers within seven days, describing it as a "beautiful vignette of male tenderness and emotional expression". "Alan, Nick (Mohammed) and David (Olusoga), you were just absolutely sublime," she added. Another big win went to Sir David Attenborough, who was named Best Presenter in his 100th birthday year, beating popular duo Ant and Dec, whose 23-year winning streak was broken by Gary Lineker last year. While not in attendance, Attenborough's long-time collaborator Mark Brownlow accepted the award on his behalf and shared a message from the broadcaster urging people to help protect the planet. "Humanity has always needed the natural world for all the practicalities of life and for our mental wellbeing," Attenborough wrote. "Now the natural world needs us too: surely we must not ignore that simple fact." Clarkson's Farm won an NTA for the second year running, taking the inaugural Celebrity-Led Reality Docuseries award. The new category also featured shows from Stacey Solomon and Joe Swash, Tyson Fury, Kelvin Fletcher, and Bob Mortimer and Paul Whitehouse. Celebrity-led programmes still featured in the Authored Documentary category, with documentaries from Olympian Sir Chris Hoy, former Little Mix singer Jesy Nelson, and Sharon Osbourne's film about her late husband Ozzy among the nominees. It was a win for a second year in a row for Jeremy Clarkson Speaking to BBC News on the red carpet, their daughter Kelly Osbourne said her family were "honoured" that the documentary about her father had been nominated, describing it as a "tragic but beautiful story". She said she had spoken to her mother Sharon just before arriving at the ceremony: "We are so close. I was on the phone with her before I got out of the car." In the end, the public chose Our Girls: The Southport Families. The BBC programme followed the families of Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, who were murdered at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in Southport in 2024. Accepting the award, Elsie's mother Jenni Stancombe told the audience: "We never expected to be stood up here, so I don't know what to say. "We know you didn't vote for us, you voted for our three girls." The parents of the Southport attack victims were recognised for their powerful film documenting the lives of their daughters In the drama categories, Vicky McClure won Best Drama Performance for her role in crime thriller Trigger Point, from the first all-female shortlist in the category's history. She told BBC News in the winners' room: "Over the years it has not been our space, and here we are dominating that category. "I feel honoured to be amongst those wonderful women." Vicky McClure came out on top in a list of nominees dominated by female actors Among those nominated alongside McClure was Sheridan Smith for her portrayal of campaigner Ann Ming in ITV true crime drama I Fought The Law. While Smith missed out on the individual prize, I Fought The Law went on to win New Drama. Away from the awards, nominee Graham Norton revealed his red carpet outfit had already had one high-profile outing this year. "This is what I wore to Taylor Swift's wedding," he told BBC News. Norton said guests had agreed not to reveal details of the celebrations. "I had a wonderful time and we all agreed by saying yes to going, we weren't going to blab about it." Norton, who also featured in Swift's music video for Opalite earlier this year, said working with the singer showed him "what leadership is like at that level". "It was such a happy set. Everyone was working as hard as they could for her," he said. Graham Norton revealed he wore the same suit to the NTAs as he did to Taylor Swift's wedding I'm A Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here!
