title: Why Reform UK undercover donations claims are legally complicated
description: A look at the key allegations concerning foreign donations and where they sit with the law.
body: Reform UK has been hit by a row over foreign donations as the party's leaders and supporters gather for their annual conference. The row centres on allegations which surfaced during undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations - founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting - and broadcast by Channel 4 News on Thursday. The party denies any wrongdoing and says it is investigating. Robert Jenrick, Reform's economy spokesperson, said the two senior aides in the film had been suspended, telling the BBC's Today programme: "Nigel [Farage] got rid of the two people who did this…he acted swiftly, they've gone." Both Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported Reform to the Metropolitan Police, which says it is assessing the claims but has not launched an investigation. The Electoral Commission says it is "in touch" with the police. We have looked at each of the three main allegations and where they sit with the law. In the film, Nigel Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform's head of policy James Orr suggest a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party, one of which would have totaled £500,000. Jukes meets an undercover reporter posing as a UK-based son of a wealthy American financier, who voices concern that his father could not directly donate to Reform within the law. Jukes tells him: "You do realise that you can do it?" According to Channel 4, Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the son's name, even though the money would have come from his American father. A similar arrangement is also mooted in a meeting with Orr. Farage is shown saying "it's all above board" and expressing thanks. On Friday, Farage said he was in fact asking whether it was above board. Channel 4 says the proposed £500,000 donation was never made. Under electoral law, you must be a UK registered voter or a company registered in the UK to be a "permissable" donor to a UK political party. In this instance, the son would be a permissible donor, but his father would not be. Any donation of more than £500 from an impermissible source must be declared to the Electoral Commission and returned within 30 days. If the party keeps it beyond that, it is deemed to have accepted the donation - and that could lead to a fine and potential criminal investigation. Two Reform officials step down after undercover donations report Farage says his aides' donor comments were 'loose pub talk' Channel 4 says Reform commissioned three opinion polls between January and July 2026, costing £32,500 in total. One was on the front page of the Telegraph newspaper under the headline "Labour would face wipeout if elections went ahead"; another on the front page of the Times with the headline "Reform vote in unions at same level as Labour". In the film, Orr suggests to the undercover reporter that perhaps the American financier could pay for opinion polling to help with Reform's campaigns. He is shown saying this would "technically be a donation in kind" but "the reality is we could easily get away with it". The public was not told who had commissioned and paid for the three polls. Polling firm JL Partners, the Telegraph and the Times have all said this was not known to them either. Farage said on Friday the polls in question had been commissioned by an independent third party and that Reform had "not done anything wrong". Any legitimate donations from permissible donors worth more than £11,180 in a calendar year must, by law, be declared to the Electoral Commission. The £32,500 polling payment does not appear to have been declared. The legal definition for a political party donation includes payments for studies and research. This video can not be played Watch: Undercover reporters posing as party donors meet with Nigel Farage The Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 specifically outlaws knowingly taking steps to disguise or conceal that a donation has come from an impermissible source. As part of this, it can be a crime for someone to conceal money spent on expenses incurred directly or indirectly by the party - and to mislead a party on the source of a donation. The maximum sentence is 12 months in prison. It is in this context that Labour is demanding the police investigate the polling and whether there is evidence of concealing who actually paid for it. But investigating this and the other claims in the film would be hugely complex - and a 30-minute TV report could not be the sole basis for a prosecution. The police would almost certainly ask Channel 4 for all the unused filmed material, research notes and plans for the documentary. Detectives would want to interview everyone involved and understand their intentions. In a statement on Friday, JL Partners said that "sometimes people with a party alignment make suggestions about potential clients who may be interested in commissioning and paying for polling" in the UK and abroad, and that it would not expect to be told the precise relationship between Reform and the US-based company. Nick Vamos, former head of specialist crime at the Crown Prosecution Service, explained: "It is very common for allegations of electoral offences to be reported to the police, especially by political rivals looking to score points," adding the police would assess the evidence neutrally to decide whether a full investigation is required. Such offences very rarely lead to prosecution. Between 2011 and 2021, the Electoral Commission referred eight cases to the Met, none of which resulted in charges. Even if there were an investigation, it would take months to get near specialist detectives or prosecutors. Elsewhere in the film, Jukes appears to list other supporters of Reform UK who have potentially donated to the party through UK residents. The names, made in the context of discussing the proposed £500,000 arrangement, are bleeped out. He is shown telling the undercover reporter: "But,

title: Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach
description: Nigel Farage's admirers in the party are calling for a stronger operation as the party aims for power.
body: "It makes us look a bit like a pirate ship," a senior Reform figure acknowledges privately, deeply frustrated that after a year in which they say the party has "radically professionalised" the events of the last few days could still happen. It was the recurring conversation throughout Reform UK's conference in Birmingham: the consequences of the undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4 News which has cost two senior party figures their jobs, at least for now. How much damage does it cause to Reform? And what does it tell us about them? "A key part of the appeal of us is the sense of us being cavaliers. Doing things differently. Standing out. And that's great. We have roundheads too. Those who ask the boring questions. Do the checks. We need more of them," this same senior figure adds. The story of Reform over the last 12 months can be summarised in three words: defections, elections and money. Farage says his aides' donor comments were 'loose pub talk' Reform donations row overshadows party's moment to lay out big ideas Farage threatens to overhaul Lords and judges to meet his pledges Defections, those who leave one party and join another, have been a big part of the party's growth in the last year – not least the recruitment of former Conservative cabinet ministers Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman. Elections have been as well - Reform's gains in the English local elections and the devolved parliament elections in Wales and in Scotland. But so too has money. The backdrop to this conference was the swirl of questions about money even before Channel 4 News', and Verbatim Investigations', endeavours. In the hour or two before its broadcast on Thursday night, senior Reform figures, including those directly caught up in it, projected a sense of being relatively relaxed about it. Awkward, embarrassing, but survivable. Once it was broadcast, things changed. There was fury, I am told, and very quickly there was a sense of its gravity. "A few bottles of red were had, and we knew we had to act," is how one source described it to me. The conversations went on into the early hours. Firstly, there was anger that it would drown out a conference that has been months in the planning. And yes, it has dominated conversation here in Birmingham. Secondly, there was widespread concern about the image it projected, the impression it would leave. Reform wants to project itself as ready to run the country. Some saw James Orr's work as head of policy as key to that professionalisation. Orr as well as Dan Jukes, a close aide to Nigel Farage, have been suspended and both deny wrongdoing. "We need people to see the reality that Reform is getting ready for government," I am told. And yet the headlines allow critics to claim they are not just ramshackle and amateurish but can point to what looks like a pattern of activity, consciously pursued, to breach the law. Absolutely not, Nigel Farage insisted to me, there was no such pattern. But what of the ethos of the party? Journalist Tim Shipman in The Spectator writes , externalthat "it is the experience of everyone I have ever known near the summit of politics that political operations take their character and operating logic from the person at the apex of the triangle. Leaders set culture." There is something in this. Take Rishi Sunak's Downing Street operation and Boris Johnson's. They were wildly different culturally, reflecting the very different characters at their helm. Would all the things that happened during Partygate under Johnson have happened under Sunak? Unlikely, I would have thought. Some within Reform, who are full of admiration for Nigel Farage's chutzpah and gift as a communicator, are desperate to see a behind-the-scenes cultural shift that minimises the chances of further embarrassments. And, alongside that, a step up in the infrastructure and personnel to match. Farage's team express frustration that this is precisely what they have been doing, but some are telling them internally they need to move more quickly. Both Orr and Jukes will be missed profoundly by those inside the party. Privately, some wonder if Orr may yet return. Jukes, who has been a pivotal and loyal figure in Team Farage for years, was already dividing his time between the UK and the United States as his wife and baby are on the other side of the Atlantic. Perhaps, some senior figures suggest, his immediate future might be in America. Does he return when the general election is nearer? Let's see. Reform leave Birmingham winded and wounded by the last few days, their days in the sun overshadowed. The question is how they deal with this and respond to it, in the coming weeks and months. title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
description: With Argentina's President Milei promising "winds of change" over the Falklands, will Donald Trump shift his stance on British rule?
body: Argentine President Javier Milei enjoys a warm relationship with President Trump The tone over the Falkland Islands dispute has been sharpening in Argentina from well before President Javier Milei's late-night national address on sanctions earlier this week. It's tempting to see a visual representation of the tension in the jubilant Argentine players celebrating their hard-fought win over England at the Fifa World Cup this summer holding a banner which read "Las Malvinas son Argentinas" - the Falklands are Argentine - in front of their deliriously happy fans. However, the ill-feeling has been fomenting for much longer. President Milei began his Thursday address with a brief history of the Falklands, very much from the Argentine perspective. He repeated the refrain at the heart of their position: the islands "rightfully belong" to Argentina. The British had invaded and colonially occupied the islands in 1833, he said, violently wrestling the territory from Argentina's hands. UK support for Falkland Islands 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims, No 10 says The UK Government would say he conveniently overlooked a few details. The European powers interchanged control over the islands throughout the 17th and 18th centuries. In December 1831, an Argentine settlement was largely dismantled not by the British but by an American warship, the USS Lexington, amid a dispute over local fishing and sealing rights, after which many inhabitants left. An Argentine garrison which arrived in 1832 was expelled by the British when they reoccupied the land in 1833. Still, if the Americans had a hand in forcing the Argentines out two centuries ago, they may now play a central role in strengthening the Argentine claim. President Milei certainly thinks so. "Winds of change" were blowing, he assured the Argentine people, after President Trump said he was "re-evaluating" the US position on the Falklands. The US recognises Britain's rule over the Falklands - but Trump has suggested he is "re-evaluating" the US position That position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course, given that President Reagan provided material support to Margaret Thatcher during the Falklands War in 1982 – an act which reinforced the long-standing alliance between London and Washington in times of conflict. For Trump, however, that mutual support – the "Special Relationship" – was eroded by Sir Keir Starmer when the UK Government chose not to join the US war on Iran. "You weren't there to help me", the president retorted in an interview with GB News this week. The Falklands were "a long way away", he said. The Falkland Islanders – who voted almost unanimously to remain a British overseas territory in 2013 – would point out that distance from London to the Falklands is fractionally shorter than the distance between Washington DC and the US territory of Guam, in the western Pacific. Still, Trump's words have undoubtedly galvanised Milei. As have the opinion polls. He urgently needs a boost ahead of a presidential election next year in which one of his challengers, his estranged vice-president, Victoria Villarruel, has presented herself as a tougher defender of national sovereignty and attacked Milei's diplomatic approach on the Falklands as failing. Fifa fined the Argentine Football Association after players held up a banner claiming the Falklands, breaching rules against political messaging Domestic politics can rarely be ruled out of the equation when the Falklands issue flares back up. However, Buenos Aires argues that the matter has become urgent: "A clear and urgent danger", as Milei put it. With two energy companies – the Israeli-owned Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration from the UK – due to undertake work on the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, the issue has new impetus. Argentina "cannot allow" the companies to "appropriate the oil reserves under our sea", he said. "We will not stand by with our arms folded," he added. On Saturday morning Milei's office said on X that it was launching sanctions proceedings against 45 people and companies. The announcement did not identify those targeted and it is not yet clear what impact they will have. In his speech, Javier Milei painted Argentina as a reliable and "trustworthy partner" to Washington and he enjoys Trump's support, both ideologically and personally. The two men are close allies in a vision of the Western Hemisphere which Trump calls the "Don-roe Doctrine", a play on words on the 19th Century 'Monroe Doctrine' which exerted American domination over the continent. In essence, the two presidents want to see only like-minded leaders in power in the Americas. Within such a new partnership and a reordering of the spheres of influence, it's more than conceivable that Trump favours the Argentine leader over the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, even if the issues at play transcend personality and party politics. Perhaps the key question for the coming months, then, is whether the strength of the so-called "Don-roe Doctrine" outweighs the lasting history of the "Special Relationship". Correction 11 September: An earlier version of this report said that a US warship had forced out an Argentine settlement from the Falklands in 1831, leaving the islands uninhabited. In fact, while many inhabitants left, some remained. An Argentine garrison was also expelled when the British reoccupied the land in 1833. The article was amended to reflect this. title: Why do ex-MPs join the 'Chiltern Hundreds' list?
description: Sir Keir Starmer is the latest person to take the office as a means of resigning as an MP.
body: Sir Keir Starmer and Boris Johnson are two of hundreds of MPs who resigned by taking the Chiltern Hundreds position Sir Keir Starmer and Boris Johnson have this in common: They both stepped down as Prime Minister before their term was up, and within three years of winning an election. Their subsequent resignation as a sitting MP means they have also shared the unusual office of "Steward and Bailiff of the Three Hundreds of Chiltern". Sir Keir is the latest person to pick up the title after resigning as an MP this week. What is it, and what does it have to do with the Chilterns? MPs across the generations have used the mechanism to resign from their role Thanks to a law dating back to 1624, Members of Parliament (MPs) in the UK are not technically permitted to resign. "Unless they die or are expelled, they must become disqualified if they wish to retire before the end of a Parliament," according to the UK Parliament website. This is because back in the 17th Century, MPs often accepted the role reluctantly, so leaving the job was not to be encouraged. A "parliamentary loophole" was created to get around this, according to the History of Parliament blog, external. "An MP can do this by requesting, and accepting, office as either the Steward and Bailiff of the Chiltern Hundreds, or Steward and Bailiff of the Manor of Northstead," wrote Dr Martin Spychal. "Both offices (or jobs) are nominal. They exist in name only, have no responsibilities and are unpaid." Anyone with these titles is disqualified from being an MP – originally in order to prevent royal influence on politics – but later used by parliamentarians who were unhappy with their lot. High Wycombe is one of the towns in the Chiltern Hundreds region The "hundreds" were areas that belonged to the Crown as far back as the 13th Century. The three Chiltern Hundreds mentioned today refer to Stoke, Desborough and Burnham in Buckinghamshire. The regions include the towns of Amersham, Beaconsfield, High Wycombe, Marlow, Eton and Chesham. Coincidentally, these are near to the prime minister's countryside residence in Buckinghamshire – Chequers. Because a steward of the hundreds might be able to benefit financially from the role, or promote the interests of the crown, it was seen as a conflict of interest. "Resourceful MPs discovered that they could request appointment to these offices, which then disqualified them from sitting in the Commons," wrote Spychal. Nigel Farage and Nadine Dorries are among those to be appointed to the Manor of Northstead or the Chiltern Hundreds The House of Commons Information Office said: "The Stewardship of the Chiltern Hundreds is thought to have been used for the first time as a means of resignation from the House of Commons on 17 January 1751 by John Pitt, who wanted to vacate his seat for Wareham and stand for Dorchester." The Manor of Northstead, in North Yorkshire, is the other remaining office given to resigning MPs. Its most recent recipient was Reform UK's Nigel Farage who resigned in order to stand for re-election in his own constituency. The titles are given out alternately, in case two MPs wish to step down at the same time, and each new appointment replaces the previous one. Spychal said there have been calls to reform the system since 1775 - but in 2026, the peculiar British formality lives on. Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below. title: Michael Owen doesn't tell his children he loves them - how big a deal is that?
description: His comments sparked discussions around parenting, gender and culture, and just how important those three simple words are.
body: England football legend Michael Owen sparked debate this week after saying he "never ever" tells his children he loves them - despite them being "the most dearest things in the world" to him. "I don't say anything like that," the father-of-four told Jamie Laing in a podcast interview., external "I just assume my actions would show them that I love them. I think most of us are like that." While some were surprised at Owen's comments, saying they always make sure to tell their children how they feel, other parents say they share the ex-striker's outlook. The exchange has highlighted different attitudes around parenting, gender and culture, and raises the question - just how important are those three simple words? Experts tell us making your child feel loved comes from more than just a simple turn of phrase. Educational psychologist Dr Patricia Britto says while words can often be crucial, the most important thing is that a child feels "safe, valued and emotionally secure". "We shouldn't conclude that children have been psychologically damaged and harmed simply because they don't hear those words," she tells the BBC. "They may experience love very clearly through actions." Dr Britto says the bigger issue for many children is whether they feel affection is "consistently communicated" which can come through both words and actions, or better yet a combination of the two. "If you said to a child 'I love you, I love you' but you never turn up to any of their football games or shows, they might not actually feel loved. They might just feel they are empty words." Michael Owen with eldest daughter and Love Island star Gemma - and the pair together in 2005, when he played for Newcastle Dad Aaron Dale, host of the Raisingboys2men podcast and author of a book on parenting, agrees. "It's not words or actions - they shouldn't compete against each other, they should complement each other. "Words are to speak the message and actions are the evidence." Dale pointed to how his own father would often tell him "I love you" after letting him down, diminishing the meaning of the words. However, some parents believe it is absolutely crucial their child hears that they are loved. One father of a seven-year-old daughter, told us he was surprised by Owen's comments, describing them as "awful". "You should always tell your children you love them no matter what, when they're bad, when they're good," he said. And reacting online to the clip of Owen, another parent wrote: "Parents and potential parents do not listen to this man. Tell your kids you love them everyday, even when it annoys them." To the outside observer, Owen's love for his children is not in doubt. The trailer for his new show, Meet the Owens, shows glimpses of what appears to be a happy home life with his wife and children. And in 2024, the former England striker spoke movingly about his son James's sight loss, saying: "If I could give him my eyes... I would." Pushed by podcast host Laing to explain why he doesn't let the 'I love yous' flow freely, Owen told Laing that "I would love to be a little bit soft". "I'm definitely getting softer," he said, "but still not soft enough to say anything like that." Using the word "soft" to describe telling your children you love them reflects long-standing attitudes many fathers have towards parenting, both Dale and Dr Britto suggest. They say it's a result of different contexts, such as culture, class, gender and a generational divide "I think that's the dangerous part there," Dale says, "the belief of what men should and what men shouldn't do." Many fathers believe their role is simply to "provide", but they can do so much more, he says. "Men are much more than just providers... what about our emotional capacity and willingness to have conversations and be there as fathers? And maybe we can't provide, but you know what? Our presence is at full capacity." He adds that he thinks people's style of parenting "always stems from somewhere", including whether they were often told they were loved as a child. Aaron Dale writes and posts about parenting on TikTok, and says he believes our parenting style comes from how our own parents behaved Gender expectations and masculinity are not the only element at play, Dr Britto says. "In some cultures they don't even use those words [I love you] at all," she says. "They may ask things like 'Have you eaten?' as a sign of love rather than actually saying 'I love you'." She adds: "As an African myself, in Nigerian culture parents don't always say 'I love you'... but I still felt loved." Parents also suggest that different generations may approach showing love for their children in different ways. Reacting on social media, one says Owen is right to suggest actions speak louder than words: "My dad never said the words, but it was also never in doubt." Another writes: "What's the big deal? My dad - and I'm sure most dads of our generation - didn't. He did something far, far better than emotional words he 'showed us' by his actions." While Owen's comments may have triggered strong feelings, it is clear there are countless ways parents communicate love to their children. Above all, says Dr Britto, it's about making sure children feel a sense of belonging. "Do they feel loved?" she says. "Do they feel wanted? "Do they feel that they matter, rather than simply hearing the words?" Our family fell out. title: New GP and wellbeing hub 'a major milestone'
description: The £21m hub brings together primary care, community wellbeing and leisure services in one location.
body: Dr Paul Moore says the new hub will reinforce the message that "your GP is there for you" A cluster of empty and under‑used buildings in East Sussex has been transformed into a £21m modern health hub. Wellbeing Square in Newhaven, which brings together primary care, community wellbeing and leisure services in one location, officially opened on Thursday. The project was led by Lewes District Council, which said it would "deliver a high‑quality, modern healthcare environment that residents so richly deserve". Council leader Zoe Nicholson called the venue a "major milestone in the history of the town". "Not only is it transformational for people living in Newhaven but is also central to our wider regeneration plans," she said. The completed scheme includes two state‑of‑the‑art GP practices, a new pharmacy, an extension to Seahaven Swim & Fitness Centre operated by Wave Active, and a creative/co‑working space. Lewes councillor Zoe Nicholson says the hub is "transformational" The council says the plan is to create an environment which can offer healthcare, wellbeing and community services delivered side‑by‑side. The two GP surgeries combined will serve more than 15,000 local residents, with more than 5.500 appointments offered on the site each month. Dr Paul Moore, a GP at Quayside Medical Practice, said: "We are encouraging people to be as healthy as they can." He says the new hub will reinforce the message that "your GP is there for you". Allison Cannon, chief nursing officer for NHS Sussex and Surrey, says the new hub will make it easier for people to access support closer to home and at a convenient time. "This is exactly the kind of neighbourhood approach we want to see more of across Surrey and Sussex," she said. "It's where health services, local partners and communities come together to help people stay well, tackle health inequalities and support healthier lives." title: Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference
description: The party's continued prominence has brought what prominence always brings: scrutiny, says BBC political editor Chris Mason.
body: Reform UK begin their annual conference in Birmingham a bigger party than they were a year ago, their numbers swelled at Westminster, at Holyrood, in the Senedd and in local authorities. But they also gather amid significant political headwinds, much of which revolve around money. There was that whopping £5m gift to Nigel Farage from Christopher Harborne, the Thailand based British billionaire, and the long running row about whether the money should have been declared by Farage once he became an MP. Then there is, among other things, the Metropolitan Police investigation into donations to the party during the last general election campaign. Reform insists that it "takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations." When the party got together in the same West Midlands venue a year ago, they were an insurgency provoking intrigue and attention and demonstrating plenty of momentum. Indeed that momentum was so significant that it was a major factor, perhaps the major factor, in accelerating the demise of Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister, because the potential prospect of a Reform government frightened the Labour Party to its core. Would Starmer, its then desperately unpopular leader, help or hinder their attempts to take on Farage? Hinder was the eventually overwhelming view within Labour, and so Starmer was a goner. But politics can change, and change quickly. With Starmer out and Burnham in, there is early evidence of some support for Labour picking up. No longer are Reform comfortably leading in all the opinion polls - in some they're not leading at all. Add to this a more confident and prominent Kemi Badenoch leading the Conservatives and the recent rise too of Restore Britain, the outfit set up by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. And the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru won and so beat them in the devolved elections in Scotland and Wales respectively. In other words, collectively Reform's opponents appear more energised and popular. Make no mistake, no party at a UK wide level is popular at the moment, but the scrap appears more evenly matched than it did. This video can not be played Watch: 'I firmly believe I have broken no rules,' Farage tells BBC Into that mix, Reform's continued prominence has brought what prominence always brings: scrutiny. Nigel Farage is a candidate for prime minister; his senior team candidates for the great offices of state. When I interviewed Farage at Reform HQ yesterday, on the specifics of the £5m gift and the police investigation he maintained they've acted appropriately. But he offered an insight into how he perceives the hurricane of questions he faces. "I think what you're seeing is the establishment - in a very coordinated way - fighting back," he claimed. I suggested he sounded like a conspiracy theorist, implying the whole world was out to get him. His answer was instructive: "When you read in the newspaper you're under investigation, and you don't even know a complaint's been made, you can see the degree of collusion that has gone on between interested parties. This will not stop. They will continually try and do this to us." Who's they? I pressed. He mentioned the House of Commons and House of Lords – full of his political opponents – but didn't name anyone or anything else. "I'm talking about normal human behaviour. People who, people who hold positions of power, influence, and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding." Let's be clear – it is a big claim to allege collusion between institutions or organisations collectively seeking to undermine him and his party, and there is no evidence for it. But, crucially, you hear in his answer a sense of why he perceives that - that is what it feels like. The question, as Reform's conference gets under way, is how the party approaches the coming days and the coming months. Will Nigel Farage ditch the "aggrieved" tone he has been accused of adopting recently? Reform up against 'complainants' society', Farage tells BBC Yes, his clear hint to me. "I've generally, you know, gone through politics with a smile…I'll go back to doing what I've been doing for the last 34 years," he said. And as for their pitch to you at conference? A Reform government would achieve, and achieve quickly, they claim. The party is promising a list of promises it would deliver in the first 100 days of a majority government, with every senior minister in a Farage government making and delivering one clear pledge. But would they be able to if there is validity in their current claim that plenty of institutions are trying to stymie them? Do you have any views, comments or questions about this story? title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse
description: The things you're doing to make your sleep better could actually be making your sleep worse.
body: Sleep scores, magnesium, white noise machines - what was once the simple act of sleeping has become a minefield. Trying to optimise sleep in this way is called "sleepmaxxing". Take it too far, and you could end up with "orthosomnia" - the clinical term for an obsession with achieving perfect sleep. While it's not formally recognised as a condition in the UK, doctors tell the BBC they've noticed signs of orthosomnia in their patients, with some bringing their sleep tracker data into appointments convinced, wrongly, that they have a sleep disorder. That fixation is actually making people's sleep worse, they warn. So how and why did sleep become so complicated? And if sleepmaxxing isn't the answer, what is the elusive secret to a good night's sleep? The first commercial fitness tracker to incorporate sleep analysis was the Fitbit Classic in 2009. Since then, many others - including Garmin, Whoop and Apple - have integrated sleep trackers into wrist-worn devices, as have smart rings such as Oura, Ultrahuman and RingConn. These devices vary, but in general they all provide users with a report of their night, broken down by sleep stages - time awake, light sleep, deep sleep, and REM (rapid eye movement). Many also give users a "sleep score". But the concept of a sleep score is "completely made up", according to Dr Alanna Hare, consultant of sleep medicine at the Royal Brompton Hospital in London. "There's nothing recognised in sleep science that is a 'sleep score'," she tells the BBC. "That's just been created by manufacturers." This video can not be played How sleep-tracking can make your sleep worse Hare says she's noticed trackers causing anxiety among her patients. "I've noticed more patients coming to me with data from various trackers, with lots of questions about sleep that... is probably contributing to their sleep difficulties," she says. Even though some have had medical tests with reassuring results, this hasn't allayed their fears, she adds. "It's great that there's more focus on sleep as part of wellness," she adds. "But sleep just does not respond well to attempts to perfect it." One proposed lawsuit against Oura, filed last month in San Francisco, alleges that Oura rings are unable to accurately measure sleep quality and sleep stages, and instead rely on AI-generated estimates that have "a coin flip's chance of being correct". In response, Oura told the BBC that it "stand[s] behind our science, research and accuracy claims". "We're committed to clearly communicating what Oura measures, what it estimates, and how members should use that information," the company added. Studies also show sleep trackers can affect how you function during the day, even if they're not accurate. In one study, external from the University of Oxford, participants were given sleep trackers which assigned them a sleep score. The scores were randomised, however, and had no relation to how the participants had actually slept. The next day participants rated their mood, fatigue levels and alertness, before tests checking their focus and reaction times. Researchers found that the people told they'd slept badly reported feeling more fatigued, and were less mentally alert - even though the sleep scores were all fake. This is something Jess Hill says she noticed in herself after getting a Garmin watch several years ago. "I started to rely on the watch as my Bible for whether I slept well or not," the 32-year-old HR professional from London tells the BBC. "I would think, 'I've had awful sleep so I'm going to really struggle today', even if I actually probably had okay sleep. If I'd slept really well, I'd be convinced I'd have to be on top - even though I was tired, I was pushing through things." Jess Hill was "obsessed" with her Garmin's sleep scores for about three years Her "obsession", as she describes it, with getting a high sleep score lasted three years, until earlier this year, when she started to notice the watch wasn't reflecting how she'd actually slept. "I was awake the other week for four hours in the night, and my watch was like 'wow, great sleep!' - I literally was awake from 01:00 until 05:00," she says. The BBC has approached Garmin for comment. Jess's sleep scores weren't matching how she actually felt Dr Neil Stanley, sleep expert and author of the book How to Sleep Well, argues that gamifying sleep is creating more disordered sleeping. "The thing with tracking your sleep is that it gives you a number, and this means you have a target," he tells the BBC. "So you get into this cycle of worrying about your quality of sleep or the quantity of sleep based on figures." He says he carried out research into actigraphy - wrist-worn sleep trackers - around 40 years ago. Though commercial trackers now are a bit more sophisticated, they work in much the same way - by measuring your movement - and have the same limitations, he says. "If you want to measure sleep, you have to measure the brain," Stanley adds. "Unless you're measuring the brain's activities, you're not measuring sleep." Keeping your bedroom cool, dark and quiet - within reason. "That doesn't mean it needs to be pitch black, exactly 16C or totally silent," she says. "It should be coolish, darkish and quietish." Seeing bright light in the morning, which is good for regulating your circadian rhythm - that is, your body's natural clock. Doing light exercise, and eating a "healthy, Mediterranean-style diet with plenty of plant variability". Above all, keeping it simple - "anything else, you don't need it". title: Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics
description: Burnham's exchanges with Kemi Badenoch slipped into familiar territory of trading barbs, writes Alex Forsyth.
body: Throughout the summer Andy Burnham's been attempting to cultivate a new style of communicating with a steady stream of social media videos designed to speak directly to the public. But alongside his digital push, the prime minister still has to master one of Westminster's weekly traditions; the political back and forth that is Prime Minister's Questions. To some it might seem outdated in a modern media world, but the exchange across the despatch box is still deemed vital by many in Westminster as a moment of scrutiny; a chance for the public to peer into Parliament's workings and a crucial factor in setting the mood among backbench MPs as they watch – and judge – the performance of party leaders. So the debut of a new prime minister matters. Badenoch presses Burnham on borrowing costs at his first Prime Minister's Questions Burnham took his place in the House of Commons chamber to raucous cheers from the packed Labour benches and struck a confident tone from the start, clearly keen to maintain the sense of optimism he's promised the country. His initial exchanges with Kemi Badenoch were vaguely jocular. The Conservative leader started with a joke about the prime minister's stamina after a marathon Commons' session on Tuesday when he took questions for more than three hours; there was laughter from MPs and a cautious smile from Burnham. But if there was an early twinkle in the eye of either party leader their exchanges soon slipped into more familiar territory, trading barbs over tax and borrowing with Badenoch making claims of profligate government spending. Burnham, despite his promises to end what he's called political "point scoring" was soon pointing the finger at the Tories for their economic record, referencing the budget of former Prime Minister Liz Truss while promising he'd deliver fiscal discipline. He's not the first prime minister to pledge a new style of politics only to find it hard to dodge the adversarial nature of PMQs. David Cameron said he'd end "Punch and Judy politics" when he became Tory leader only to find himself in regular political knockabouts across the despatch box. But while the political barbs continued it's clear that Burnham is a more comfortable communicator than his predecessor. His real challenge will be delivering more than a change in tone. Andy Burnham speaking during his first Prime Minister's Questions in the House of Commons, London, with Conservative MPs including party leader Kemi Badenoch watching on The backdrop to his first few days as prime minister with Westminster in full swing has been the increased cost of borrowing – a global trend but one to which the UK is exposed and which looks likely to limit the chancellor's room for manoeuvre at the budget come the end of October. Burnham has promised a transformational government but he's facing many of the same challenges as Sir Keir Starmer, with difficult decisions on defence spending, welfare and social care - to name just a few - hurtling towards him. These are the pressure points his political opponents will seek to exploit, as evidenced by Badenoch's approach at Prime Minister's Questions when she quizzed him over plans for taxes, spending and borrowing. Burnham pointed to his early actions in office, cutting VAT on domestic electricity bills and business rates for pubs and music venues as a sign of his priorities, but he gave little more away – leaning back on another familiar refrain that prime ministers don't write budgets from the despatch box. In reality, it would be unfair to expect much more in the way of detail about Burnham's plans for the economy during his very first session of PMQs, but these are questions his government will eventually have to answer. And what is clear is that despite the promise of a more consensual style of politics, when it comes to the substance there are sharp ideological differences across the Commons. Burnham's diagnosis for the country's problems centres on privatisation and deindustrialisation over recent decades, as well as Brexit. Badenoch disagrees, pointing instead to high taxes and spending as constraints on economic growth. While Burnham's early weeks in office have seen a shift in style with a summer tour around the country and heavy social media presence, the economic arguments between him and his political opponents remain, and now Westminster is back in session there will likely be a clamour for more detail about his planned direction. Today's Prime Minister's Questions is a taste of what's to come. As well as smart communications, the choices the prime minister makes against a tricky economic background will take careful navigation if he's to deliver the optimistic future he's promised. title: Five takeaways from Burnham's Commons debut as PM
description: The prime minister's first appearance in Parliament comes more than six weeks after he entered No 10.
body: Andy Burnham has taken questions from MPs in the House of Commons for the first time since taking over as prime minister. The statement on his future plans for power comes six weeks after he took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July, just before Parliament's summer recess. Here are the main points from what he said. Burnham told MPs his time as mayor of Greater Manchester had given him a "clear theory of growth" that further devolution of power away from Westminster would help boost the UK's economic prospects. But he said he wanted to avoid a "two-tier England" - where areas that have already been given greater powers pull away from those that have not. He announced that work was under way with Cornwall council and its six MPs on a devolution deal, "with or without" an elected mayor, to help the rural economy. Burnham's move to grant the county greater powers, without requiring it to team up with councils in neighbouring areas, could open the door to more devolution for other single counties. Burnham also said he would meet leaders in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to explore more local powers there. The statement was the first chance for Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to grill Burnham on defence spending following headlines on the issue over the summer. Chancellor John Healey was appointed by Burnham after quitting as defence secretary under Sir Keir Starmer, calling for the UK to spend 3% of gross domestic product (GDP) on defence by 2030. However, since entering the Treasury, Healey is yet to attach a date to this spending target, and has faced pressure to do so in recent days. Healey has said a target date for increasing spending to 3% of GDP will be set out at the next government spending review, expected in spring next year. But in a potential signal of his intentions in this area, Burham said the arguments Healey had made about defence spending in his former role were a key reason why he had put him in charge of the Treasury. Andy Burnham chaired his first Number 10 North meeting in July Burnham confirmed he would attend the COP31 climate summit in November, as he vowed to "meet the climate challenge". The annual UN climate change conference will take place in Antalya, Turkey, allowing Burnham to come face to face with many world leaders and senior officials. While Sir Keir attended COP summits when he was prime minister, Rishi Sunak was criticised in 2022 for not going because he had "other pressing domestic commitments". Burnham's pledge to attend the summit comes as he faces a looming decision about whether to allow drilling to start in the Rosebank oilfield and Jackdaw gasfield, in the North Sea, which have been in legal limbo for a year. Labour's 2024 election manifesto promised to "finally bring the feudal leasehold system to an end", after campaigners said it was unfair that flat owners had little control over spiralling property costs. A draft Leasehold and Commonhold Reform Bill published by Starmer's government earlier this year included plans to cap ground rent at £250, ban the sale of new leasehold flats and give homeowners greater control over how their buildings are managed. Under the bill, leasehold would be banned "except in limited cases", and developers would no longer be allowed to sell new flats as leasehold. That bill is yet to be introduced to Parliament, but Burnham confirmed he intended to "bring forward" a Commonhold and Leasehold Bill during the current session of Parliament, which began in May and would normally last around a year. Burnham kicked off his Commons statement by paying tribute to his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, who had announced he was resigning as MP for Holborn and St Pancras just hours earlier. Sir Keir had given the UK "a lifetime of service", Burnham said, including delivering the Hillsborough Law which demands more accountability from public officials during official inquiries, as well as work to achieve peace in Ukraine. He also praised Sir Keir for leading Labour to one of its "best victories" in the 2024 election. He said Sir Keir had "created a platform to change this country for the better" which the new government would "use well". Burnham to tell MPs optimism at heart of his vision for UK Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost? title: Emergency measures needed to stop teachers quitting, say Lib Dems
description: A survey by the party suggested almost half of teachers reported considering quitting the classroom in the next five years.
body: The Lib Dems say schools are approaching an "existential crisis" in teacher retention Burnt out teachers urgently need better working hours and more support to stop them leaving the profession, the Liberal Democrats say, as the new term approaches. Nearly half of the teachers surveyed by the party in England said they were planning to quit the classroom in the next five years, with many saying they felt overworked and stressed. The Lib Dems are urging new Education Secretary Lucy Powell to fully fund teachers' pay, rather than raiding school budgets to cover increases, and to bring in limits on overtime. The Department for Education said last year saw the lowest rate of teachers leaving the profession since 2010 but acknowledged there was "more to do". The survey asked more than 900 teachers, headteachers and Special Educational Needs Coordinators (SENCOs) across England how long they planned to stay in teaching. Almost half of those in post said they were considering leaving teaching in the next five years, while one in ten were planning to spend less than a year in the job. More than three quarters of those surveyed, which included former teachers, said they had felt "frequently or constantly burnt out" while at work. Respondents cited high workloads on marking, lesson preparation and other tasks, which they said gave them less time in the classroom. The Liberal Democrats' schools spokesperson Caroline Voaden said this pointed to a government that is "not listening" to the profession. "We rely on teachers to educate our children, the least we can do is make sure they want to come back after the summer," she said. Teacher retention is a challenge successive governments have had to grapple with. The National Education Union (NEU) reported that 4 in 10 teachers were planning to quit over "huge workloads and excessive accountability" in 2019. This latest survey was also conducted with the help of the NEU, as well as the Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL). "After over a decade of austerity and chronic underfunding in our schools the system is on its knees" said the NEU's general secretary Daniel Kebede. "The new academic year is the perfect time for Andy Burnham to signal a fresh start for our schools" he added. "That means fully funding the pay award and properly funding all our schools and colleges to stem the recruitment and retention crisis and give children the education they deserve." "As Lucy Powell enters her first term as education secretary the Liberal Democrats are calling for her first act to be to introduce an emergency package of 'back to school' measures to face this crisis head on," Voaden said. The Lib Dem proposals include the government fully funding teacher's pay, which will increase in England by 3.5% from September, with an additional 3% the year after. Currently, half of the pay increase will come from existing school budgets. The party is also calling for proper enforcement of teacher's legally mandated working hours, the introduction of reasonable limits on overtime, and for all schools to be required to introduce flexible working policies. The party did not identify where funding might come from to pay for the policies. An education department spokesperson said: "We know teachers do an incredible job and we're determined to make sure that dedication is matched with the right support. "Last year saw one of the lowest rates of teachers leaving the profession since 2010, and a record number of teachers returning to the classroom, but we know there's more to do. "We're taking action by announcing pay awards of almost 17% over two years, funding schools to improve maternity pay and offering targeted support to normalise flexible working and manageable workloads so that more teachers stay in our classrooms and thrive." title: Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost?
description: The prime minister says he will keep hundreds more criminals behind bars but doing so requires complex changes.
body: This video can not be played Watch: PM confirms PC Harper's killers will remain in prison The prime minister's announcement that he will keep hundreds of criminals behind bars who would otherwise have been released early is one he has wanted to make for weeks. Andy Burnham had already expanded the list of people ineligible for early release and had consistently said he wanted to go further. What is not clear is exactly what has changed to allow him to do so. Earlier this month, the Ministry of Justice warned that exempting any more prisoners risked "prisons reaching capacity and collapsing". The prime minister himself previously said he had "pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do". In his exclusive interview with BBC Breakfast, Burnham picked out the release of people on controversial indefinite sentences and the deportation of foreign criminals as measures that had made his latest intervention possible. It is understood extra capacity will also be created by immediately beginning work to create new cells in existing prisons. But none of these are short-term solutions. Ending indefinite sentences will require new legislation, meaning it could be years before space is freed up. Previous governments have struggled to quickly deport foreign offenders and there are not thought to be any new returns agreements with other countries. The case of grooming gang ringleader Shabir Ahmed, who Pakistan has resisted attempts to deport, is one example. Retrofitting prisons to create more cells is also expected to take months. People in government concede that in the short-term, Burnham will only be able to follow through on today's announcement by making prisons even more full. With the adult male prison estate already running at 98% capacity, it is a move that could worry some in the sector. But in the end, the prime minister believed he simply had to act. The extra exemptions Burnham has announced are being described within government as a "political decision". That is not surprising given the intense pressure that had built up, especially around the potential for PC Andrew Harper's killers to be released early. Burnham's inner circle are mindful that political misjudgements at the start of Sir Keir Starmer's premiership caused long-lasting damage. They believe Sir Keir never recovered from early rows over freebies and winter fuel payments, and point to a lack of major mishaps in Burnham's first six weeks in office as evidence of a more slick political operation. There was some surprise in Downing Street about how much media attention the issue of early release received over the summer. That is one reason why the prime minister's aides are relishing the new parliamentary term, when news stories come along at a faster rate and so are less likely to linger in the headlines. After the initial flip-flopping on whether the government would be able to exempt more prisoners, the mother of PC Harper told BBC Breakfast that the handling of the situation had been a "hash". Government officials working on the plans have spoken to the families of victims, who made it clear they did not want the new measures to be dripped out in leaks to the media. Instead it was decided one big announcement would be the neatest option. It had seemed likely that would come in the form of a parliamentary statement on Tuesday from the justice secretary. Instead, the prime minister decided to make the announcement himself in an interview with BBC Breakfast. It is understood Burnham was mindful of mounting speculation and wanted to give victims and the public as much certainty at the earliest possible opportunity. In doing so, he may have risked the ire of the Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle, who is generally disdainful of governments that make major announcements outside of Parliament. He may also have offered up ammunition to the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who has already accused Burnham of being a "people pleaser" who finds it difficult to say no to people. That characterisation is likely to be tested again when more stories inevitably appear about the victims of prisoners who will still be released early. It already started on Sunday morning, when the domestic abuse commissioner said she remained "deeply concerned about the number of abusers" still set to be freed. While this is not the first time Burnham has said he has pushed the system to the limit, Whitehall sources are now adamant there will be no more additional exemptions. title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier
description: Parenting experts give their top tips on how to make sure back-to-school runs as smoothly as possible.
body: The BBC spoke to parents and experts to find out their back-to-school tips It's back-to-school time again - and families brace for the challenge of swapping summer lie-ins for school routines, easing first-day nerves and getting ready for the year ahead. While children in Scotland returned to school in mid-August, children in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will be returning in the coming week as September begins. We spoke to experts to find out their six key tips to make going back to school as stress-free as possible. Cerys Parker, a teacher and blogger, says one of the best ways to keep organised during school time is to keep a consistent morning routine. Her morning starts 30 minutes before her children wake up, for some alone time and a hot coffee. She then makes them the same breakfast every morning, which they eat together with no screens, then it's upstairs for showers and getting ready for school. Parker also keeps copies of her children's timetables so she knows what to prepare on specific days, such as when they have PE She grabs their lunch boxes and they leave the house at 07:30 for the bus, or 07:50 if Parker is dropping them at school on the way to her own job. The night before, she makes sure school bags are packed, shoes are ready, uniform is laid out and lunch is packed for the morning. "We have things in the same place, so the bags are always in the same location, the keys, and that makes the morning smoother. There's no panic about where everything's going to be." It is easy to forget non-uniform days, sports days or study sessions. Parker recommends having a family calendar pinned to your wall or your fridge - somewhere you can easily see it every day. "It's an academic year calendar with a space for each of us, and then an events section, so as soon as a notice comes in, I write it down." This could include things like meal plans, after-school activities or - depending on your child's age - exams. Parker's calendar from June, detailing exams, activities and meal plans for herself and her children It's worth reminding yourself of the school holiday dates, while Parker also notes down key days for her children's school year, such as: Children in Need, on Friday, 13 November World Book Day, on Thursday, 4 March 2027 Red Nose Day, on Friday, 19 March 2027 Earth Day, on Thursday, 22 April 2027 She also keeps a small purse of coins throughout the year in case her children need some change for non-uniform days or bake sales. After school, many children are tired and are not up for discussion about their day, so Will Shield, professor of child and educational psychology at the University of Exeter, suggests changing your approach to the conversation. "Ask some open questions, instead of interrogating them," he says. "Ask what made you smile today? Or who did you play with at lunchtime?" These sorts of questions are a lot easier to answer for a child, he says, instead of asking what they did. Martha Deiros Collado says children getting emotional at the school gates is perfectly normal Parker suggests similar questions, like: "What was the silliest thing that happened, or what made you laugh today?" For younger children, clinical psychologist Dr Martha Deiros Collado told CBeebies Parenting Download that pick-up time should not be a "sign of alarm". "See it as part of the process of separating and loving you, missing you, which is really important." Many families will have children attending school for the first time, which can be just as big a moment for parents as it is for new pupils. Shield says parents should "reassure themselves" about the routine they will need to follow on school mornings. "Visit the school, walk or drive past it, bring bedtimes back a bit earlier so it's not just a big start in the first week," he says. He also encourages parents to introduce their child into the concept of school, through things like: Going through the school website Trying on the new school uniform or PE kit Shield adds that you don't want to overwhelm your child with information about school, but get them to a point where it feels "familiar" Deiros Collado says school readiness is not about "numbers and letters". "It's about much more basic things, like feeling comfortable and safe to be in a classroom with other children," she says. Building independence can also help bridge the gap between home and school life, she says, by encouraging your child to do some things by themselves, such as zipping up their own coat. "It's just building that sense of, I'm ready to do this without you," she says. But Deiros Collado also stresses that your child should be able to ask for help when they need it. "One of the best skills you can give your little ones is being able to say to an adult, 'Help me,' because you want your kid to be able to say that to a teacher." She also suggests a "goodbye ritual" with your child to practise separation, such as blowing a kiss. Katharine Radice says that focusing too much on the homework outcome you want for your child can be "demotivating" for them Katharine Radice, teacher and author, recommends putting together a homework timetable. "Doing this puts boundaries around homework and makes it easier to ring-fence distraction-free time," she says. This could be different every week depending on different activities, but Radice stresses there should be a plan in advance so it's not left to the last minute. For supporting children with homework, Radice suggests approaching the task in a "positive and open way" and listening to what they might be finding difficult. She also recommends looking for opportunities to praise your child's effort in doing work to help them "stay motivated." title: We helped create UK emergency alert system - but question how government is using it
description: Millions across England and Wales received a wildfire alert on their phones earlier this month, but it partly backfired.
body: There are calls for ministers to launch a review of how emergency alerts are used As the Conservative minister who launched the UK's emergency alert system, Oliver Dowden was more than familiar with the loud bleeping sound coming from his phone earlier this month. What took him by a surprise was the message on the screen. Like millions of people across England and Wales, the "severe alert" on 14 August warned him of a "very high risk of wildfires nationally" and against doing anything that could start a fire, including lighting disposable barbecues. It was the biggest use of the system to date - but Dowden has now weighed in to question whether it was strictly necessary. Dowden and two officials who helped create the government's emergency alert system are calling for Labour ministers to be up front with the public on what it could be used for in future. "I was surprised at the decision to issue this nationwide alert and it raises some serious questions," Dowden, who served as deputy prime minister under Rishi Sunak, tells BBC News. "The government needs to clarify the criteria for its use and why this alert met those criteria." When he fronted the launch of the alert system in April 2023, he says it was intended for as narrow a geographic area as possible where the threat to life is imminent. The government's own webpage, external for emergency alerts says they are only sent for "life-threatening emergencies", listing wildfires, severe flooding and extreme storms. Two national tests of the system took place in 2023 and 2025, while 10 local alerts have been sent since its launch, all related to weather or flooding bar one in Plymouth for a World War Two bomb removal. The day before the alert was sent earlier this month, 19 homes burned down in the west Midlands town of Stourbridge after a wildfire. The day of the alert, ministers say they were asked directly by fire chiefs to send one as crews dealt with 43 wildfires and 11 major incidents across the country. Oliver Dowden oversaw the public campaign when the alert was launched in 2023 The government's Cobra emergency committee met to discuss how to respond. After sign off from Prime Minister Andy Burnham's de facto deputy Louise Haigh, the alert was sent at 19:00 on 14 August. It triggered a backlash on social media with some vowing to opt out of further alerts in their phone settings, domestic abuse charities and survivors saying victims with hidden phones were put at risk, and confusion about alerts sent multiple times. Dowden's worry is that the wildfire alert was more like a public information campaign than an imminent threat to life across all of England and Wales. "People need to know that when they receive an alert, it is a genuine imminent emergency," the Conservative MP says. "If that confidence is lost, people will simply ignore it." A Cabinet Office report during trials in 2014 warned of this "cry wolf" effect, while pointing out there was strong support among the public for the alerts. "Alerts should not be issued just because the government wants to be seen to be doing something," Dowden adds. The National Fire Chiefs Council said the alert heightened people's awareness and public behaviour, while government insiders point out wildfire alerts are commonplace in many European countries. "By following the guidance that was issued, people were able to take the necessary steps to keep themselves safe and front line services recorded a significant decrease in incidents in the following days," a government spokesperson said. But Frazer Rhodes, who worked in government across a decade to help build the technology and devise high thresholds for the alerts, feels a review is now necessary to avoid future ones backfiring. He was in a bar in Halifax, West Yorkshire, with his wife when the sound of pinging phones began echoing around. "Everybody around was just going, 'what's this?' What's this?'" he tells us. "Then my wife shouted, 'he did that'." His wife's joke aside, he said his "immediate thought" was whether it met the threshold for sending one. He explains: "At its heart are three criteria: urgency, severity and certainty. So, in simple terms, how bad, how soon, and how sure?" Rhodes thinks the wildfire alert arguably met the bar for urgency and severity, but perhaps not for certainty of a threat to life. "It should be very rare to get an alert," he points out. Frazer Rhodes was closely involved in building the emergency alert system He thinks ministers should accept there has been a divided response and launch a review to ask themselves: "How do we do this differently?" Rhodes, a service delivery specialist, adds: "The national protocol should be a public document… I think that document is almost like a contract with us to say 'this is when we're going to use it, these are the parameters, this is who can use it'." Back in 2021 when designing the alerts, he says these were the scenarios considered valid for future alerts: Severe weather and environmental alerts such as flood risk Major hazards such as the Buncefield oil depot fire in 2005 When building the UK alert system, which cost up to £25.3m in its first three years, officials looked to Australia, external and New Zealand, external where emergency alerts have no "opt out" option for the public, unlike in the UK. They also considered minor types of public safety alerts which are sent in the US for issues such as missing children. The alert targets individual cell towers with a radiowave-like signal, allowing all mobile phones in the area to pick it up without needing to know people's mobile numbers. This cell broadcast technology is used instead of SMS texts or an app. It comes as the Cabinet Office plans to launch a separate campaign in the autumn about how people can make themselves and their homes more prepared for extreme weather and cyber-attacks. title: One in eight young people still out of work or education ahead of major review
description: Just under one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training (Neet).
body: Just under one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - according to data published ahead of a major report about a "lost generation". The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) suggests 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 were Neet between April and June. That is about one in eight people in that age group. The final instalment of a major report by former minister Alan Milburn is expected to set out recommendations for tackling the problem in the coming weeks. Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told the BBC ministers would "take those [recommendations] forward". Want your job application to stand out? Employers say they look for these six skills Competition for degree apprenticeships quadruples as university costs rise The new data suggests the number of young people who are Neet has fallen compared to the first three months of the year, when it was over one million, or 13.5% of the total population of people aged 16 to 24. But it has risen by 3% compared to the same period last year, when it was 951,000 young people. The estimates are based on information from a sample of households. The ONS says looking at a smaller subset, like Neets, leads to more "variability" - which can explain small changes from quarter to quarter and means it is best to look at long-term, rather than short-term, changes. Asia Mason, 22, from London, says she spent more than two years applying for jobs before she finally secured her first role in the NHS. After leaving college with a health and social care qualification, Mason hoped to work in maternity. She applied for more than 30 jobs but was repeatedly told she lacked experience. "I remember thinking, 'How am I supposed to get experience if nobody is willing to give me the opportunity to gain it?'" she says. She ended up securing her first NHS role after completing a social care programme run by The King's Trust charity, which helped her gain experience and confidence. Asia eventually wants to be a midwife Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the UK labour market was "in a robust position" but there had been "a long-term challenge for young people". He said he was "looking forward" to recommendations on how to tackle the issue from Milburn. "We'll have proposals, legislation, if necessary, to take those forward," he said. McFadden spoke to the BBC during a visit to Boots in Nottingham, where young people had started jobs in a pilot of the government's Jobs Guarantee scheme. Over the next three years, it aims to support 90,000 young people who have been claiming Universal Credit and looking for work for 18 months. It funds 25 hours of paid work every week for half a year. What Skills Do You Need For The Jobs Market? According to ONS data, the latest figures suggest 981,000 people aged 16-24 were Neet between April and June McFadden said there were also plans for 300,000 more work experience placements and 50,000 more youth apprenticeship starts, adding that the government had already rolled out £3,000 hiring incentives for employers who take on young people who have been out of work for six months. But shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately criticised the government's policies, claiming Labour had "destroyed job opportunities for young people" through increased taxes, such as employer National Insurance contributions. For the Liberal Democrats, Munira Wilson said the sheer number of Neets represented a "generational betrayal", and said the government needed to make it "more attractive for businesses to take on apprentices, boosting the number of degree apprenticeships, and crucially, reversing Labour's damaging job tax". The rise in the number of Neets between April and June compared to the same time last year was largely an increase among men. An extra 25,000 men were estimated to be Neet, compared to another 4,000 young women. In May, the first part of Milburn's report, which was commissioned by the government, said the reasons for the rise in rates among men were "complex", but could be down to more health issues, the "erosion of traditional employment routes" and "a growing gap in educational outcomes". He also said the "Neet problem is grounded in social disadvantage" and highlighted higher rates among certain groups, including young people who: have grown up in poverty have special educational needs or disabilities (SEND) don't have a GCSE-level qualification are Black, African and Caribbean The report warned that one in six young people would be out of work in five years without action, adding: "We are at risk of a lost generation." It said young jobseekers were submitting dozens, sometimes hundreds of applications, but rejections had become the norm. Last week, analysis by the BBC found that competition for degree apprenticeships in England through the government's "find an apprenticeship" service, for example, had quadrupled over the past three years. The second, and final, instalment of Milburn's report - including recommendations for how to tackle the problems - is expected in the coming weeks.
